title: Database Concepts for Industrial Engineers
text:
Preface
This book is intended as a textbook for an undergraduate course on database concepts for industrial engineering students. It is written for engineers who will design, query, and depend on databases in their work on production, inventory, logistics, quality, and service systems. It is not a computer science text: it does not cover the theory and internals of database management systems, such as relational algebra, storage structures, or query optimization.
The book assumes no earlier course on databases. Its first eight chapters need only comfort with a computer and the patience to check an answer by hand. Two later chapters use more: 10  Programming with Databases assumes a first course in programming, in any language, and introduces the Kotlin it uses as it goes; and 12  Databases for Simulation and Analytics assumes a first course in probability and statistics, and is most useful to a reader who has met, or is meeting, discrete-event simulation. Everything else, from SQL to data modeling, is taught from the beginning.

title: Database Concepts for Industrial Engineers
text:
Approach
I have taught databases to industrial engineering students at the University of Arkansas for thirty years, in the course now numbered INEG 38303 and in its predecessors. Over that time the question the course answers has not changed, although the tools have:

How should an engineer keep, find, and trust the data a system runs on?

Industrial engineers are rarely asked to build a database management system, and seldom asked to administer one. They are asked, constantly, to find out what a system’s records say, to design the records a new process or study will need, and to decide whether a number in a report can be believed. This book is organized around those three tasks. It teaches SQL early and thoroughly, because querying is what an engineer does first and most. It teaches design through UML class models, because a model states what a business records in terms its people can check, and then maps the model to tables by explicit rules. It asks, throughout, that every result be checked, by working it out by hand on a few rows before trusting the computer with thousands.
Every example uses the same company, HG Industries, a small maker of hand trucks and garden carts, whose database grows a few tables at a time as the chapters need them. A student who has queried its orders in 3  Querying Tables meets the same orders again when they are modeled in 5  Class Modeling with UML, normalized in 7  Normalization, programmed against in 10  Programming with Databases, and summarized in a warehouse in 11  Data Warehousing and Decision Support. The setting stays familiar so that the new idea is the only new thing.

title: Database Concepts for Industrial Engineers
text:
How this book is organized
The chapters move from reading and querying a database, to designing and building one, to using databases in engineering work:

Reading and querying a database: why industrial systems need databases (1  Databases in Industrial Engineering); the relational model, enough to read an existing database and find your way around it (2  The Relational Model); and SQL, querying one table and then many (3  Querying Tables), then aggregation and analytical queries (4  Aggregation and Analytical Queries).
Designing and building a database: describing the data a system needs with UML class models (5  Class Modeling with UML); mapping a class model to tables in the tradition of Blaha and Premerlani (1998) (6  From Class Models to Tables); normalization (7  Normalization); defining and populating tables (8  Defining and Populating Tables); and views, transactions, and security (9  Views, Transactions, and Concurrency).
Databases in practice: programming with databases in Kotlin (10  Programming with Databases), data warehousing for decision support (11  Data Warehousing and Decision Support), and the databases that feed and record simulation and analytics studies (12  Databases for Simulation and Analytics).

Each chapter closes with exercises at several levels: terms and short conceptual questions, true-or-false questions aimed at common misunderstandings, design problems, query problems, and programming problems. Most use HG Industries’ database. Some use small settings of their own, a transit agency or a tool crib, and some use public sample databases, so that you practice on schemas that other people designed.
The appendices hold what a reader needs beside the chapters: installing PostgreSQL and its tools (Appendix A — Installing PostgreSQL and Its Tools) and the Kotlin tools (Appendix B — Kotlin and KSL Setup); the book’s databases and how to load them (Appendix C — The Book’s Databases); translating between the book’s UML and the crow’s foot diagrams of other books and tools (Appendix D — Translating Between Crow’s Foot and UML); software for drawing both kinds of diagram (Appendix E — Tools for Drawing UML and ER Diagrams); a quick reference to the SQL the book teaches (Appendix F — SQL Quick Reference); and embedded databases, SQLite and DuckDB, which a program or a study can keep in a single file (Appendix G — Embedded Databases: SQLite and DuckDB).

title: Database Concepts for Industrial Engineers
text:
Software
PostgreSQL is the database management system used throughout the book. It is free, it runs on every major platform, and its dialect of SQL follows the standard closely, so what you learn here carries over to other systems. Where PostgreSQL departs from the standard, the text says so. You install and run your own server. DataGrip and DBeaver are the tools used to connect to it, write queries, and inspect results. PostgreSQL’s own tools, psql and pgAdmin, are introduced briefly so that you recognize them. Appendix A — Installing PostgreSQL and Its Tools covers installing all of them.
Data models are drawn as UML class diagrams. Much of the database literature, and many tools, use crow’s foot entity-relationship diagrams instead; Appendix D — Translating Between Crow’s Foot and UML shows how to translate between the two notations.
Kotlin and the Kotlin Simulation Library (KSL) carry the programming work, through the KSL’s database utilities. Appendix B — Kotlin and KSL Setup covers installing the tools and running your first program. The KSL is developed and documented separately; see Simulation Modeling using the KSL for a full treatment of the library.
The book’s examples use small databases created for it, each designed to be understood in a sitting. The SQL scripts that create and populate them, and the Kotlin examples, are distributed with the book as a companion code project, https://github.com/rossetti/DbConceptsBookCode. For practice at a larger scale, Appendix C — The Book’s Databases describes four public sample databases and a loader that fetches each from its original source; they are not distributed with the book.

title: Database Concepts for Industrial Engineers
text:
How this book was written
This book began as course notes. Over thirty years the course accumulated lecture slides, breakout-session handouts, homework sets, exams, SQL scripts for teaching databases, and a Kotlin starter project, and I drew on it to decide what the book covers and in what order. The raw material was plentiful. What it lacked was a single running example, a single notation, and a consistent standard of proof that a result printed on the page is the result the database actually returns. It also mixed my own questions with questions from the textbooks I taught from over the years. Every archived question was traced to its origin before any idea from it was used, and none from another book appears here; where an old question tested a concept worth testing, the book tests it with a new question on its own data.
The book is written in Quarto. Each chapter is a Markdown file, and one source renders to both the website and the PDF. The whole book, including its databases, its code, and its build scripts, lives in a version-controlled repository, so every change to a chapter is recorded alongside the data and code that support it.
Every result is computed, not typed. The book’s databases are built by SQL scripts, one stage at a time, and each stage is loaded into a PostgreSQL database of its own; every query shown with its result in a chapter runs against its stage’s database when the book is rendered, and the result on the page is what PostgreSQL returned. The relational schemas printed in the chapters are read from those databases; the product structure trees and instance diagrams are drawn from them; the output of every Kotlin program is pasted from a real run; and the result of every query in the solutions is produced by running it. The diagrams are written as text and rendered by a script, so a model and its figure cannot drift apart. In addition, a set of scripts checks the cross-references, the citations, the spelling, the consistency of the prose with a written style guide, and the separation of the instructor’s solutions from the student’s book, on every build. Thus, when the book quotes a number, a query or a program produced it, and a check will fail if it changes.
I wrote this book with the help of an AI assistant, Claude, developed by Anthropic. That is, I used it the way I would use a fast and patient research assistant. It turned thirty years of course materials into draft sections under the style guide derived from my simulation textbook; it designed, with me, and then built the book’s databases, and wrote the scripts that load them, render their results, and check the book; it wrote and tested the companion code; it worked the exercise solutions and produced their results from the databases; and it traced the origin of every question in the course archive, so that no other author’s work entered the book. For example, the transit exercises of 5  Class Modeling with UML were drawn from a study I led for the Transportation Research Board (Rossetti 1999), and each model was redrawn from the report before any exercise was written against it. The decisions were mine: what the book covers and in what order, the design of HG Industries and its database, the conventions for naming and keys, the notations, and what a student should be able to do at the end of each chapter. I reviewed every section, and the assistant’s work was held to the same standard as my own, which is that a result is accepted when the database confirms it. Any errors that remain are my responsibility.

title: About the Author
text:
Dr. Manuel Rossetti, P.E. Dr. Rossetti is a University Professor of Industrial Engineering at the University of Arkansas. He served as the inaugural Director for the University of Arkansas Data Science program from 2019-2024. In addition, Dr. Rossetti served as the Director for the NSF I/UCRC Center for Excellence in Logistics and Distribution (CELDi) from 2013-2020. Dr. Rossetti has published over 125 journal and conference articles in the areas of simulation, logistics/inventory, and healthcare and has been the PI or Co-PI on funded research projects totaling over 6.4 million dollars. He was selected as a Lilly Teaching Fellow in 1997/98 and was voted Best IE Teacher by IE students in 2007, 2009, and 2017. He won the IE Department Outstanding Teacher Award in 2001-02, 2007-08, and 2010-11. He received the College of Engineering Imhoff Teaching Award in 2012 and was elected an IIE Fellow. In 2013, the UA Alumni Association awarded Dr. Rossetti the Charles and Nadine Baum Faculty Teaching Award, the highest award for teaching at the university. In 2015, Dr. Rossetti served as Program Chair for the Winter Simulation Conference. In 2024, Dr. Rossetti served as the General Chair for the Winter Simulation Conference. He is also the author of the book, Simulation Modeling and Arena, published by John Wiley & Sons.
Dr. Rossetti grew up in Canton, Ohio and is an ardent Cleveland sports fan. He received his Ph.D. and MSIE degrees in Industrial and Systems Engineering from The Ohio State University and his BSIE degree from the University of Cincinnati. He is a registered professional engineer in the State of Arkansas.

title: 1  Databases in Industrial Engineering
text:
1.1 From files and spreadsheets to databases
Industrial engineers design and improve systems that make, move, and serve: production lines, warehouses, supply chains, hospitals, transit networks. Every such system runs on records. An order is taken, a part is made, a lot is inspected, a shipment leaves, and each event is written down somewhere, by someone, so that the next person can act on it. The quality of those records limits the quality of every decision made from them, from tomorrow’s schedule to next year’s capacity plan.
This chapter asks why those records belong in a database and what that means for an engineer. It shows what goes wrong when a system’s data lives in spreadsheets, surveys the data that industrial systems generate, describes the parts of a database system and the people who use it, and lays out the path the book follows, from a model of a system’s data to a working database. It ends by introducing the small company whose database the rest of the book builds.
This section shows the problems a spreadsheet of operational records runs into, and what a database does about them.
HG Industries, the manufacturer of hand trucks and garden carts that this book follows, took its first orders the way many small companies do: in a spreadsheet kept by the sales office. Each row records one line of an order, with everything the office needed to know about it. Table 1.1 shows the log’s first seven rows: every line of the company’s first three orders of January 2026, and the first line of its fourth.
The log is easy to start and easy to read, and for a few dozen orders it works. Look closer at what it stores, though. Riverside Hardware’s city and state appear on three of the log’s seven rows, and the description of the HT-100 on three. Each row mixes facts about four different things: an order, a customer, a product, and the quantity and price of one product on one order. Thus, most facts in the log are stored many times, and nothing ties the copies together. Four problems follow, each a request the log handles badly.
The first three are the anomalies of a table that stores several kinds of fact together, and Section 7.2 studies them precisely as update, insertion, and deletion anomalies. The fourth is not an anomaly. The log holds no rules, so nothing can enforce them. Two more problems appear as soon as more than one person needs the log. Two clerks editing their copies of the file on the same afternoon produce two versions, and one clerk’s work is lost when the other’s is saved. And a question that crosses the log and the warehouse’s own spreadsheet of stock (which products are ordered but not in stock?) means copying and matching rows by hand.
A database is an organized collection of related data, stored so that many people and programs can share it, with the rules the data must obey stored alongside it. In HG Industries’ database, each customer is recorded once, in a table of customers; each product once, in a table of products; each order once; and each line of an order once, referring to its order and its product rather than copying them. Moving Riverside Hardware changes one row. The GC-400 is a row in the products table with no orders. Canceling SO-5002 removes the order, not the customer. The database refuses a product number that does not exist, a quantity that is not a number, and, if told to, an order date outside a sensible range. The next chapter describes these tables and how they refer to one another.
None of this makes spreadsheets the wrong tool. A spreadsheet is the right place to explore a set of numbers, chart them, or try a what-if calculation, and engineers use them every day. The distinction is between records that a business keeps and shares, which belong in a database, and an analysis of some of those records, which may well belong in a spreadsheet filled by a query. The next section surveys the records an industrial system keeps.

Changing a fact. Riverside Hardware moves to Rogers. Every one of its rows must be changed, and a row missed leaves the company in two cities at once, with no way to tell which is right.

text:
1.2 Data in industrial systems
This section surveys the data that industrial systems generate and the decisions that use it.
Every function an industrial engineer works on produces records, and each record serves a decision. Table 1.2 lists the common ones, with an example from HG Industries and the kind of decision each supports.



Table 1.2: Data in an Industrial System

Two kinds of use run through Table 1.2. The first is operational: recording and looking up the individual events of the business, one order or one inspection at a time, as they happen. The second is analytical: summarizing many events to see a pattern, such as on-time performance by carrier over a year or the capability of a process over a quarter. The same records serve both, but the two uses ask different things of a database, and Chapter 11 explains why a company often keeps its data twice, once for each.
Notice also that the functions of Table 1.2 share their data. The product that sales takes an order for is the part that production makes and quality inspects, and the operator who welds a frame is the one whose certification the plant records. Thus, the records of an industrial system form one connected body of data, and a database that holds them should connect them too, rather than leave each department with its own copy. That connected body of data is what a database system manages.

title: 1  Databases in Industrial Engineering
text:
1.3 Database systems and their users
This section describes the parts of a database system and the people who work with it.
A database management system (DBMS) is the software that stores a database and does everything with it on behalf of the people and programs that use it. This book uses PostgreSQL, a DBMS that is free, widely used in industry, and close to the SQL standard; others include Oracle, Microsoft SQL Server, MySQL, and SQLite. Figure 1.1 shows how the parts fit together.






Figure 1.1: The Parts of a Database System



Read Figure 1.1 from the left. People do not open a database directly. They use database tools, such as DataGrip and DBeaver, the tools this book teaches, or psql, which comes with PostgreSQL; or they use programs written for a purpose, a report, a scheduling application, a simulation that reads its inputs from the database. Tools and programs alike communicate with the DBMS in SQL, the standard language for defining, changing, and querying relational databases, which Chapter 3 begins to teach. The DBMS does the work: it stores the rows, finds the ones a query asks for, and keeps a catalog of metadata, the data about the data, recording what tables exist, their columns and types, and the rules each must obey.
The DBMS also provides services that no spreadsheet does. Integrity, concurrency, and querying answer three problems of Section 1.1: the rules nothing kept, the clerk’s lost work, and the question that crossed two files. Recovery and security answer two problems that section did not raise, a failure in the middle of a change and a user who should not see everything.

Integrity. The rules stored with the data (a product number must be one that exists, a quantity must be a positive whole number) are enforced on every change, by every program. Chapter 8 shows how they are declared.
Concurrency. Many people can read and change the database at once, and the DBMS keeps their work from interfering. Chapter 9 shows how.
Recovery. A change is either made completely or not at all, and a change the DBMS has confirmed survives a power failure.
Security. Each user can be allowed to see and change only what their work requires.
Querying. Any question the data can answer can be asked in SQL, without writing a program for it and without copying the data first.

The people around a database system have different roles, and you may hold several of them. End users record and look up data, usually through programs built for them, without seeing SQL. Analysts query the database to answer questions and build reports, which is where most industrial engineers begin. Application programmers write the programs that others use. Database designers decide what the database records and how, the work of Chapter 5 through Chapter 7. A database administrator installs and runs the DBMS, grants access, and keeps backups. An industrial engineer is often the analyst of a system and, on an improvement project, its designer too; the next section describes how design proceeds.

title: 1  Databases in Industrial Engineering
section: 1.4 From a model to a database
text:
1.4 From a model to a database
This section lays out the path from a business’s needs to a working database, which is the path the book follows.
Building a database begins well before any table is created. It begins with what people need to record and to know, and with a model of the business that says what the database must hold. Figure 1.2 shows the steps.






Figure 1.2: From a Business’s Requests to a Working Database



The steps of Figure 1.2 fall into two parts, and the difference between them is one of the most useful ideas in this book. Modeling describes the business: what things it records, what it records about each, and how they are related, independently of any software. The book’s models are UML class diagrams (Chapter 5), the notation used throughout software and systems engineering. Implementing turns the model into a database a DBMS can hold: tables with keys that link them (Chapter 6), checked so that each fact is stored once (Chapter 7), created and loaded with SQL (Chapter 8), and then used by queries (Chapter 3 and Chapter 4), programs (Chapter 10), and analyses (Chapter 11 and Chapter 12).
The two parts answer different questions, and mixing them causes most bad designs. That is, “Can a customer have more than one address?” is a modeling question, answered by the business; “Should the address be a separate table?” is an implementation question, answered by the model and the rules of Chapter 6. Thus, you should settle what the business records before you decide how to store it. The book, however, starts in the middle, with tables and queries (Chapter 2 through Chapter 4), because a reader who has queried a well-designed database knows what good design produces before learning how to produce it.

title: 1  Databases in Industrial Engineering
text:
1.5 The databases in this book
This section introduces the databases the book’s examples and exercises use.
Almost every example in the book uses one database, built for it: the records of HG Industries, the small manufacturer of Table 1.1. HG makes four products, two hand trucks and two garden carts, in a plant in Fayetteville, Arkansas, and sells them to hardware stores, farm stores, and distributors from warehouses in Fayetteville and Tulsa, Oklahoma. Its database has a part for each department that keeps records: distribution (customers, orders, products, stock, shipments), production (parts, bills of materials, work centers, machines, operators, routings, work orders), and quality (characteristics, inspections, measurements, defects). Later chapters add a year of history, a star schema for analyzing sales, and the output of a simulation of the plant.
The database is small on purpose. Its base data holds eight customers and twelve orders, few enough that you can check any query’s answer by hand, and the book asks you to, before you trust the computer to do it. The year of history that later chapters add brings the database to 30 customers and 614 orders, for the questions that need more data than a reader checks by hand. The database is also introduced in stages, a few tables at a time, as each chapter needs them, so that a new idea arrives against tables you already know. Appendix C describes the whole database and how to load it into your own PostgreSQL server (Appendix A).
Exercises also use a second database of the book’s own, Millbrook Transit, a week of service of a small town’s bus agency (Section C.10), and four public sample databases, among them a music store and a food importer (Section C.11), so that you practice on schemas designed by other people as well. The next chapter begins with HG Industries’ first tables.

title: 1  Databases in Industrial Engineering
text:
1.6 Summary
Operational records belong in a database, not in spreadsheets. A spreadsheet that mixes facts about several things stores each fact many times, so changing, adding, and removing facts goes wrong, nothing enforces the rules, and sharing it loses work. A database stores each fact once, enforces its rules, and lets many people use it at once.
Industrial systems generate connected data. Orders, inventory, production, quality, logistics, and people and equipment each produce records that serve decisions, and the records of one function refer to those of another. The same data serves operational work, one event at a time, and analysis, many events at once.
A database management system does the work. It stores the data and a catalog of metadata, runs SQL for tools and programs, and provides integrity, concurrency, recovery, security, and querying. Its users range from end users through analysts and programmers to designers and administrators.
Modeling comes before implementing. A class model describes what the business records; mapping, normalization, and SQL turn it into tables that a DBMS holds and that queries, programs, and analyses use.
The book’s examples use one small database, introduced in stages. HG Industries’ base data is small enough to check by hand; Millbrook Transit and four public databases give the exercises other settings.

A work order is for exactly one manufactured part.
The work_order table has a foreign key column manufactured_part_fk.
An operator may be certified on many machines, with a date and a level for each.
Quantities are stored as INTEGER.
A shipment may carry the lines of only one order.



Exercise 1.7 For each use, say whether a spreadsheet or a database is the better tool, and why.

The record of every customer order HG Industries takes.
A chart of last quarter’s on-time shipments, prepared for one meeting.
The inspection results that quality engineers, production supervisors, and an auditor all consult.
An engineer’s what-if calculation of the capacity added by a third welder.



Exercise 1.8 Using Table 1.2 and Section 1.5, say which of HG Industries’ departments’ records each question needs, and which questions need records of more than one department.

How many HT-100 hand trucks are on hand in Tulsa?
Which operators inspected lots whose weld strength was below its minimum?
Which customers ordered products made on the saw?
How many work orders for the wheel assembly were completed late in March?

title: 2  The Relational Model
text:
2.1 Tables, rows, and domains
Most engineers meet a database that someone else built. An intern is handed a connection to the plant’s order system and asked how many orders shipped late last quarter; a quality engineer needs the inspection results for one lot. In both cases the first task is the same: find out what the database holds, and how its parts fit together. This chapter presents the ideas that make that possible.
Chapter 1 described why industrial data belongs in a database and introduced HG Industries, the manufacturer of hand trucks and garden carts whose databases this book uses. This chapter presents the relational model, the way nearly every database in industrial use organizes its data. We begin with tables, rows, columns, and the values they may hold, and with the properties that set a table apart from a spreadsheet. We then take up keys, which identify rows and connect tables, and the integrity rules a database enforces to keep those connections sound. With those ideas in place, we write a database’s schema down in a compact notation that shows every table’s keys and how they connect, and we find that the database stores the same description of itself. We then explore a real database with the tools you will use throughout the book. The chapter closes with a brief look at the other ways databases organize data.
The chapter does not ask you to design anything. Every table in it already exists, and our job is to read it. Designing tables of your own begins in Chapter 5, after the SQL chapters have shown what a well-built database lets you do.
This section presents the building blocks of the relational model: tables, their rows and columns, and the values a column may hold.
Codd (1970) proposed the relational model in 1970, and it has been the basis of commercial databases ever since. In the model, all data is held in relations. A relation has a fixed set of named attributes, and each attribute draws its values from a domain, the set of values that are allowed for it. Formally, a relation is a set of tuples, and each tuple holds one value for each attribute. That is, if a relation has the attributes of a customer, each tuple describes one customer.
In practice a relation is drawn and stored as a table. Each attribute is a column, and each tuple is a row. This book uses the words table, row, and column throughout, and it treats tuple and row as meaning the same thing. A table looks like a spreadsheet, but it obeys rules that a spreadsheet does not, and Section 2.1.1 states them.
Let’s look at a real table. HG Industries’ distribution department keeps a table of its customers. The following query asks for every column (the *) of every row of the table named after FROM. Queries are the subject of Chapter 3; for now, notice only what comes back.

The structure of a table (its name, its columns, and their domains) is called its schema, and the rows it holds at a given moment are called its state. The schema changes rarely, when the database is redesigned; the state changes every time a row is added, changed, or removed. A database schema is the collection of all its tables’ schemas. In other words, the schema is what the database can hold, and the state is what it holds now. Section 2.2 shows why the difference matters when we look for keys.

title: 2  The Relational Model
text:
2.1.1 The properties of a relation
This subsection presents the six properties that every relation has and that a well-built table keeps. A row holds one value in each column, and the place where a row and a column meet is called a cell, as in a spreadsheet. The six properties are:

Each cell holds one value that cannot be broken into parts, or none at all.
The values of each column come from one domain.
Each column has a name that no other column of its table shares.
No two rows are identical.
The order of the rows carries no meaning.
The order of the columns carries no meaning.

For each property, we state what it says, see what it means for the customer table of Table 2.1, and see what goes wrong without it.
The first property concerns what one cell may hold. Notice in Table 2.1 that each value is a single item, one name or one state. A value that is one member of its column’s domain, rather than several values joined in one, is called atomic, and the relational model requires every value to be atomic. A column holding “Fayetteville, AR” would break that rule. A query for the customers in Arkansas would have to pick the state out of the text, and an entry typed as “Fayetteville AR” or “Fayetteville, Ark.” would slip past it. That is why the city and the state are separate columns.
Whether a value is atomic depends on its domain and on how it is used; how it looks does not settle it. Prairie Garden Center’s city in Table 2.1 is “Fort Smith”, two words with a space between them, and it is atomic. “Fort Smith” is one member of the domain of cities, and no query, rule, or sort ever needs “Fort” alone. Nor does atomic mean a single character: AR is two characters, one value, and no one ever needs the A alone. A date has a year, a month, and a day, yet it is one value of the date domain. Its data type defines those parts and keeps them well formed, so a query can ask for a date’s month (Section 3.5) and no date can have a 13th month. “Fayetteville, AR” joins members of two domains, a city and a state, in a text value whose parts the database does not know. Thus, the database cannot pick out the state reliably, and it cannot check that the state is a real one. The test is a question about use: does any query, rule, or sort need part of the value on its own, in a way the value’s domain does not supply? If so, the parts belong in separate columns.
The same test settles values that have a structure of their own. A telephone number that is always stored and searched whole is atomic, since nothing needs its area code alone. A location’s latitude and longitude are two values, because a question such as which warehouse lies north of Joplin, or which is nearest a customer, needs each one alone. An address is atomic only if nothing ever asks for its city or its ZIP code. Section 5.3.1 returns to such values when it models attributes that have parts.
The first property allows one thing besides an atomic value: a cell with no value at all. A NULL marks a value that is unknown or that does not apply. For example, an order placed without a requested ship date has NULL in that column. NULL is neither zero nor an empty string, and Section 3.3 explains how queries treat it. Every row of Table 2.1 has a value in every column, because each column of the customer table is declared to require one.
The first property has a companion that spreadsheets break just as often. Suppose that HG Industries recorded up to two telephone numbers per customer, in columns named phone1 and phone2. Each cell then holds one value, yet the two columns hold the same attribute, a telephone number, told apart only by position. Several columns that hold the same attribute are called a repeating group, and the relational model forbids them. A customer with a third number would need a new column, and a search for one number would have to look in every column of the group. The model records such facts as rows of a table of their own, one row per telephone number, and Section 7.4 returns to repeating groups when it defines first normal form.
The second property says that a column’s values all come from its domain. A domain is more than a data type, although in SQL the data type is its main expression. For example, the state column is declared CHAR(2), a string of exactly two characters. The domain of US state codes is smaller than that: it has about fifty members, and ZZ is not one of them. A database can narrow a column’s domain further with a rule that every value must pass, a CHECK constraint, which Chapter 8 presents. Thus, the data type is the first line of defense for a domain, and it is usually not the last.
The data type is enforced on every value. The customer_pk column is declared INTEGER. An UPDATE changes values in the rows its WHERE names; the following one tries to set Riverside Hardware’s customer_pk to the text 'ten'. PostgreSQL refuses it:

UPDATE distribution.customer
SET customer_pk = 'ten'
WHERE customer_number = 'C-1001';
ERROR:  invalid input syntax for type integer: "ten"
LINE 2: SET customer_pk = 'ten'
                          ^

Notice that the message names the type and the value, and points to the value in the statement. PostgreSQL refuses the statement for the type alone, before it considers anything else about the change (Section 2.3 shows that it refuses a new number in customer_pk too, for another reason). A refused statement changes nothing, so the table is as it was before. Without the second property, a column of quantities could hold 10, ten, and a dozen, and no sum or comparison over it would mean anything.
The third property says that each column of a table has its own name. A query finds a column by its name: city means the same column of the customer table whatever other columns the table holds. Two columns named city would make every mention of city ambiguous, and PostgreSQL refuses to create a table that has them. Suppose that a designer wanted both a billing city and a shipping city for each customer. The designer names each column for its role, billing_city and shipping_city, and every mention of either is then clear. A query result is more lenient than a table: a query may ask for the same column twice, and its result then has two columns with one name. Thus, the third property is enforced for the tables a database stores, and a query that repeats a name is best avoided.
The fourth property says that no two rows of a relation are identical. Each row states a fact (here, that a customer with this number, name, city, and state exists), and a fact stated twice is still one fact. Were Riverside Hardware’s row stored twice, a count of the customers in Arkansas would report six where there are five, and every sum over the rows would count its figures twice. In addition, the two copies could not be told apart: no condition in a query could pick out one of them and leave the other. Here SQL departs from the model. SQL does not require a table to be a true set, so a table with no key can hold two identical rows, which a relation never can. The keys of Section 2.2 are what prevent that, and every table in the book’s database has one. A query result has no key and may also repeat a row, and a query can ask for each different row only once (Section 3.1).
The fifth property says that the rows of a table have no order. A spreadsheet has a row 1 and a row 2; a table does not, and a database may return the same rows in a different order the next time you ask. When order matters, a query must ask for its rows in an order (Section 3.4). Suppose that someone treated the last row of the customer table as the newest customer. That meaning would vanish the first time the rows came back in another order. A fact that matters, such as the date a customer was added, belongs in a column of its own.
The sixth property says that the columns of a relation have no order either. Each column is known by its name (the third property), so name holds the customer’s name whether it is the third column or the fifth. Here SQL departs from the model again. A table keeps the order in which its columns were declared, and a query that asks for every column returns them in that order, as Table 2.1 shows. A statement that adds a row without naming its columns also depends on that order, matching its values to the columns by position. A new column changes what a query for every column returns. A table rebuilt with its columns in another order would send such a statement’s values into the wrong columns, or have it refused. Thus, a statement that must keep working as the table changes should name its columns, and a statement that adds a row should always name them.
Table 2.2 collects the six properties, what goes wrong without each, and where SQL departs from the model. Notice that the second and fifth properties hold in SQL as the model states them, and that each departure has a remedy in how you write a table or a query.



Table 2.2: The Properties of a Relation










Property
What goes wrong without it
Where SQL departs




1. One atomic value or NULL per cell
A query must pick values out of text, and variants slip past it
PostgreSQL also offers array and document types, which the book uses only in its appendix on NoSQL (Section H.4)


2. One domain per column
Sums and comparisons over the column mean nothing
None: the data type enforces the domain, and CHECK narrows it


3. Unique column names
A mention of a column is ambiguous
A query result may repeat a name, as in SELECT city, city


4. No identical rows
Counts and sums are inflated, and the copies cannot be told apart
A table with no key, and a query result, may hold identical rows; keys and DISTINCT restore the rule


5. No order of rows
Meaning carried by position is lost when the order changes
None: order must be asked for with ORDER BY


6. No order of columns
Meaning carried by position is lost when a column is added
A table keeps its declared column order, so SELECT * and an INSERT with no column list depend on it; name the columns






The properties are easiest to see where they are broken. Table 2.3 shows how the same customers might be kept in a spreadsheet. Its rows are customers of Table 2.1, and its telephone numbers are invented, since the book’s database holds none.

Let’s walk through Table 2.3 one break at a time.

The Location cells hold a city and a state together, which breaks the first property: “Fayetteville, AR” is not atomic.
Phone 1 and Phone 2 hold the same attribute, which makes them a repeating group. Summit Farm Supply’s third number would need a third column.
Riverside Hardware appears twice, which breaks the fourth property. A count of the sheet’s customers gives five where there are four.
The row “Missouri customers” describes no customer, so its Customer cell holds a value outside the column’s domain, which breaks the second property. Joplin and Springfield are in Missouri only because their rows sit under that heading, which breaks the fifth property. Sort the sheet by name, and the two customers lose their state.

Undoing each break gives back the customer table. Splitting Location into a City column and a State column makes every value atomic. Moving the telephone numbers to a table of their own removes the repeating group, and the customer table of stage D1 holds no telephone numbers at all. Deleting the second Riverside Hardware row leaves each customer once. Finally, deleting the heading row and writing MO in the State cell of each Missouri customer puts the meaning of the heading into values. What remains has the columns of Table 2.1 except customer_pk, the internal key that Section 2.2 explains.
Taken together, the six properties say one thing: a table’s meaning lives in its values and its names, never in the position of a row or a column or in the layout of a sheet. That is what lets a query say what it wants (the customers whose state is MO) without saying how to walk through the rows to find them. It is also why a new column leaves a query that names its columns unaffected, and why the database is free to return rows in whatever order is quickest without changing an answer. One property takes more than care to keep: a table holds no identical rows only if it has a way to tell its rows apart, and that is the subject of keys.

title: 2  The Relational Model
text:
2.2 Keys
This section presents keys: the columns that identify a row and, in another role, connect one table to another.
A table must give us a way to tell its rows apart. A superkey is a set of one or more columns whose values identify a row: no two rows of the table may ever have the same values in all of them. The set of all of a table’s columns is always a superkey, since two rows that agree in every column would be the same row. Superkeys usually carry more columns than they need, so the model asks for the smallest ones. A candidate key is a superkey from which no column can be removed without losing the property. That is, a candidate key satisfies two conditions:

The table will never contain two rows that agree on all the columns of the candidate key.
No smaller set of those columns satisfies the first condition.

The word never in the first condition is the important one. A candidate key is a rule about every state the table could ever be in, which makes it a fact about the business the table describes. The rows the table holds today can show that a set of columns is not a key, by containing two rows that agree on it; however, they can never prove that it is one.

Example 2.1 (Finding the candidate keys of the customer table) The system. HG Industries records each customer it sells to in the customer table of Table 2.1, which has the columns customer_pk, customer_number, name, city, and state.
The request. Which columns, alone or together, identify a customer?
Let’s examine each column against the eight rows of Table 2.1, and then against what we know about the business. The following table records the check.



Table 2.4: Checking the Columns of the Customer Table

Notice that the data rules out only state. The names and cities of the eight customers happen to be different, yet neither column is a candidate key, because nothing about the business stops a second hardware store from opening in Fayetteville. Indeed, the year of history in stage G adds a second customer in Springfield, Missouri. In contrast, customer_number is a key because the company promises it is: it is the identifier on every invoice.
The check. Each candidate key found has a single column, so the second condition holds automatically: there is no smaller set to try. The same condition settles the columns taken together. Any larger set that contains customer_pk or customer_number identifies a customer, but it is not minimal, so it is not a candidate key. The only sets left are combinations of name, city, and state, and no rule of the business makes any of them unique: two stores of the same name may open in the same city.
Interpretation. The customer table has two candidate keys, customer_pk and customer_number. A query that must find one customer should look it up by one of them. A report that groups customers by city is doing something else: it gathers customers together, and it never needs a city to single one out.
Where it breaks. If the company ever reused the number of a customer who had closed, customer_number would stop being a key, and every report that assumed it was one would silently merge two customers’ histories.

A table often has more than one candidate key, and the designer chooses one to be the primary key, the key by which the table’s rows are identified and referred to. The candidate keys not chosen are called alternate keys. In Example 2.1, the primary key is customer_pk and customer_number is an alternate key. The database enforces both: it rejects any row that would repeat a value of either. For example, when we tried to add a second customer numbered C-1001, PostgreSQL refused with this message:
ERROR:  duplicate key value violates unique constraint "customer_customer_number_key"
DETAIL:  Key (customer_number)=(C-1001) already exists.
The two candidate keys of the customer table are of different kinds. A natural key is made of data that means something to the business, such as a customer number or a part number. A surrogate key is a value the database generates only to identify rows, such as customer_pk, and it means nothing outside the database. Almost every table in the book’s database has a surrogate primary key, named for its table with the suffix _pk, and keeps its natural key as an alternate key. Section 6.6 discusses when each kind is the better choice. For reading a database, it is enough to recognize both.
A key may also need more than one column. A key of several columns is called a composite key. For example, HG Industries numbers the lines of each order 1, 2, 3, and so on. A line number alone identifies nothing, since every order has a line 1; the order and the line number together identify one line. Thus, the pair (customer_order_fk, line_number) is a candidate key of the order_line table, which Section 2.4 shows.
The last kind of key connects tables. A foreign key is a set of columns in one table whose values must match the values of a candidate key in another table (or, occasionally, in the same table). The foreign key refers to the other table’s rows. Recall that each customer places orders. Its value in each row is the customer_pk of the customer who placed the order, so it is a foreign key that refers to the customer table. For example, order SO-5001 has customer_fk 1, and the customer whose customer_pk is 1 in Table 2.1 is Riverside Hardware. Customer 1 appears three times in the customer_fk column, and customer 8 (Northgate Hardware) does not appear at all. That pattern, one customer with many orders and some customers with none, is what a foreign key records. The next section presents the rules that keep such references sound.

title: 2  The Relational Model
text:
2.3 Integrity rules
This section presents the two rules that every relational database enforces on its keys.
The first rule protects primary keys. The entity integrity rule states that no column of a primary key may be NULL. The reason is simple: a primary key is how a row is identified, and a row whose identifier is unknown cannot be found or referred to. PostgreSQL applies the rule automatically; declaring a column part of a primary key also declares that it may not be NULL.
The second rule protects foreign keys. The referential integrity rule states that every value of a foreign key must either match a value of the key it refers to or be NULL. In other words, a reference must point to a row that exists. An order that refers to customer 9 when there is no customer 9 would be an orphan: an order that no one placed. The database enforces the rule in both directions, as the following attempts on stage D2 illustrate.
First, suppose that we try to record an order for customer 9, who does not exist. An INSERT adds a row to the table it names, with the values it lists for the columns it lists:

INSERT INTO distribution.customer_order
    (order_number, order_date, customer_fk)
VALUES ('SO-5013', '2026-03-12', 9);

PostgreSQL rejects the new row and names the rule it would break:
ERROR:  insert or update on table "customer_order" violates foreign key constraint "customer_order_customer_fk_fkey"
DETAIL:  Key (customer_fk)=(9) is not present in table "customer".
Second, suppose that we try to remove Riverside Hardware (C-1001), who has placed three orders. A DELETE removes the rows its WHERE names; this one names Riverside Hardware’s row:

DELETE FROM distribution.customer
WHERE customer_number = 'C-1001';

Deleting the customer would leave its three orders pointing at nothing, so PostgreSQL refuses again:
ERROR:  update or delete on table "customer" violates foreign key constraint "customer_order_customer_fk_fkey" on table "customer_order"
DETAIL:  Key (customer_pk)=(1) is still referenced from table "customer_order".
Notice what the second message says: the key is still referenced. The same statement for Northgate Hardware (C-1008), which has no orders, succeeds, because no row refers to it. Thus, referential integrity depends on the state of the database as well as on its schema.
Notice that the two attempts changed different tables. The first added a row to the table that holds the foreign key; the second removed a row from the table the foreign key refers to. A change to either table can break referential integrity, but not every change can. Table 2.6 considers each kind of change to the two tables of stage D2.



Table 2.6: Changes That Can Break Referential Integrity











Table
Change
Can it break the rule?

Let’s read Table 2.6 one table at a time. A new customer is referred to by no order, so adding one is always safe; removing an order leaves no reference behind, so it is always safe too. An order that is added, or whose customer_fk is changed, may refer to a customer who does not exist. The only sound response is to refuse the change, as PostgreSQL did with order SO-5013.
The remaining rows change the table that is referred to. When a customer who has orders is removed, or its customer_pk is changed, the database has four possible responses. The designer chooses one for each foreign key when the table is defined:

refuse the change, as PostgreSQL did with Riverside Hardware (NO ACTION, the default, or RESTRICT);
cascade the change: remove the customer’s orders along with it, or change their customer_fk to the new value (CASCADE);
set NULL: keep the orders but set their customer_fk to NULL, so that they refer to no customer (SET NULL);
set a default: set their customer_fk to the column’s default value, which must itself match a customer that exists (SET DEFAULT).

In PostgreSQL, NO ACTION and RESTRICT both refuse; they differ only in when the check is made, which matters only inside the transactions of Chapter 9.
Almost every foreign key in the book’s database refuses: its definition names no response, so it takes the default. The exceptions cascade deletions from a whole to its parts, such as an order’s lines, which cannot exist without their order; Chapter 6 explains why. The foreign key of customer_order refuses, as the Riverside Hardware attempt showed. Setting NULL could never succeed in the book’s database, since every foreign key column in it is declared NOT NULL. In addition, the surrogate key customer_pk refuses any value we supply. PostgreSQL generates its values, and it rejects an attempt to set one:

UPDATE distribution.customer
SET customer_pk = 20
WHERE customer_number = 'C-1001';
ERROR:  column "customer_pk" can only be updated to DEFAULT
DETAIL:  Column "customer_pk" is an identity column defined as GENERATED ALWAYS.

Notice that the message allows one change: the column may be set to DEFAULT, which draws a new generated value. Nothing about a customer ever requires that, because the value means nothing outside the database. Thus, a surrogate key is not meant to change, and a reference to one never needs to follow a change. That is one reason for surrogate keys, which Section 6.6 takes up, and Chapter 8 shows how to declare each response. For reading a database, the lesson is that a foreign key is a promise the database keeps. When you query a table with a foreign key, every value in it that is not NULL has a matching row in the table it refers to, and a query can rely on that.

title: 2  The Relational Model
text:
2.4 Writing down a schema
This section presents a compact way to write down a database’s schema: its tables, their keys, and the references that connect them.
Recall from Section 2.1 that a database schema is the collection of all its tables’ schemas. To read a database, we need that collection in front of us, with the keys of Section 2.2 marked. This book writes a database schema down in a compact text notation, which we call a relational schema. At a minimum, a relational schema gives:

each table’s name, followed by its columns in parentheses;
each table’s primary key, and its alternate keys;
each foreign key, with the key it refers to, the table that holds that key, and whether the foreign key may be NULL.

A key of several columns is written in parentheses. Listing 2.1 gives the relational schema of stage D2.




Listing 2.1: The Relational Schema of Stage D2


customer (customer_pk, customer_number, name, city, state)
    primary key: customer_pk
    alternate key: customer_number

customer_order (customer_order_pk, order_number, order_date,
                requested_ship_date, customer_fk)
    primary key: customer_order_pk
    alternate key: order_number
    customer_fk references customer_pk in customer,
        must not be NULL




The first entry of Listing 2.1 says that the customer table has five columns, that customer_pk is its primary key, and that customer_number is its alternate key: the keys found in Example 2.1. The last line of the customer_order entry is its foreign key. It says that customer_fk refers to customer_pk in the customer table and must not be NULL, so every order has a customer. Read in the other direction, the same line says that a customer may be referred to by any number of orders, including none.
Notice that the book’s key names do some of the work. A column ending in _pk is its table’s primary key, and a column ending in _fk is a foreign key named for the table it refers to, or sometimes for the role the referenced row plays (a bill of materials line names an assembly and one of its components, as assembly_fk and component_fk). The relational schema states the keys anyway, because a key of several columns, an alternate key, and a database named by someone else’s rules all need saying.
The minimal form leaves out what is needed to build the tables rather than read them. A complete relational schema adds each column’s data type and whether it may be NULL, the CHECK constraints that narrow each domain, and each foreign key’s response to deleting or updating the row it refers to (Table 2.6). Listing 2.2 gives the complete relational schema of the customer_order table.




Listing 2.2: The Complete Relational Schema of the Customer Order Table


customer_order
    customer_order_pk    INTEGER      not NULL, generated
    order_number         VARCHAR(10)  not NULL
    order_date           DATE         not NULL
    requested_ship_date  DATE         may be NULL
    customer_fk          INTEGER      not NULL
    primary key: customer_order_pk
    alternate key: order_number
    customer_fk references customer_pk in customer,
        must not be NULL
    customer_fk: on delete no action, on update no action
    check: requested_ship_date >= order_date




The column lines of Listing 2.2 confirm what Table 2.5 showed: requested_ship_date is the one column that may be NULL. The word generated on customer_order_pk says that the database generates its values, which is what makes it a surrogate key. The line that begins customer_fk: on delete records the response chosen for the foreign key, no action, which means refuse. The check line narrows the domain of requested_ship_date: a customer cannot ask for an order to ship before the order was placed. In other words, a complete relational schema holds everything needed to write the statements that create the tables, which Chapter 8 presents.
The relational schema of stage D5, the whole distribution schema, is too long for one listing, so it is given in two. Listing 2.3 gives the tables of orders and products, and Listing 2.4 the tables of warehouses and shipments.




Listing 2.3: The Relational Schema of Stage D5: Orders and Products


customer (customer_pk, customer_number, name, city, state)
    primary key: customer_pk
    alternate key: customer_number

customer_order (customer_order_pk, order_number, order_date,
                requested_ship_date, customer_fk)
    primary key: customer_order_pk
    alternate key: order_number
    customer_fk references customer_pk in customer,
        must not be NULL

product (product_pk, product_number, description,
         list_price)
    primary key: product_pk
    alternate key: product_number

order_line (order_line_pk, customer_order_fk, line_number,
            product_fk, quantity, unit_price)
    primary key: order_line_pk
    alternate key: (customer_order_fk, line_number)
    customer_order_fk references customer_order_pk in
        customer_order, must not be NULL
    product_fk references product_pk in product,
        must not be NULL








Listing 2.4: The Relational Schema of Stage D5: Warehouses and Shipments


warehouse (warehouse_pk, warehouse_code, city, state)
    primary key: warehouse_pk
    alternate key: warehouse_code

stock_level (stock_level_pk, warehouse_fk, product_fk,
             quantity_on_hand, reorder_point)
    primary key: stock_level_pk
    alternate key: (warehouse_fk, product_fk)
    warehouse_fk references warehouse_pk in warehouse,
        must not be NULL
    product_fk references product_pk in product,
        must not be NULL

shipment (shipment_pk, shipment_number, shipped_on, carrier,
          customer_order_fk, warehouse_fk)
    primary key: shipment_pk
    alternate key: shipment_number
    customer_order_fk references customer_order_pk in
        customer_order, must not be NULL
    warehouse_fk references warehouse_pk in warehouse,
        must not be NULL

shipment_line (shipment_line_pk, shipment_fk, order_line_fk,
               quantity)
    primary key: shipment_line_pk
    alternate key: (shipment_fk, order_line_fk)
    shipment_fk references shipment_pk in shipment,
        must not be NULL
    order_line_fk references order_line_pk in order_line,
        must not be NULL




The foreign key lines of Listing 2.3 and Listing 2.4 sort the eight tables into three groups. Three tables have none, so they refer to nothing: customer, product, and warehouse. Four refer only to those three or to each other: an order refers to a customer, an order line to an order and a product, a stock level to a warehouse and a product, and a shipment to an order and a warehouse. The last, shipment_line, refers to a shipment and to the order line it ships. Notice also the three alternate keys written in parentheses. The first, in order_line, is the composite key of Section 2.2, an order and a line number. The second, in stock_level, says that a warehouse holds at most one stock level for each product. The third, in shipment_line, says that a shipment ships a given order line at most once.
The tables of the book’s database also carry a schema name, the name of a group of tables within the database. The distribution tables belong to the schema distribution, so a query names the customer table distribution.customer, as the queries of this chapter have. The production and quality departments’ tables belong to schemas of their own, and Appendix C shows all of them.
The main use of a relational schema is to find where the answer to a question lives, before any query is written. The following example illustrates the process.

Example 2.2 (Tracing a request through the schema) The system. The distribution schema of Listing 2.3 and Listing 2.4.
The request. The sales manager asks: which customers have ordered the GC-300 steel garden cart?
The request names two things, customers and a product, so we begin by finding the tables that describe them: customer and product. Neither refers to the other, so we look for a path of foreign keys between them. The foreign keys of order_line refer to product and to customer_order, and the foreign key of customer_order refers to customer. Thus, the path runs from product to order_line, then to customer_order, and finally to customer. The columns along the path are the keys that connect each pair:



Table 2.7: The Path from a Product to Its Customers





Foreign key
Refers to




order_line.product_fk
product.product_pk


order_line.customer_order_fk
customer_order.customer_order_pk


customer_order.customer_fk
customer.customer_pk






The check. Every step of Table 2.7 is a foreign key line of Listing 2.3, and every step matches a foreign key to the primary key it refers to, so each connection is guaranteed by referential integrity.
Interpretation. Four tables answer the question. A query needs the product’s number from product, the customers’ names from customer, and the two tables between them only to make the connection.
Where it breaks. The path finds customers who ordered the cart. A manager who asks which customers received one needs a different path, through shipment_line and shipment, because an order line that has not shipped is still an order.

Tracing a path of keys through a schema is the reasoning behind a join, the operation Section 3.6 presents. So far the schema has been given to us as a listing. The next section shows that the database holds the same description itself, where anyone can ask for it.

title: 2  The Relational Model
text:
2.5 A database describes itself
This section shows that a relational database stores the description of its own tables, and that the description is queried like any other data.
Recall from Section 1.3 that a DBMS keeps a catalog of metadata, the data about the data. The relational schemas of Section 2.4 are metadata: they say what tables exist, what columns each has, and which keys and rules apply, without listing a single customer. A database that stores this description inside itself, where people and programs can read it, is called self-describing. Every relational database is self-describing, and it holds the description the relational way, in tables.
Compare the sales office’s order log of Table 1.1. Its only description is its heading row. The heading “Qty” names a column, but nothing in the spreadsheet records that a quantity must be a positive whole number or that an order number identifies one order. Those rules live in the heads of the people who keep the log, and they hold only as long as those people are careful. In a database, the same rules are part of the catalog, and the DBMS reads them on every change.
The SQL standard defines a set of views of the catalog, called the information_schema, which every system that follows the standard provides. Its views are queried with the same SQL as the data. The following query asks the catalog of stage D5 which tables the distribution schema holds. Unlike the queries before it, it names the columns it wants after SELECT, keeps only the rows its WHERE allows, and sorts them with ORDER BY.



Table 2.8: The Tables of the Distribution Schema, from the Catalog


SELECT table_name, table_type
FROM information_schema.tables
WHERE table_schema = 'distribution'
ORDER BY table_name;





table_name


table_type






customer


BASE TABLE




customer_order


BASE TABLE




order_line


BASE TABLE




product


BASE TABLE




shipment


BASE TABLE




shipment_line


BASE TABLE




stock_level


BASE TABLE




warehouse


BASE TABLE








Table 2.8 lists the eight tables of Listing 2.3 and Listing 2.4. Each is a BASE TABLE, a table that stores rows; the catalog also lists views, which Section 9.1 presents. The next query asks the catalog about the columns of one table. Its WHERE keeps the rows that meet both conditions joined by AND, and AS gives the column character_maximum_length the shorter name length in the result.



Table 2.9: The Columns of the Customer Order Table, from the Catalog


SELECT column_name, data_type,
       character_maximum_length AS length,
       is_nullable
FROM information_schema.columns
WHERE table_schema = 'distribution'
  AND table_name = 'customer_order'
ORDER BY ordinal_position;





column_name


data_type


length


is_nullable






customer_order_pk


integer


NULL


NO




order_number

10

order_date
