Exercise 5.2 Using Figure 5.7, write each association as two sentences, one in each direction, of the form “each … is linked to …”. Then say, for each end, whether an object may exist without a link at that end.


Exercise 5.3 At stage D5, each shipment leaves from one warehouse, and the two warehouses have made eleven shipments between them.

Draw a cloud instance diagram of the warehouses, the shipments SH-9001 to SH-9005, and the links between them. The query of Exercise 3.11 shows how to find each shipment’s warehouse.
Read the multiplicity at each end from your diagram.
In the sample, every warehouse has at least one shipment. Which minimum is a rule of the business that the diagram cannot show? Explain.



Exercise 5.4 The Shipment class of stage D5 records its carrier as the attribute carrier. The distribution manager now wants to record each carrier’s contract rate per pound and its dispatcher’s phone number, and to keep a list of approved carriers that includes carriers not yet used. Treat a customer pickup as one of the carriers on the list.

Should the carrier remain an attribute? Give the test of Section 5.3 that decides it.
Sketch the change to the class model, with multiplicities, and read the new association both ways.



Exercise 5.5 The production schema of stage P3 records, for each operator certified on a machine, the date of the certification and its level.

Explain why neither the date nor the level is an attribute of Operator or of Machine.
Model the certification with an association class, and give the multiplicities.
Could an operator be certified on the same machine twice, say at level 1 in 2020 and at level 3 in 2024? What would the association class model say, and what would the business need to decide?



Exercise 5.6 The plant extends the certifications of Exercise 5.5 with two more facts. Each certification is signed off by an operator who holds a level 3 certification on the same machine. And each machine has one lead operator, responsible for its upkeep; an operator may lead any number of machines, or none.

Draw a class model in which Certification is an association class of Operator and Machine, and add an association for the operator who signed each certification off and one for each machine’s lead. Name the roles and give every multiplicity.
Draw a second model in which Certification is an ordinary class, associated with Operator twice and with Machine once.
Four certifications of stage P3 are to be recorded with their sign-offs: Maria Lopez (E-201) on M-04 and Aisha Patel (E-205) on M-05, both signed off by Linda Nguyen (E-203); Robert Hayes (E-204) on M-01, signed off by Maria Lopez; and Linda Nguyen on M-06, signed off by Robert Hayes. Linda Nguyen leads M-04 and M-05, Maria Lopez leads M-01, and Robert Hayes leads M-06. Draw a cloud instance diagram of these facts, in the manner of Figure 5.6, for each model.
Name a set of objects and links that the model of part (b) allows and the model of part (a) forbids. Would the plant want it?
Neither model enforces the rule that the signer holds a level 3 certification on the same machine. State that rule in words beside the diagram, and say what else a signer must not be.



Exercise 5.7 HG Industries decides to record where each product is stored within a warehouse. Each warehouse is divided into bins, identified by a bin code such as A-03 that is unique within its warehouse; two warehouses may both have a bin A-03.

Model warehouses and bins without a qualifier, and give the multiplicities.
Model them with a qualifier, and explain how the multiplicity at the bin end changes.
What composite key would the qualifier become in a table?



Exercise 5.8 Consider the six hypothetical runs of Figure 5.14.

List the links as triples (operator, machine, work order), with their hours.
Replace the ternary association with three binary associations (operator with machine, machine with work order, operator with work order), and list the links each would hold.
List every triple consistent with the three binary associations, that is, every operator, machine, and work order whose three pairs are all links of part (b). Mark the triples that are not runs.
Remove Maria Lopez’s run of M-01 on WO-7003 from the data. Show that every triple consistent with the binary associations is now a real run. Does that make the binary model right for these runs? Explain.
Where would the hours be recorded in the binary model? Explain why that is a problem.



Exercise 5.9 For each association, say whether it is a composition, an aggregation, or an ordinary association, and give the question of Section 5.6 that decides it.

ManufacturedPart and its Operations (stage P3).
WorkCenter and Machine (stage P3).
Customer and CustomerOrder (stage D2).
ManufacturedPart and Part in the bill of materials (stage P2).
Part and its quality Characteristics (stage Q).



Exercise 5.10 Using Figure 5.17 and Figure 5.18:

List the attributes an object of PurchasedPart has, and say where each comes from.
Why does the assembly end of the bill of materials attach to ManufacturedPart rather than Part? (Figure 5.20 shows the bill of materials.)
HG Industries considers buying wheel assemblies from a supplier when the plant is at capacity, while still making them at other times. Which of {disjoint, complete} would that break, and what are two ways to change the model?



Exercise 5.11 For each proposal, say whether it should be a subclass or a role name, and why.

Inspector, a subclass of Operator, for the operators who inspect parts.
RetailCustomer and WholesaleCustomer, subclasses of Customer, where wholesale customers have a credit limit and a sales representative and retail customers pay on order.
ReferringCustomer, a subclass of Customer, for customers who have referred another customer to HG Industries.



Exercise 5.12 A new analyst proposes the following model of part of stage D5, written as text:

Product (productNumber, description, listPrice, fayetteville_on_hand, tulsa_on_hand, reorder_point)
Warehouse (warehouse_pk, warehouseCode, city, state)
Shipment (shipmentNumber, shippedOn, carrier, warehouse_fk, customerName)

Review it with the questions of Table 5.6. List every problem you find, say which question finds it, and describe the repair.


Exercise 5.13 HG Industries’ quality department inspects lots of manufactured parts. An inspector measures a sample of parts from a lot against the part’s characteristics, each with a lower and an upper specification limit, and counts defects by type. The department wants to know which lots failed, which characteristics drift, and whether inspectors agree.

Write a problem statement for the department’s inspection records, answering the six questions of Section 5.2, and say what the system will not do.
Name the actors and at least three use cases, and draw the use case diagram.
Write the description of one use case, in the form of Table 5.1.
Write three requirements in the form “The system shall …”, at least one of which is a request the model must answer.



Exercise 5.14 The receiving dock writes:

Parts that HG Industries buys arrive from suppliers by truck. Each delivery brings the parts of one purchase order, though an order may arrive in several deliveries. A purchase order lists, for each part, the quantity ordered and the price agreed. At the dock, a receiving clerk counts each part in the delivery and records the quantity received and any quantity rejected as damaged. Accounts payable pays suppliers from the receipts, which this system does not handle. The buyer needs to know which purchase orders are still open and how often each supplier delivers late.


List every candidate class in the statement.
Decide each candidate as Table 5.5 does: a class, an attribute, or eliminated, with the reason.
Apply the four tests of step 3 to the classes you kept. Which candidate is closest to failing the more than a name test, and what would the buyer have to want recorded for it to pass?
Name each association, its kind from Table 5.4, and its multiplicities, and draw the class model.
Which requirement in the statement does your model answer with a derived value rather than a stored one?



Exercise 5.15 Write a domain specification for each attribute, and say which of the four ways (enumeration, citation, acceptance rule, range) you used.

PurchasedPart.leadTimeDays, the days a supplier needs to deliver.
Customer.state.
Inspection.result, an attribute the department proposes to add, which records whether a lot was accepted or rejected.
Measurement.measuredValue of a diameter, measured in inches.
An analyst wrote, for OrderLine.unitPrice, “Domain: a decimal number.” Say what is wrong with it, and write a better specification.



Exercise 5.16 A supplier’s catalog system is drawn in crow’s foot notation with three entity types, Supplier, CatalogItem, and PurchasedPart. The line from Supplier to CatalogItem has two bars at Supplier and a bar with a crow’s foot at CatalogItem. The line from CatalogItem to PurchasedPart has a circle with a crow’s foot at CatalogItem and two bars at PurchasedPart. CatalogItem has the attributes supplierPartNumber and unitPrice.

Translate each line into a UML association with multiplicities, and read each both ways.
CatalogItem connects a supplier and a purchased part and carries a price. Should it be an association class of an association between Supplier and PurchasedPart? Consider whether a supplier might list the same part twice, say in two package sizes.



Exercise 5.17 HG Industries wants to record machine maintenance. Model the following in a class diagram, with multiplicities, and write a class description for each new class.
Each machine receives preventive maintenance on a schedule: a maintenance plan for a machine lists tasks, each with an interval in days, and a task is numbered within its plan. When a technician performs a task, the plant records the date, the technician, and the minutes it took. Technicians are employees but not operators, although an operator may be trained as a technician. A machine may also break down; each breakdown is recorded with its start and end times and the technician who repaired it.
Say which parts of your model are compositions, which multiplicities are decisions the business must confirm, and how you modeled “an operator may be trained as a technician”.

The exercises from here on model settings outside HG Industries, each a short statement of business rules in plain English. Model each with the constructs of this chapter, give every multiplicity, and read each association both ways before you trust it. Where a statement leaves a rule open, say what you assumed. Chapter 6 maps several of these models to tables, starting from the instructor’s model of each.

Exercise 5.18 A plant’s tool crib lends tools to its mechanics. Each tool has a tool number, unique in the crib, a description, and the date it was purchased. Each mechanic has an employee number and a name. When a mechanic checks out a tool, the crib records the time; when the tool comes back, it records the return time. Over its life a tool is checked out many times, by many mechanics, and a mechanic often checks out the same tool again. A tool is out with at most one mechanic at a time, and a mechanic may have several tools out at once. New tools have never been checked out.

Model the tools, the mechanics, and the checkouts, with multiplicities.
Explain why a checkout cannot be an association class of an association between Tool and Mechanic.
Which rule of the statement can no multiplicity in the diagram state? How would you record it?



Exercise 5.19 A quality department keeps its gauges calibrated. Each gauge has a serial number, a type (such as micrometer or caliper), a measuring range, and a calibration interval in days. Calibrations are done by outside laboratories, each with a name and an accreditation number. Each calibration of a gauge records the date, the result (passed, adjusted, or failed), and the certificate the laboratory issued. A laboratory numbers its certificates itself, so two laboratories may both issue a certificate numbered 1047. A gauge may be calibrated by different laboratories over the years, and a newly bought gauge has not yet been calibrated. A laboratory is recorded only once it has calibrated a gauge.

Model the gauges, laboratories, and calibrations, with multiplicities.
Model the certificate number with a qualifier, and say what the qualifier states that an attribute of Calibration would not.
The department also wants each gauge’s next due date. Is it an attribute to record? Explain.



Exercise 5.20 A machining cell pulls parts with kanban containers. Give the multiplicity at each end of each association, and read each association both ways.

Each container is dedicated to one part number. Each part number circulates in at least two containers, since the cell runs a two-bin system.
Each container belongs to the loop of one cell; a cell’s loop may hold containers of many part numbers, and a new cell has none yet.
A kanban card is printed for one container and is never moved to another. A container carries at most one card; a new container has none until its card is printed.
Draw the class model of parts (a) to (c), with PartNumber, Container, Cell, and Card and attributes of your choosing.
Should the card be a class of its own, or attributes of Container? Give one argument each way.



Exercise 5.21 A plant’s occupational health clinic schedules appointments. Each appointment is for one employee, with one provider (a nurse or a physician), in one exam room, at a date and time, for a number of minutes, with a reason and a status (scheduled, completed, or missed). An employee has many appointments over the years, often with the same provider in the same room.

Model the employees, providers, exam rooms, and appointments.
A classmate models the appointment as a ternary association of Employee, Provider, and ExamRoom, with an association class. Explain, with the rule of Section 5.4 about links, why that model cannot record the clinic’s appointments.
Each provider has a home exam room, and a room is the home of at most one provider. Add this to your model.



Exercise 5.22 A project scheduler records projects and their activities. Each project has a name and a start date. Each activity belongs to one project, has an identifier unique within its project (such as A, B, C), a description, and a duration in days. An activity may have predecessors, activities that must finish before it can start, and it may be a predecessor of several other activities; the first activities of a project have no predecessors. Each precedence may carry a lag, a number of days that must pass between the end of the predecessor and the start of its successor.

Model projects, activities, and precedences, with role names on the recursive association.
Where does the lag belong, and why?
A precedence must join two activities of the same project, and no chain of precedences may lead from an activity back to itself. Can the diagram state either rule?



Exercise 5.23 A company records the places in its plants: each site has buildings, each building has areas, and each area may have production lines. Every building is in one site, every area in one building, and every line in one area. A site has at least one building, and a building at least one area.

Model the four levels as four classes.
Model the same places with one class, Location, and a recursive association.
The company acquires a plant whose areas are divided into zones, and zones into lines. What must change in each model?
Which model states a request for everything inside a building as one idea, whatever the depth, and which lets SQL answer it without a recursive query? Recall Section 4.6.



Exercise 5.24 A city’s bike share has stations, each with a name and a location. Each station has docks, numbered 1, 2, 3, and so on within the station. A bike, identified by its bike number, is locked in at most one dock, and a dock holds at most one bike. Members, with a member number and a name, take rides: a ride uses one bike, starts at one station at a time, and ends at a station at a later time, often a different station; a ride in progress has not yet ended.

Model the stations, docks, bikes, members, and rides.
Explain the role names your model needs, and why.
What does the qualifier on the dock number state, and what would change if docks were numbered across the whole city instead?



Exercise 5.25 A port’s container yard is divided into blocks, each identified by a block code within the yard. A place for a container in a block is a slot, identified by its bay, row, and tier numbers together; a slot may be refrigerated. Each shipping container has a container number, a size in feet, and an owner, and occupies at most one slot while in the yard; a slot holds at most one container.

Model the yard, its blocks, slots, and containers, using qualifiers.
Which associations are compositions? Apply the questions of Section 5.6.
A qualifier of three attributes, bay, row, and tier: what composite key would it become in a table?



Exercise 5.26 A hospital’s emergency department records each patient visit: the arrival time and, when the patient leaves, the departure time. On arrival a nurse assigns the visit a triage level from 1 (resuscitation) to 5 (non-urgent); each level has a description and a target number of minutes within which the patient should be seen. During a visit a patient may be moved between beds, and may return to a bed used earlier in the same visit; each move records when the patient took the bed and when the patient left it. Each bed has a code and a type (such as trauma or general).

Model patients, visits, triage levels, beds, and bed assignments.
Is the triage level an attribute of Visit or a class? Give the argument for your choice.
Why is the bed assignment a class and not an association class between Visit and Bed?



Exercise 5.27 An equipment rental yard rents units of equipment, each unit identified by its serial number and of one equipment type (such as a 20-foot scissor lift). Rates depend on the type and the rental period: a scissor lift rents for one amount per day, another per week, and another per month, and every unit of the type rents at the same rates. Customers rent units; each rental is of one unit and records the date out, the date due, the date returned, and the rental period it is charged at.

Model equipment types, units, rate periods, rates, customers, and rentals.
Where does the rate’s amount belong, and why is it not an attribute of EquipmentUnit?
The distinction between a type and its units recurs in many settings. Name one other pair from this chapter’s exercises or from HG Industries.



Exercise 5.28 A fleet manager tracks the plant’s vehicles. Every vehicle has a unit number, a make, a model year, and an hour meter. Trucks and vans are road vehicles, with a license plate, a registration expiry date, and an odometer; trucks also have a payload and a number of axles, and vans a cargo volume. Forklifts are not road vehicles; they have a lift capacity and a fuel type. Every vehicle is a truck, a van, or a forklift, and never more than one.

Model the vehicles with generalization, placing each attribute on the highest class it applies to, and state the constraints.
Some vehicles are leased and some are owned. Should LeasedVehicle be a subclass? Recall Exercise 5.11.



Exercise 5.29 For each pair, say whether the association is a composition, an aggregation, or an ordinary association, and give the question of Section 5.6 that decides it.

A pallet and the cartons stacked on it.
An aircraft and its engines, which are removed for overhaul and installed on other aircraft.
An invoice and its lines.
A building and its rooms.
A maintenance crew and its technicians.
A kit and the parts packed in it for an assembly station.


The next six exercises model one system, a transit agency’s monitoring system, adapted from a Transportation Research Board study (Rossetti 1999). Each models one part of it; together they cover its routes, stops, schedules, operations, fares, and the record of each trip a vehicle makes.

Exercise 5.30 A transit agency runs bus routes. Each route has a number, a name, a color on the system map, and the distance the agency publishes for it. The places on the network are points, each with a name and a latitude and longitude. A route is a sequence of segments, in the order the bus travels them; each segment starts at one point and ends at another and has a length. Each segment belongs to exactly one route; two routes that run along the same street have segments of their own. A point may lie on many routes, and a route has at least one segment. Points of interest, such as a shopping center or a hospital, each with a name and an address, are recorded with the points near them; a point of interest is near at least one point.

Model routes, segments, points, and points of interest.
A route’s points, in order, are also wanted. Should the model have an association between Route and Point? Explain what it would add and what it would cost.
Read the association between Segment and Point both ways, for each role.



Exercise 5.31 Some points of the network of Exercise 5.30 are access points, where passengers may board or leave the bus; the others are places such as timing points and turnarounds. An access point records where it is on its block (midblock, near side, or far side of an intersection), the capacity of its waiting area, its number of benches, and whether it has a shelter. Some access points are scheduled points, which appear on the printed timetables and record whether a timetable is posted there.

Model the three kinds of point with generalization, and state each generalization’s constraints.
A rider asks for a stop where the bus will drop off only on request. Is a RequestStop a new subclass, or an attribute? Explain.



Exercise 5.32 Each route of Exercise 5.30 has one or more schedules, each with a name (such as “Weekday” or “Saturday”), the date it was last updated, and the headway, the minutes between buses. A schedule applies to one or more days of the week, and a day of the week is covered by schedules of many routes. A schedule lists, in order, the times a bus is due at the scheduled points of Exercise 5.31: each line gives one scheduled point, an arrival time, and a departure time. A scheduled point appears on many lines of many schedules.

Model routes, schedules, days of the week, schedule lines, and scheduled points.
Why is the schedule line a class of its own rather than an association class between Schedule and ScheduledPoint?



Exercise 5.33 A transit manager assigns a driver to a vehicle on a route for a period of time, with a start time, an end time, and comments. Over a month the same driver drives the same bus on the same route on many days, and a driver drives many vehicles, a vehicle is driven by many drivers, and a route is served by many vehicles and drivers. Each driver has a name and a license number; each vehicle has a vehicle number and a seating capacity.

Model the assignment first as a ternary association with an association class, then as a class with three binary associations.
Which model can record the month described above? Use the rule of Section 5.4.
The study this exercise is adapted from made the assignment a class. What else does the class allow that the ternary association does not?



Exercise 5.34 The agency sells smart cards, each with a card number and the date issued. Every card is either a debit card, which holds a balance that each trip draws down, or a credit card, whose trips are billed to an account; an account, with an account number and a balance, has one or more credit cards. Each account has one holder, a person, who may authorize other people to use the account’s cards; a person may hold several accounts and be authorized on others. A person has a name and, optionally, a rider category (student, senior, or standard), and may have a mailing address, which several people in one household may share. Each trip is made with one card, from an origin point to a destination point of Exercise 5.30, at a start and end time, for a fare. Payments are made to an account, each with a date, an amount, and a payment type (cash, check, or charge).

Model the cards, accounts, people, addresses, trips, and payments, recording the address by one of the choices of Section 5.3.1.
State the generalization’s constraints, and say what they rule out.
Read the two associations between Person and Account both ways.
Where would you record that a person may use an account’s cards only until a given date?



Exercise 5.35 Each time a vehicle runs a route of Exercise 5.30, the monitoring system records a route traversal, with a start and end time. A route traversal consists of point traversals, one for each point the bus reached, in order, each with the arrival and departure times and the numbers of passengers boarding and alighting; and link traversals, one for each segment the bus traveled between two point traversals, in order, each with a start time, an end time, and an average speed. Each point traversal is at one point, and each link traversal travels one segment.

Model route traversals, point traversals, and link traversals, with their associations to vehicles, routes, points, and segments.
The structure of a traversal mirrors the structure of a route. Explain the correspondence, class by class.
Which rules connecting the two structures can the diagram not state? Give two.


The last six exercises reverse the direction: each gives a class diagram and asks for the English description a business reader could check. For each diagram, write every association as two sentences, one in each direction, with the multiplicities in words; state each constraint; describe each association class and qualifier; and name one rule of the business that the diagram does not state.

Exercise 5.36 Figure 5.22 is part of the monitoring system of the transit exercises, the summary statistics computed from trips and traversals. Describe it in English.






Figure 5.22: Summary Statistics of the Monitoring System





Exercise 5.37 Figure 5.23 shows the event logs a vehicle’s data terminal records and the office imports. Describe it in English, and explain what the generalization’s {disjoint, incomplete} allows.






Figure 5.23: Event Logs of the Monitoring System





Exercise 5.38 Figure 5.24 shows transfers between access points. Describe it in English, and give an example of a transfer that is not symmetric.






Figure 5.24: Transfers Between Access Points





Exercise 5.39 Figure 5.25 shows a testing laboratory’s samples and their chain of custody. Describe it in English. What does the qualifier on the sample number say about how samples are numbered?






Figure 5.25: A Laboratory’s Samples and Their Chain of Custody





Exercise 5.40 Figure 5.26 shows cycle counting in a distribution center. Describe it in English. Can a count exist whose item is not stocked at its location? What does the diagram say, and what should the business decide?






Figure 5.26: Cycle Counting in a Distribution Center





Exercise 5.41 Figure 5.27 shows engineering drawings and their revisions. Describe it in English, including the two associations between Revision and Engineer and what the generalization’s constraints mean for a drawing.






Figure 5.27: Engineering Drawings and Their Revisions

Jacobson, Ivar, Magnus Christerson, Patrik Jonsson, and Gunnar Övergaard. 1992. Object-Oriented Software Engineering: A Use Case Driven Approach. Addison-Wesley.


Larman, Craig. 2004. Applying UML and Patterns: An Introduction to Object-Oriented Analysis and Design and Iterative Development. 3rd ed. Prentice Hall.


Rossetti, Manuel D. 1999. Transit Integrated Monitoring System. IDEA Program Final Report TRANSIT-19. Transportation Research Board, National Research Council.


Rumbaugh, James, Michael Blaha, William Premerlani, Frederick Eddy, and William Lorensen. 1991. Object-Oriented Modeling and Design. Prentice Hall.

title: 6  From Class Models to Tables
text:
6.1 The mapping process
Chapter 5 built class models of HG Industries: what the business records and how the things it records are related. Chapter 2 read the tables that implement those models. This chapter connects the two. It presents the rules that turn each construct of a class diagram into tables, columns, keys, and constraints, following Blaha and Premerlani (Blaha and Premerlani 1998), and it applies them to the models of Chapter 5 to produce, step by step, the tables of the book’s database.
The chapter begins with the whole process, seven steps from a reviewed class model to a complete relational schema, and then illustrates each step on the models of Chapter 5, showing each time the part of the class diagram being mapped and where each of its parts goes in the tables. The rules are few, and most of them are mechanical once the class model is right. That is the point of designing in a class model first: the judgment goes into the model, where the business can review it, and the mapping carries the model’s meaning into tables without adding any. Every mapping in this chapter ends in a complete relational schema, in the notation of Section 2.4, that holds everything needed to create the tables, which Chapter 8 does.
This section presents the whole mapping, from a class model to tables, as a sequence of steps, before the sections that illustrate each step.
Designing a database has two phases. The first turns a class model into a relational schema: the tables, their columns, their keys, and the rules that connect them. The second turns the relational schema into statements that a database system runs to create the tables. This chapter presents the first phase, and Chapter 8 the second. Figure 6.1 shows the first phase as seven steps.
The steps of Figure 6.1 are applied to a whole model, one step at a time: all of its classes, then all of their attributes, and so on, since a later step needs the tables and keys of the earlier ones. In words, they are:
The result is a complete relational schema, in the notation of Section 2.4: every table with its columns, types, NULL rules, keys, checks, and the deletion rule of each foreign key. It holds everything Chapter 8 needs to create the tables. The sections that follow illustrate the steps in order:
Step 7 deserves a word before the details. When a mapping seems hard, the trouble is usually in the class model, not the rules. The remedy is the one of Section 5.4: draw a cloud instance diagram of a few objects and links, and put the same objects and links into the tables as rows. If the rows cannot hold what the diagram shows, or hold something it forbids, the model or the mapping is wrong, and the diagram says where.
crumbs: 6  From Class Models to Tables

title: 6  From Class Models to Tables
text:
Figure 6.1: The Steps of Mapping a Class Model to Tables





Map each class to a table. Every class becomes a table of its own, named for the class.
Map each attribute to a column, with its domain. Each column gets a type that holds the attribute’s values, NOT NULL unless the attribute may be missing, and a CHECK for a domain narrower than its type.
Give each table its identity. Each table gets a primary key, which the class model does not name, and each business identifier becomes an alternate key.
Map each association by its multiplicity. An association becomes a foreign key in one of its classes’ tables when a link can be recorded there as a single value, and a table of its own when it cannot.
Map each generalization. A superclass and its subclasses become tables that share a key, or are combined, in one of three ways.
Choose what a deletion does to each foreign key. A foreign key refuses the deletion of the row it refers to, unless its association is a composition, whose parts go with their whole.
Check the tables. Put a few objects and links into the tables, as rows, and see whether they hold them without loss or contradiction; then review the tables’ normal form, which Chapter 7 presents. A check that fails sends the designer back to the class model, along the dashed arrow of the figure.





Table 6.1: The Steps of the Mapping and Where They Are Illustrated









Step
Illustrated in




1 to 3: classes, attributes, identity
Section 6.2, and in depth Section 6.6


4 and 6: associations and deletions
Section 6.3 and Section 6.4


5: generalization
Section 6.5


7: checking the tables
the check and the interpretation of Example 6.3

title: 6  From Class Models to Tables
text:
6.2 Mapping classes
This section illustrates steps 1 to 3 of Figure 6.1: how a class becomes a table, its attributes become columns, and the table gets its keys. Figure 6.2 shows the Customer class of Figure 5.1, with a note that says where each of its parts goes.






Figure 6.2: Mapping a Class



Each class maps to a table, as the note of Figure 6.2 begins. The table is named for the class, in the snake_case of Section 2.4 (CustomerOrder becomes customer_order), and in the singular, since the table implements the class and the class describes one object. Each attribute maps to a column, named the same way (customerNumber becomes customer_number). Recall from Section 5.3.1 that a value split into parts, such as a point’s location, is several attributes (latitude and longitude), and so becomes several columns.
Each column needs a data type, and the type comes from the attribute’s domain (Section 5.3). Choosing it is the first place where a design meets the implementation, and it is best done in two steps. The first specifies each attribute’s domain in words, with whether the attribute may be missing; the second chooses the SQL type and the constraints that implement each domain. For the Customer class of Figure 5.1, the two steps give:



Table 6.2: Specifying the Domains of the Customer Class











Attribute
Domain
May be missing?
SQL type and constraints




customerNumber
a number assigned by the company, C- and four digits
no
VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL UNIQUE


name
the business’s name
no
VARCHAR(60) NOT NULL


city
a city name
no
VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL


state
a two-letter US state code
no
CHAR(2) NOT NULL






Three things in Table 6.2 come straight from the class model. An attribute without a multiplicity has exactly one value, so its column is NOT NULL; an attribute marked [0..1], such as requestedShipDate, becomes a column that allows NULL. A business identifier becomes a UNIQUE column, since the business promises that no two objects share it; customerNumber is the alternate key found in Example 2.1. And a domain narrower than any SQL type, such as a price that must be positive, becomes a CHECK constraint, as list_price > 0 does for products.
Each table needs a primary key, and here the class model gives no help, deliberately: objects are distinguishable in themselves, and a class model names no identifier (Section 5.3). The mapping must supply one. The book’s database supplies a surrogate key for every table: a column named for its table with the suffix _pk, whose values PostgreSQL generates. The business identifier stays a UNIQUE column beside it. Section 6.6 weighs this choice against using the business identifier itself as the primary key.
With a key chosen, the class is fully mapped. Listing 6.1 gives the complete relational schema of the customer table of stage D1, the result of mapping Table 6.2.




Listing 6.1: The Complete Relational Schema of the Customer Table


customer
    customer_pk      INTEGER      not NULL, generated
    customer_number  VARCHAR(10)  not NULL
    name             VARCHAR(60)  not NULL
    city             VARCHAR(40)  not NULL
    state            CHAR(2)      not NULL
    primary key: customer_pk
    alternate key: customer_number




Every line of Listing 6.1 traces back to the model or to a decision of this section: the columns to the attributes, not NULL to the attributes’ multiplicities, the alternate key to the business identifier, and the primary key, generated by the database, to the surrogate key. The table has no foreign key, since Customer in stage D1 has no associations. The next section adds them.

title: 6  From Class Models to Tables
text:
6.3 Mapping associations
This section illustrates steps 4 and 6 of Figure 6.1: how each kind of association becomes a foreign key or a table, according to its multiplicities, and what a deletion does to it.
Recall the cloud instance diagram of Figure 5.5: each link of the association between customers and their orders is a line from one customer dot to one order dot. A table has no lines. It records a link as a value: the row of each order holds the key of the customer it is linked to, in a foreign key column. That works because each order has exactly one link. Every rule of this section follows from one question: where can a link be recorded as a single value? Each case below shows the fragment of a class diagram being mapped, with a note on the class whose table receives what the association becomes.

6.3.1 One-to-many associations
Figure 6.3 shows the association between customers and their orders of Figure 5.1.






Figure 6.3: Mapping a One-to-Many Association



Read the multiplicities of Figure 6.3 from the CustomerOrder end. Each order is linked to exactly 1 customer, so each order’s row can hold its customer’s key; the note on the link says so. A one-to-many association therefore maps to a foreign key in the table of the many end: customer_fk in customer_order, referring to customer_pk. The minimum at the one end decides NULL. The 1 at the Customer end has a minimum of one, so every order must have its customer and customer_fk is NOT NULL, as the note on CustomerOrder says; a minimum of 0 there would allow NULL for an order with no customer. The 0..* at the CustomerOrder end needs nothing in the tables: a customer with no orders is simply a customer whose key appears in no order’s customer_fk. Listing 6.2 gives the resulting relational schema.




Listing 6.2: The Relational Schema of the One-to-Many Association


customer (customer_pk, customer_number, name, city, state)
    primary key: customer_pk
    alternate key: customer_number

customer_order (customer_order_pk, order_number, order_date,
                requested_ship_date, customer_fk)
    primary key: customer_order_pk
    alternate key: order_number
    customer_fk references customer_pk in customer,
        must not be NULL




Each element of Figure 6.3 has a line in Listing 6.2. The two classes are the two tables; the association is the last line, the foreign key that references customer_pk; and the minimum of 1 at the Customer end is its must not be NULL. This is the schema of stage D2 that Chapter 2 read in Listing 2.1, now seen as the product of a mapping.


6.3.2 One-to-one associations
The book’s database has no one-to-one association of its own, but the maintenance model of Exercise 5.17 has one: each machine has at most one maintenance plan, and each plan belongs to exactly one machine, as Figure 6.4 shows.






Figure 6.4: Mapping a One-to-One Association



Each object at each end of Figure 6.4 has at most one link, so either table could hold the foreign key. The note puts it in the table of the end whose objects always have a link, the plan’s, so that it can be NOT NULL: every plan has its machine. A second constraint keeps the association one-to-one. Without it, two plans could name the same machine, and the 0..1 at the plan end would become 0..*. A one-to-one association therefore maps to a foreign key made UNIQUE: machine_fk in maintenance_plan, NOT NULL and UNIQUE. The machine table is stage P3’s, as Listing 6.3 gives it.




Listing 6.3: The Relational Schema of the Machine Table


machine (machine_pk, machine_number, model, installed_on,
         work_center_fk)
    primary key: machine_pk
    alternate key: machine_number
    work_center_fk references work_center_pk in work_center,
        must not be NULL




The maintenance_plan table is hypothetical, since the book’s database holds no maintenance plans, so Listing 6.4 is written out by hand, in the notation of the book’s generated listings.



Listing 6.4: The Relational Schema of the Maintenance Plan (Hypothetical)


maintenance_plan (maintenance_plan_pk, effective_from,
                  machine_fk)
    primary key: maintenance_plan_pk
    alternate key: machine_fk
    machine_fk references machine_pk in machine,
        must not be NULL



The UNIQUE constraint on machine_fk appears in Listing 6.4 as an alternate key, which is what it is: no two plans share a machine, so a machine identifies at most one plan. The machine table of Listing 6.3 is unchanged by the association, as the 0..1 at the plan end requires nothing of it.


6.3.3 Choosing the side of a one-to-one association
In Figure 6.4 the minimums decided the side: one end is mandatory and the other optional, so the foreign key went in the table of the objects that always have a link, where it could be NOT NULL. When both ends are 1, or both are 0..1, the multiplicities treat the two tables alike, and either side gives a correct schema. The choice is then a design decision, and the business context decides it. You should weigh three questions, in order:

Does one object depend on the other? An object that exists only for the other, or is always created after it, holds the foreign key: a maintenance plan exists for its machine. If the association is a composition, step 6 then lets the dependent object’s row be deleted with its whole.
Which end could become many? A rule that holds today may loosen. Put the foreign key in the table of the end that could become many; if the rule loosens, the association becomes one-to-many, and the change is only to drop the UNIQUE constraint.
Which table do users start from? The question asked most often names one object and wants that object’s own facts with its partner’s identifier. A foreign key in that object’s table answers it from one table, with no join, provided the column holds an identifier that people read.

The order matters. A schema that must be changed when the business changes costs more than a join, so the second question outranks the third.
Two other mappings complete the choices. When both ends are 1 and the two objects are created and removed together, one table can hold the attributes of both classes, and no foreign key is needed. When both ends are 0..1, a foreign key on either side would often be NULL; a table of its own for the association, holding the two foreign keys, each UNIQUE, records only the links that exist.
Whichever side holds it, one foreign key enforces one end fully and the other end only in part. A foreign key that is NOT NULL and UNIQUE gives each row of its table exactly one partner, the 1 at the partner’s end, and lets no two rows share a partner, the maximum of the 1 at its own end. Nothing makes every row of the other table a partner, so the minimum of that 1 is left to the application, or to a query that looks for the rows it misses.

Example 6.1 (Assigning lockers to operators) The system. The production schema of stage P3 holds the plant’s six operators. Suppose the plant also tracks the locker room: each locker is numbered on its door (L-101 to L-106), every operator has exactly one locker, and, apart from the day between an operator leaving and the next hire, every locker has exactly one operator. Figure 6.5 models the rule: the 1 at the Locker end says that each operator has exactly one locker, and the 1 at the Operator end that each locker has exactly one operator.






Figure 6.5: Assigning Lockers to Operators, a One-to-One Association



The request. Human resources asks almost every day for an operator’s details with the number of the operator’s locker, to issue a key or to welcome a new hire. “Who uses locker L-104?” is asked only when a locker is found open.
The design. Both ends of Figure 6.5 are 1, so the minimums do not decide, and we take the three questions in turn. Neither object depends on the other: the lockers are fixtures of the room, and operators are hired and leave. The second question asks the business about the future, and the plant’s answer is that operators on different shifts may one day share a locker. The operator end could then become many, so the foreign key belongs in the operator table. The third question agrees: human resources starts from the operator and wants the operator’s own details with the locker’s number.
Under the book’s convention of surrogate keys (Section 6.6), the operator’s row would hold locker_fk, the locker’s locker_pk, as Listing 6.5 gives it.



Listing 6.5: Lockers and Operators, with a Surrogate Foreign Key (Hypothetical)


locker (locker_pk, locker_number, location)
    primary key: locker_pk
    alternate key: locker_number

operator (operator_pk, employee_number, name, hire_date,
          locker_fk)
    primary key: operator_pk
    alternate keys: employee_number, locker_fk
    locker_fk references locker_pk in locker,
        must not be NULL



A locker_fk of 4 means nothing to a clerk, so the everyday question still needs a join to locker to print L-104, although the foreign key sits in the table the question starts from. Recall from Section 2.2 that a foreign key refers to a candidate key, not only to the primary key, so any column declared UNIQUE will do. Referring to the locker’s number instead, as Listing 6.6 does, puts the identifier people read in the operator’s row. The column keeps the name of the key it holds, locker_number, rather than locker_fk, which the book keeps for a column that holds another table’s surrogate key.



Listing 6.6: Lockers and Operators, with a Foreign Key to the Locker’s Number (Hypothetical)


locker (locker_pk, locker_number, location)
    primary key: locker_pk
    alternate key: locker_number

operator (operator_pk, employee_number, name, hire_date,
          locker_number)
    primary key: operator_pk
    alternate keys: employee_number, locker_number
    locker_number references locker_number in locker,
        must not be NULL



The result. With the tables of Listing 6.6, the everyday question reads one table:



Table 6.3: Each Operator with a Locker, from One Table (Hypothetical Lockers)


SELECT employee_number, name, locker_number
FROM production.operator
ORDER BY employee_number;





employee_number


name


locker_number






E-201


Maria Lopez


L-104




E-202


James Carter


L-101




E-203


Linda Nguyen


L-106




E-204


Robert Hayes


L-102




E-205


Aisha Patel


L-105




E-206


Tom Becker


L-103








The check. Each operator’s row holds one locker number, so the query returns one row per operator, six in all, which Table 6.3 has. The six locker numbers are all different, as the alternate key on locker_number requires.
Interpretation. The design follows the plant’s own answers: the foreign key sits where a shared locker would put it, and the question human resources asks every day needs no join. “Who uses locker L-104?” still has an answer, through the operator table, which Table 6.3 shows is Maria Lopez.
Where it breaks. Two conditions break the design. First, the locker numbers must stay as they are: if the plant renumbered its lockers, every operator’s locker_number would have to change with them, which the response of cascading an update (Section 2.3), declared as ON UPDATE CASCADE, can do. Second, the foreign key enforces the 1 at the Locker end, but only the maximum of the 1 at the Operator end. A locker that no operator is assigned to breaks the minimum of that 1, and nothing refuses it:

INSERT INTO production.locker (locker_number, location)
VALUES ('L-107', 'Locker room, row 2');




Table 6.4: A Locker That No Operator Uses (Hypothetical Lockers)


SELECT l.locker_number, l.location
FROM production.locker AS l
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT *
                  FROM production.operator AS o
                  WHERE o.locker_number = l.locker_number);





locker_number


location






L-107


Locker room, row 2








The insert of L-107 is accepted, and only a query like that of Table 6.4 finds it. A business that changed its mind about the second question, deciding instead that an operator might be given a second locker for tools, would reverse the design: the locker end could become many, and the foreign key would belong in locker, at the price of a join for the everyday question.



6.3.4 Many-to-many associations and association classes
Figure 6.6 shows the association of warehouses and products from Figure 5.7, with its association class StockLevel.






Figure 6.6: Mapping an Association Class



Both ends of Figure 6.6 are 0..*, so an object at either end may have many partners, and neither end’s table can hold its links as a single value. A many-to-many association therefore maps to a table of its own, whose rows are the links: each row holds two foreign keys, one to each end. The association class supplies the rest of the row, its attributes, which is why the note sits on StockLevel: the association and its class map together to the stock_level table, with warehouse_fk, product_fk, quantity_on_hand, and reorder_point. Recall Figure 5.6: each line there, with its quantity, is now one row.
The rule of Section 5.4, one link per pair of objects, also maps, as the note’s UNIQUE line says. Two rows of stock_level with the same warehouse and product would be two links between one pair, so the pair of foreign keys is a key of the table: UNIQUE (warehouse_fk, product_fk). The database then enforces the rule. An attempt to add a second stock level for the HT-100 at Fayetteville, at stage D4, fails:

INSERT INTO distribution.stock_level
    (warehouse_fk, product_fk,
     quantity_on_hand, reorder_point)
VALUES (1, 1, 5, 10);

ERROR:  duplicate key value violates unique constraint "stock_level_warehouse_fk_product_fk_key"
DETAIL:  Key (warehouse_fk, product_fk)=(1, 1) already exists.
Thus, an association class maps to a table whose foreign keys, taken together, are a key. In the book’s database that table also has a surrogate key, stock_level_pk, and the pair of foreign keys is an alternate key; Section 6.6 explains why. Listing 6.7 gives the resulting relational schema of the three tables.




Listing 6.7: The Relational Schema of the Association Class


product (product_pk, product_number, description,
         list_price)
    primary key: product_pk
    alternate key: product_number

warehouse (warehouse_pk, warehouse_code, city, state)
    primary key: warehouse_pk
    alternate key: warehouse_code

stock_level (stock_level_pk, warehouse_fk, product_fk,
             quantity_on_hand, reorder_point)
    primary key: stock_level_pk
    alternate key: (warehouse_fk, product_fk)
    warehouse_fk references warehouse_pk in warehouse,
        must not be NULL
    product_fk references product_pk in product,
        must not be NULL




The two classes of Figure 6.6 map to product and warehouse, which the association leaves unchanged, and the association with its class maps to stock_level: its two foreign keys are the two ends of each line of Figure 5.6, its alternate key is the rule of one link per pair, and its other columns are the class’s attributes.


6.3.5 Recursive associations
A recursive association maps by the same rules as any other; its ends happen to attach to the same class, or to a class and one of its subclasses. Only where the rules end up is new. In a one-to-many recursive association, both ends are the same table, so the table’s foreign key refers to the table itself. This subsection maps one of each kind, a one-to-many association first.

Example 6.2 (Mapping each operator’s lead) The system. The production schema of stage P3 holds the plant’s six operators. Suppose the plant organizes them into crews: each operator reports to at most one lead operator, and a lead may lead any number of operators. No operator is the operator’s own lead. Robert Hayes leads the plant and reports to no one. Figure 6.7 models the rule as an association of Operator with itself, with a role name at each end: the 0..1 at the lead end says that each operator has at most one lead, and the 0..* at the crewMember end that a lead has any number of crew members.






Figure 6.7: Mapping a Recursive One-to-Many Association (Hypothetical Leads)



The request. Map the association so that the database records who leads whom.
The design. Both ends of Figure 6.7 attach to one class, so both ends are the operator table, and the rule that the foreign key goes in the table of the many end no longer says enough. The question becomes which rows hold the foreign key, and whose key they hold. A cloud instance diagram answers it, as Figure 5.13 did for the bill of materials, by drawing the class once for each role. Figure 6.8 draws the six operators twice: on the left as crew members, on the right as leads. Each line is one link, from a crew member to the crew member’s lead.






Figure 6.8: The Six Operators, Drawn Once as Crew Members and Once as Leads (Hypothetical Leads)



Read Figure 6.8 from the crew-member cloud. Every dot has at most one line: James Carter’s goes to Maria Lopez, Maria Lopez’s to Robert Hayes, and Robert Hayes’s dot has none. Each operator’s link can therefore be recorded as one value in that operator’s own row, the row of the crew member. The row is the crew member’s, and the value it holds is the lead’s key: the rule of one-to-many, read once per role. Read the other cloud, and the dots have any number of lines: Robert Hayes has two, and James Carter none. A lead’s row cannot hold its crew, just as a customer’s row cannot hold its orders.
Four details complete the mapping. The foreign key is named for the role of the operator it refers to, lead_fk, since a column named operator_fk would not say which of the two operators it means, and crew_fk would name the wrong one. It refers to operator_pk in its own table. The 0..1 at the lead end lets it be NULL, for the operator with no lead. A CHECK that lead_fk differs from operator_pk implements the rule that no operator is the operator’s own lead, which the class model states only in words. And by step 6 the foreign key refuses a deletion: a lead’s row cannot be deleted while any row’s lead_fk holds its key. Listing 6.8 gives the relational schema; the column is hypothetical, since the book’s database records no leads.



Listing 6.8: The Operator Table with Each Operator’s Lead (Hypothetical)


operator (operator_pk, employee_number, name, hire_date,
          lead_fk)
    primary key: operator_pk
    alternate key: employee_number
    lead_fk references operator_pk in operator,
        may be NULL



The result. With the column of Listing 6.8 added, each operator’s row holds the key of its lead:



Table 6.5: Each Operator’s Row with Its Lead’s Key (Hypothetical Leads)


SELECT operator_pk, employee_number, name, lead_fk
FROM production.operator
ORDER BY operator_pk;





operator_pk


employee_number


name


lead_fk

E-203


Linda Nguyen


4

NULL

E-206

A key means nothing to a reader, so a query that shows each operator beside the lead joins operator to itself, a self-join (Section 3.6), once as the crew member and once as the lead. A left join (Section 3.7) keeps the operator who has no lead:



Table 6.6: Each Operator and the Operator’s Lead (Hypothetical Leads)


SELECT o.name AS crew_member, l.name AS lead_name
FROM production.operator AS o
LEFT JOIN production.operator AS l
  ON l.operator_pk = o.lead_fk
ORDER BY o.employee_number;





crew_member


lead_name






Maria Lopez


Robert Hayes




James Carter


Maria Lopez




Linda Nguyen


Robert Hayes




Robert Hayes


NULL




Aisha Patel


Linda Nguyen




Tom Becker


Maria Lopez








The check. The table has six operators, so Table 6.5 has six rows, and Table 6.6 one for each of them. Figure 6.8 has five lines, and Table 6.5 has five values of lead_fk, one per line; the sixth row, Robert Hayes’s, is NULL, his dot with no line.
Interpretation. Robert Hayes leads Maria Lopez and Linda Nguyen, who lead the rest of the plant’s operators. A lead’s crew is found from the other side, as the rows whose lead_fk is the lead’s key, just as a customer’s orders are found as the rows whose customer_fk is the customer’s key.
Where it breaks. The CHECK refuses an operator as the operator’s own lead:

UPDATE production.operator
SET lead_fk = operator_pk
WHERE employee_number = 'E-204';
ERROR:  new row for relation "operator" violates check constraint "operator_check"
DETAIL:  Failing row contains (4, E-204, Robert Hayes, 2019-10-07, 4).

A longer loop is accepted, however. Were Robert Hayes’s lead set to James Carter, every row would still satisfy the foreign key and the CHECK, yet the chain of leads would never end, and a recursive query that follows it, like the one of Section 4.6, would never end either, unless a bound on its depth or a CYCLE clause stopped it. That the leads form a hierarchy is a rule the tables leave to a checking query.

The bill of materials is the other kind. Figure 6.9 shows it, a recursive association between an assembly and its components, with its association class BomLine.






Figure 6.9: Mapping a Recursive Association with an Association Class



Its ends attach to a class and its subclass. A part may be a component of many assemblies, so, unlike an operator’s lead, a part’s links cannot be recorded as one value in its own row. The association in Figure 6.9 is many-to-many with an association class, so it maps to a table of its own, bom_line, with two foreign keys and the attribute quantity_per. Both foreign keys refer to parts, so they cannot both be named part_fk; the note names them for the roles at the ends of the line, assembly_fk and component_fk, which are the two role clouds of Figure 5.13. The pair is UNIQUE, as for any association class, and a CHECK that the two differ stops a part from being its own component, a rule the class model states only in words. The complete relational schema of Listing 6.9 shows both constraints.




Listing 6.9: The Complete Relational Schema of the Bill of Materials


bom_line
    bom_line_pk   INTEGER       not NULL, generated
    assembly_fk   INTEGER       not NULL
    component_fk  INTEGER       not NULL
    quantity_per  NUMERIC(8,3)  not NULL
    primary key: bom_line_pk
    alternate key: (assembly_fk, component_fk)
    assembly_fk references part_fk in manufactured_part,
        must not be NULL
    component_fk references part_pk in part,
        must not be NULL
    assembly_fk: on delete no action, on update no action
    component_fk: on delete no action, on update no action
    check: quantity_per > 0
    check: assembly_fk <> component_fk




Notice that the two foreign keys of Listing 6.9 refer to different tables, although both lead to parts. assembly_fk refers to manufactured_part, since the assembly end of Figure 6.9 attaches to ManufacturedPart, and component_fk refers to part. The generalization between the two, mapped in Section 6.5, is what makes both refer to the same parts.
The two recursive associations of this section thus map by the rule of Section 6.3, asked of a class drawn once per role: where can a link be recorded as one value? An operator has at most one lead, so the link fits in the operator’s own row, and operator refers to itself. A part has many assemblies, so its links need a table of their own, with two foreign keys to parts.


6.3.6 Compositions and aggregations
Figure 6.10 shows the composition of an order’s lines in the order, from Figure 5.11.






Figure 6.10: Mapping a Composition



A composition is an association, so it maps by its multiplicities first: the 1 at the CustomerOrder end and the 1..* at the OrderLine end make it one-to-many, with the foreign key customer_order_fk in order_line, NOT NULL. The filled diamond adds step 6 of Figure 6.1: since a part cannot outlive its whole, deleting an order deletes its lines, and the foreign key is declared ON DELETE CASCADE, as the note says. Table 2.6 listed cascading as one of the responses a designer may choose; composition is the case that calls for it. Listing 6.10 gives the complete relational schema of the order_line table as the book’s database holds it at stage D3.




Listing 6.10: The Complete Relational Schema of the Order Line Table


order_line
    order_line_pk      INTEGER        not NULL, generated
    customer_order_fk  INTEGER        not NULL
    line_number        INTEGER        not NULL
    product_fk         INTEGER        not NULL
    quantity           INTEGER        not NULL
    unit_price         NUMERIC(10,2)  not NULL
    primary key: order_line_pk
    alternate key: (customer_order_fk, line_number)
    customer_order_fk references customer_order_pk in
        customer_order, must not be NULL
    product_fk references product_pk in product,
        must not be NULL
    customer_order_fk: on delete cascade, on update
        no action
    product_fk: on delete no action, on update no action
    check: line_number > 0
    check: quantity > 0
    check: unit_price > 0




The composition of Figure 6.10 is the line customer_order_fk: on delete cascade. The other foreign key, to product, maps an ordinary association and refuses, which Example 6.3 interprets. An aggregation, the hollow diamond, maps like an ordinary association, and its foreign key refuses, since its parts outlive the whole: machine.work_center_fk refuses the deletion of a work center that still has machines.


6.3.7 Ternary associations
A ternary association maps to a table with three foreign keys. Each link of Figure 5.14 connects an operator, a machine, and a work order, so each row holds three keys, and the attribute of the association class Run of Figure 5.15, the hours, joins them. Which columns form a key depends on the multiplicities. With 0..* at every end, as in Figure 5.15, a link can be recorded only in a table of its own, as for a many-to-many association, and the three foreign keys together are its key. The runs are hypothetical, so Listing 6.11 is written out by hand.



Listing 6.11: The Relational Schema of the Ternary Association (Hypothetical)


run (run_pk, operator_fk, machine_fk, work_order_fk, hours)
    primary key: run_pk
    alternate key: (operator_fk, machine_fk, work_order_fk)
    operator_fk references operator_pk in operator,
        must not be NULL
    machine_fk references machine_pk in machine,
        must not be NULL
    work_order_fk references work_order_pk in work_order,
        must not be NULL



Each ring of Figure 5.14 is one row of run, and its three lines are the row’s three foreign keys. The alternate key of the three says that one association holds at most one link among a given operator, machine, and work order. A plant that records several runs of the same three on different days would add the date to the key, or promote the run to a class of its own, as the review of Example 5.3 suggested. The class Run then maps by step 1, and its association with each of the three classes by the one-to-many rule. That gives the same columns with no key over the three foreign keys, so the table holds any number of runs of the same three.
The following example maps a whole model and checks the result against it.

Example 6.3 (Mapping the refined order model of stage D3) The system. The class model of Figure 5.11: customers, their orders, the order lines composed in each order, and the products the lines are for.
The request. Produce the tables that implement the model, with their keys, foreign keys, and deletion rules.
Let’s apply the rules one construct at a time, and record where each element of the model goes:



Table 6.7: Mapping the Refined Order Model, Construct by Construct










Model construct
Rule
Result in the tables




Classes Customer, CustomerOrder, OrderLine, Product
a table each, with a surrogate key
customer, customer_order, order_line, product, each with a _pk


Business identifiers customerNumber, orderNumber, productNumber
a UNIQUE column
alternate keys


requestedShipDate [0..1]
a column that allows NULL
requested_ship_date may be NULL


The other attributes: name, city, state, orderDate, description, listPrice, quantity, unitPrice
a column each, NOT NULL
name, city, state, order_date, description, list_price, quantity, unit_price


Customer 1 to 0..* CustomerOrder
a foreign key at the many end, NOT NULL
customer_order.customer_fk


CustomerOrder 1 to 1..* OrderLine, a composition
a foreign key at the many end, NOT NULL, cascading
order_line.customer_order_fk, ON DELETE CASCADE


OrderLine 0..* to 1 Product
a foreign key at the many end, NOT NULL
order_line.product_fk






The order line’s lineNumber is left for Section 6.4, where it becomes part of a key. The relational schema of the four tables, as the book’s database holds them at stage D3, is:




Listing 6.12: The Relational Schema of the Refined Order Model


customer (customer_pk, customer_number, name, city, state)
    primary key: customer_pk
    alternate key: customer_number

customer_order (customer_order_pk, order_number, order_date,
                requested_ship_date, customer_fk)
    primary key: customer_order_pk
    alternate key: order_number
    customer_fk references customer_pk in customer,
        must not be NULL

product (product_pk, product_number, description,
         list_price)
    primary key: product_pk
    alternate key: product_number

order_line (order_line_pk, customer_order_fk, line_number,
            product_fk, quantity, unit_price)
    primary key: order_line_pk
    alternate key: (customer_order_fk, line_number)
    customer_order_fk references customer_order_pk in
        customer_order, must not be NULL
    product_fk references product_pk in product,
        must not be NULL




The check. Every row of Table 6.7 appears in a line of Listing 6.12, and every column of the listing comes from a row of the ledger: the surrogate keys from its first row, the attributes from the next three, and the foreign keys from the last three. The one exception is line_number, which Section 6.4 accounts for. The deletion rules are in the complete schema of Listing 6.10: the on delete cascade of customer_order_fk is the composition’s diamond, and the no action of product_fk says that deleting a product that has been ordered is refused.
Interpretation. The two deletion rules say what the business can and cannot undo. An order can be canceled with its lines in one statement; a product that customers have ordered cannot be removed, since the order history refers to it. For example, order SO-5012 of stage D5 has two lines and no shipments:



Table 6.8: The Lines of Order SO-5012


SELECT o.order_number, l.line_number,
       l.product_fk, l.quantity
FROM distribution.customer_order AS o
JOIN distribution.order_line AS l
  ON l.customer_order_fk = o.customer_order_pk
WHERE o.order_number = 'SO-5012';





order_number


line_number


product_fk


quantity






SO-5012


1


3


4




SO-5012


2


2


2








Both rows of Table 6.8 refer to the order through customer_order_fk. If the order is deleted, the cascade deletes these two order lines with it, and nothing else: the order’s customer and the lines’ products are untouched, since their foreign keys point the other way. Chapter 8 presents the DELETE statement and shows the cascade at work.
Where it breaks. The cascade stops at the order lines. An order that has been shipped has shipments that refer to it, and their foreign key refuses, so deleting a shipped order fails, as it should: a shipment is not part of an order, and its record must survive.

6.4 Mapping qualified associations
This section continues step 4 of Figure 6.1 with the qualified association, which becomes a composite key.
Figure 6.11 shows the order line qualified by its line number, from Figure 5.12.






Figure 6.11: Mapping a Qualified Association



Recall that a qualifier reduces the multiplicity at the far end: in Figure 6.11, given an order and a line number, there is at most one order line, the 0..1 at the OrderLine end. The qualifier’s meaning is a uniqueness rule, and a table states uniqueness with a key. A qualified association therefore maps like the association without its qualifier, and the qualifier becomes a column that, with the foreign key to the qualifying class, forms a key. For the order line, the qualifier becomes the column line_number of order_line, and the key is UNIQUE (customer_order_fk, line_number), as the note of Figure 6.11 says: the alternate key of Listing 6.10. The foreign key customer_order_fk is the one the composition already put in order_line; the qualifier adds only its column and the key. Listing 6.13 gives the resulting relational schema of the order line.




Listing 6.13: The Relational Schema of the Qualified Order Line


order_line (order_line_pk, customer_order_fk, line_number,
            product_fk, quantity, unit_price)
    primary key: order_line_pk
    alternate key: (customer_order_fk, line_number)
    customer_order_fk references customer_order_pk in
        customer_order, must not be NULL
    product_fk references product_pk in product,
        must not be NULL




Read Listing 6.13 against Figure 6.11. The qualifier box lineNumber is the column line_number, and the 0..1 it produces at the OrderLine end is the alternate key (customer_order_fk, line_number): with a given order and line number, at most one row. The rest of the listing comes from the other two associations of the order line, with its order and its product.
The key is what keeps the qualifier’s meaning. Mapping the association without the qualifier’s key, as a plain column, would let two lines of one order share a line number, which the model forbids. It is the order line’s version of the rule of one link per pair: here, one line per pair of order and line number.
The same rule maps the routing of Figure 5.16. An operation is qualified by its operation number within its manufactured part, so operation has the column operation_number and the key UNIQUE (manufactured_part_fk, operation_number); operation 10 of the axle and operation 10 of the frame are different operations. The composition of the routing makes the same foreign key cascade, so an operation goes with its part’s routing. Listing 6.14 gives the complete relational schema of the operation table of stage P3.




Listing 6.14: The Complete Relational Schema of the Operation Table


operation
    operation_pk          INTEGER       not NULL, generated
    manufactured_part_fk  INTEGER       not NULL
    operation_number      INTEGER       not NULL
    description           VARCHAR(40)   not NULL
    setup_minutes         NUMERIC(6,1)  not NULL
    run_minutes_per_unit  NUMERIC(6,2)  not NULL
    work_center_fk        INTEGER       not NULL
    primary key: operation_pk
    alternate key: (manufactured_part_fk, operation_number)
    manufactured_part_fk references part_fk in
        manufactured_part, must not be NULL
    work_center_fk references work_center_pk in work_center,
        must not be NULL
    manufactured_part_fk: on delete cascade, on update
        no action
    work_center_fk: on delete no action, on update no action
    check: operation_number > 0
    check: setup_minutes >= 0
    check: run_minutes_per_unit > 0




The qualifier of Figure 5.16 is again an alternate key, (manufactured_part_fk, operation_number), and the filled diamond is again on delete cascade. The foreign key work_center_fk maps the ordinary association of an operation with the work center that performs it, and it refuses: a work center that some routing uses cannot be deleted.
A qualifier often looks like an identifier, and it is one, but only within its qualifying object. A line number, an operation number, a bin code within a warehouse: none is unique alone, and none should be made UNIQUE alone. The test is the one Section 2.2 applied to candidate keys: ask whether the business promises uniqueness for the qualifier alone, or only within something.
An {ordered} end (Section 5.4) maps the same way. The order becomes a column, a sequence number, in the table at the ordered end, and the foreign key with the sequence number is an alternate key, as if the association were qualified by the number. A query that wants the objects in order sorts by it; the rows themselves have no order (Section 2.1).

6.5 Mapping generalization
This section illustrates step 5 of Figure 6.1: how a superclass and its subclasses become tables.
Figure 6.12 shows the generalization of stage P1, in which every part is either manufactured or purchased (Figure 5.17), with notes on the mapping the book’s database uses.






Figure 6.12: Mapping a Generalization, Table per Class



A generalization has no single obvious mapping, because a table has no notion of one kind of row being a kind of another. There are three ways to map it, and each keeps some of what the model says and gives up some. We map the parts of stage P1 all three ways.

6.5.1 A table for each class
The first mapping, the one of Figure 6.12 and of the book’s database, gives each class a table of its own. The superclass table part holds the superclass’s attributes, and each subclass table holds the subclass’s own attributes and a key. The key is the link: a subclass table’s primary key is also a foreign key to the superclass table, so a manufactured part and the part it is have the same key value in both tables. Listing 6.15 gives the resulting relational schema.




Listing 6.15: The Relational Schema of the Generalization, Table per Class


part (part_pk, part_number, description, unit_of_measure,
      standard_cost)
    primary key: part_pk
    alternate key: part_number

manufactured_part (part_fk, lot_size)
    primary key: part_fk
    part_fk references part_pk in part, must not be NULL

purchased_part (part_fk, lead_time_days)
    primary key: part_fk
    part_fk references part_pk in part, must not be NULL




Notice the name of the subclass tables’ key, part_fk. It is the primary key of manufactured_part and a foreign key to part at once, and the book names it for what it refers to, so the link to the superclass is visible in the listing. The generalization’s line of Figure 6.12 is that foreign key: every manufactured part is a part.
An object of a subclass is split across two tables, so a query that wants a whole manufactured part, its inherited attributes and its own, joins them on the shared key:



Table 6.9: The Manufactured Parts, Whole


SELECT p.part_number, p.description, m.lot_size
FROM production.part AS p
JOIN production.manufactured_part AS m
  ON m.part_fk = p.part_pk
ORDER BY p.part_number;





part_number

The table-per-class mapping keeps what the model says about associations. An association attached to a subclass maps to a foreign key that refers to the subclass’s table, and one attached to the superclass to the superclass’s table. Recall from Listing 6.9 that assembly_fk refers to manufactured_part and component_fk to part: the database itself enforces that only a manufactured part can be an assembly, while any part can be a component.
What the mapping does not keep is {disjoint, complete}. Nothing in Listing 6.15 stops a part from having a row in both subclass tables, which would break disjoint, or in neither, which would break complete. A query can find such parts, using the EXISTS of Section 3.8:



Table 6.10: Parts That Break Disjoint or Complete


SELECT p.part_number
FROM production.part AS p
WHERE (EXISTS (SELECT *
               FROM production.manufactured_part AS m
               WHERE m.part_fk = p.part_pk)
       AND EXISTS (SELECT *
                   FROM production.purchased_part AS u
                   WHERE u.part_fk = p.part_pk))
   OR (NOT EXISTS (SELECT *
                   FROM production.manufactured_part AS m
                   WHERE m.part_fk = p.part_pk)
       AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT *
                       FROM production.purchased_part AS u
                       WHERE u.part_fk = p.part_pk));





part_number












Table 6.10 is empty: every part of stage P1 is in exactly one subclass table. The query does not prevent a violation; it finds one, and it is the kind of check that step 7 of Figure 6.1 runs, and that the book’s own tests run on every stage.


6.5.2 A table for each subclass only
The second mapping drops the superclass table and repeats its attributes in each subclass table. Since the book’s database does not use it, Listing 6.16 is written out by hand.



Listing 6.16: The Generalization Mapped to Subclass Tables Only (Hypothetical)


manufactured_part (manufactured_part_pk, part_number,
                   description, unit_of_measure,
                   standard_cost, lot_size)
    primary key: manufactured_part_pk
    alternate key: part_number

purchased_part (purchased_part_pk, part_number, description,
                unit_of_measure, standard_cost,
                lead_time_days)
    primary key: purchased_part_pk
    alternate key: part_number



Each whole object is now one row, with no join, and a part cannot be in two subclasses unless it is entered twice. But the mapping loses the superclass. part_number is unique within each table, not across both, so a manufactured part and a purchased part could share a number. Worse, an association attached to the superclass has nowhere to go: component_fk must refer to any part, and a foreign key refers to one table. The bill of materials cannot be mapped at all. This mapping suits a superclass that no association and no query treats as a whole, which is rare in industrial data.


6.5.3 One table for the whole hierarchy
The third mapping puts every class’s attributes in one table, with a column that says which subclass each row belongs to. Such a column is called a discriminator. Listing 6.17 writes it out by hand.



Listing 6.17: The Generalization Mapped to One Table (Hypothetical)


part (part_pk, part_number, description, unit_of_measure,
      standard_cost, part_kind, lot_size, lead_time_days)
    primary key: part_pk
    alternate key: part_number
    may be NULL: lot_size, lead_time_days
    check: part_kind IN ('manufactured', 'purchased')
    check: (part_kind = 'manufactured'
            AND lot_size IS NOT NULL
            AND lead_time_days IS NULL)
        OR (part_kind = 'purchased'
            AND lead_time_days IS NOT NULL
            AND lot_size IS NULL)



Here disjoint and complete are enforced, and by a single column: each row has exactly one part_kind, and the first check allows only the two subclasses. The second check ties each kind to its own columns. The cost is in the NULLs, since every row leaves the other kind’s columns empty, and in the associations: assembly_fk can refer only to part, so the database can no longer stop a purchased part from being an assembly. You may read in older material that this mapping violates a normal form. It does not; every column still depends on the key. What it gives up is the ability of foreign keys to tell the subclasses apart.
Table 6.11 compares the three mappings.



Table 6.11: The Three Mappings of Generalization Compared
