The book maps every generalization a table per class, because the rows of Table 6.11 about foreign keys decide it for HG Industries: the bill of materials needs a foreign key to the superclass and one to a subclass at once. You should decide each generalization by the same test. Ask which associations attach to the superclass and which to the subclasses, and choose the mapping that lets the database enforce them.

title: 6  From Class Models to Tables
text:
6.6 Choosing and naming keys
This section returns to step 3 of Figure 6.1, a table’s identity, to weigh surrogate keys against natural keys and to state the book’s naming conventions.
A table’s primary key can come from the data or be invented for the table. A natural key, one made of the class’s own attributes, uses what the business already has: a customer’s number, a part’s number. A surrogate key, as Section 2.2 defined it, is invented: PostgreSQL generates it and it means nothing outside the database. Blaha and Premerlani call the two value-based and existence-based identity (Blaha and Premerlani 1998), and both work. Choosing between them is a design decision, made table by table, and one schema may use both. A surrogate key is a sound default, for four reasons:

A surrogate key never changes. A natural key can: a customer renumbered after a merger would need every order’s foreign key changed with it. Recall from Section 2.3 that PostgreSQL refuses even to update a generated key.
A surrogate key is one column. A natural key of a dependent class grows as the dependence deepens: an order line’s natural key is its order’s key and its line number, and a shipment line’s natural key would repeat all of that.
Every foreign key is then one column of the same type, named in the same way, which makes joins uniform to write and to read.
A surrogate key does not depend on the business’s identifiers being right. A customer entered with a mistyped number can be corrected without touching any reference to it.

A surrogate key does not replace the natural key; it adds to it. The business’s identifier is still a candidate key, and without its UNIQUE constraint the table would accept two rows for customer C-1001, each with its own surrogate key, and nothing would notice. Thus, whenever you give a table a surrogate key, you should declare its natural keys as alternate keys, as every table of the book’s database does.
A natural key earns its place, as a primary key or as the column a foreign key refers to, when the reasons above are weak for it: the business assigns it, it never changes and is never reused, it is short and one column, and people read it. The two-letter state codes of the customer table, the units of measure of parts, and the locker numbers of Example 6.1 qualify; a customer number that a merger might change does not. A foreign key may refer to any column declared UNIQUE, not only to a primary key, so a table can keep a surrogate primary key and still let other tables refer to its natural key. The referring row then carries an identifier that people read, and a question that wants only that identifier needs no join, as Table 6.3 showed. Its price is the first reason above: if the identifier ever changes, every referring row must change with it, which cascading the update (Section 2.3) can do but which a design should not have to rely on.
Many databases therefore mix the two kinds: surrogate keys for the business’s main things, such as customers, orders, and parts, and natural keys for codes and for stable identifiers that people read. The book’s database uses surrogate keys throughout, and stores codes such as states in the referring table itself rather than in a table of their own; Exercise 6.11 asks when a table of codes is worth having. That is one consistent policy, chosen so that every example follows the same rules. It is not the only sound one, and you should choose the keys of your own designs by the reasons of this section.
The names of keys follow five rules, which make the book’s schema readable without its diagram. Like the choice of surrogate keys, they are a convention: teams adopt their own, and every convention has exceptions, which a design should state when it makes one.

A table’s surrogate key is named for the table with the suffix _pk: customer_pk, order_line_pk.
A foreign key is named for the table it refers to, with the suffix _fk: customer_fk refers to customer_pk.
When a table refers to another twice, or refers to its own class, each foreign key is named for its role instead: assembly_fk and component_fk in bom_line.
A subclass table’s key, both its primary key and its reference to the superclass, is named for the superclass, part_fk, and a table that refers to the subclass names its foreign key for the subclass, manufactured_part_fk.
A foreign key that refers to a natural key keeps that key’s name, since it holds the key’s value: locker_number in Listing 6.6.

Surrogate keys have a further cost, which the following example makes concrete.

Example 6.4 (Seeing what single-column foreign keys cannot enforce) The system. The shipments of stage D5. A shipment is made for one order, and each shipment line ships a quantity of one order line.
The request. Every shipment line must ship a line of its own shipment’s order: shipment SH-9004, made for order SO-5004, must not ship a line of order SO-5001. Can the tables enforce that rule?
The rule involves two paths from a shipment line to an order: through its shipment (shipment_line.shipment_fk to shipment.customer_order_fk) and through its order line (shipment_line.order_line_fk to order_line.customer_order_fk). The rule says the two paths must reach the same order. With surrogate keys, each foreign key of shipment_line is one number, and nothing in the tables compares where the two paths lead. A query can check the rule by joining along both paths:



Table 6.12: Shipment Lines That Ship Another Order’s Line


SELECT sl.shipment_line_pk, s.shipment_number,
       l.customer_order_fk AS line_order,
       s.customer_order_fk AS shipment_order
FROM distribution.shipment_line AS sl
JOIN distribution.shipment AS s
  ON s.shipment_pk = sl.shipment_fk
JOIN distribution.order_line AS l
  ON l.order_line_pk = sl.order_line_fk
WHERE l.customer_order_fk <> s.customer_order_fk;





shipment_line_pk


shipment_number


line_order


shipment_order












Table 6.12 is empty, so the data of stage D5 obeys the rule, but only because it was loaded correctly: the database would have accepted a line that broke it.
Composite foreign keys can enforce the rule. If a shipment line holds its order’s key itself, one foreign key can pair it with the shipment and another with the order line. Natural keys supply such keys directly. With value-based identity, an order line’s key is its order and line number, so a shipment line that refers to an order line must hold the order’s key, and a shipment’s key can be made to carry its order’s key too. Listing 6.18 writes the two tables out by hand.



Listing 6.18: Shipment Lines with Composite Foreign Keys (Hypothetical)


shipment (shipment_number, customer_order_fk, shipped_on,
          carrier, warehouse_fk)
    primary key: shipment_number
    alternate key: (shipment_number, customer_order_fk)
    customer_order_fk references customer_order_pk in
        customer_order, must not be NULL
    warehouse_fk references warehouse_pk in warehouse,
        must not be NULL

shipment_line (shipment_number, customer_order_fk,
               line_number, quantity)
    primary key: (shipment_number, customer_order_fk,
                  line_number)
    (shipment_number, customer_order_fk) references
        (shipment_number, customer_order_fk) in shipment
    (customer_order_fk, line_number) references
        (customer_order_fk, line_number) in order_line



In Listing 6.18, the shipment line holds one customer_order_fk, and both of its composite foreign keys use it. The first says the shipment was made for that order; the second says the order line belongs to that order. A shipment line that shipped another order’s line would need two different values in one column, which is impossible. The rule is enforced by the structure of the keys.
The natural keys are a convenience here, not a requirement. The same two composite foreign keys work beside surrogate primary keys, if shipment_line gains a customer_order_fk column that must not be NULL and shipment and order_line each declare UNIQUE the pair of columns that a foreign key refers to. The column must not be NULL because PostgreSQL does not check a composite foreign key when one of its columns is NULL; a line with no order would pass both foreign keys. That is the real cost of surrogate keys: they do not carry the order’s key along, so a designer who wants the rule enforced must add a NOT NULL column and two constraints that the tables would not otherwise need.
The check. Table 6.12 joins along the two paths that the rule compares, one join per foreign key, and keeps only the rows where they disagree, so an empty result means that every shipment line passes.
Interpretation. The book keeps its surrogate keys, without the added column, and checks the rule with a query, a choice made for the reasons listed above. The example shows what the choice gives up, and a designer who judges this rule important enough can have the database enforce it with composite foreign keys. The tests that load the book’s database run the same check on stage D5.
Where it breaks. A check query finds a violation after it has happened; it does not stop one. A program that records shipments must therefore apply the rule itself, as the programs of Chapter 10 can.

With the keys chosen and named, a mapping is complete: every table has its columns, its keys, its foreign keys, and their deletion rules. Chapter 7 presents the review of step 7 in full, and Chapter 8 writes the result as CREATE TABLE statements.

title: 6  From Class Models to Tables
text:
6.7 Summary
Mapping follows seven steps, from a reviewed class model to a complete relational schema. Classes, attributes, identity, associations, generalization, deletion rules, and a check, in that order; a check that fails sends the designer back to the model.
Each class maps to a table, and each attribute to a column. The column’s type and constraints implement the attribute’s domain: NOT NULL from a multiplicity of one, UNIQUE from a business identifier, and CHECK for a domain narrower than its type. Each table gets a primary key the class model does not name.
An association maps according to where a link can be recorded as one value. A one-to-many association maps to a foreign key at the many end, NOT NULL when the one end’s minimum is one; a one-to-one association to a UNIQUE foreign key; a many-to-many association, with its association class, to a table of its own whose foreign keys together are a key. A recursive association maps the same way, its foreign keys named for their roles, so a recursive one-to-many association gives a table a foreign key to itself. A composition’s foreign key cascades a deletion.
The side of a one-to-one association is a design decision. When the minimums do not settle it, the dependent object, then the end that could become many, then the table users start from decide where the foreign key goes. One foreign key enforces one end fully and only the maximum of the other, and one that refers to an identifier people read saves the everyday question a join.
A qualifier maps to a composite key. The qualifier becomes a column that, with the foreign key to the qualifying class, is UNIQUE, which keeps the qualifier’s meaning in the tables.
A generalization maps in one of three ways, each keeping part of the model. A table per class keeps every association but leaves {disjoint, complete} to a checking query; subclass tables alone lose the superclass; one table with a discriminator enforces the subclasses but not associations to one of them. The associations decide which to use.
A table’s key is chosen, and a schema may mix surrogate and natural keys. A surrogate key never changes and is always one column, which makes it a sound default; a natural key earns its place when it is stable, short, and read by people, and a foreign key may refer to it. Either way, the natural key’s UNIQUE constraint is what stops duplicates. Keys are named for their tables, _pk and _fk, or for their roles. A rule comparing two paths to the same row needs composite foreign keys, which natural keys supply and surrogate keys need an added column for; without them, a query must check the rule.
Chapter 7 reviews the tables that a mapping produces, and Chapter 8 creates them.

text:
6.8 Exercises

Exercise 6.1 Specify the domains of the CustomerOrder class of Figure 5.1 in the form of Table 6.2, and give the SQL type and constraints of each column. Then compare your result with the complete relational schema of Listing 2.2, and explain each difference.


Exercise 6.2 Map the Shipment class of the stage D5 class model of Figure 5.19, with its associations to CustomerOrder and Warehouse and its association with OrderLine (Shipment 0..* to 1..* OrderLine), whose association class is ShipmentLine, in the form of Table 6.7. Give the keys of the shipment_line table. Say which foreign keys cascade and which refuse by step 6 of Figure 6.1, and why.


Exercise 6.3 Map the association class Certification between Operator and Machine (Exercise 5.5).

Give the table, its columns, and its keys.
Explain which constraint enforces the rule of one certification per operator and machine.
If the business decided to keep a history of certifications, how would the class model change, and how would the table’s keys change?



Exercise 6.4 The class model of Figure 5.16 has multiplicity 1 at the WorkCenter end of its aggregation with Machine, and the table machine has work_center_fk declared NOT NULL.

What does that say about a machine that has been bought but not yet installed, or taken out of service and stored?
Change the model so that such a machine can be recorded, and give the change to the table.
Should the foreign key cascade? Explain from the difference between aggregation and composition.



Exercise 6.5 Each machine may have at most one maintenance plan, and each plan belongs to exactly one machine (Exercise 5.17).

In which table does the foreign key go, and why?
Which two constraints does it carry, and what would go wrong without each?
Could the foreign key be placed in the other table instead? What would it cost?



Exercise 6.6 A trucking fleet tracks its toll transponders. The toll authority issues each transponder with a serial number printed on its case, and the fleet keeps no spares: each truck carries exactly one transponder, and each transponder is mounted in exactly one truck. When a truck is retired, its transponder is moved to the truck that replaces it. Trucks are identified by a fleet number painted on the cab, such as T-12.

Draw the association with its multiplicities. Do the minimums, or the first question of Section 6.3.3, decide where the foreign key goes? Why or why not?
The fleet manager says that a truck that runs in a second toll region may soon need a second transponder. Where does the foreign key go, and why?
Dispatch’s most frequent question starts from a truck and wants the truck’s own details (its model and driver) with the serial number of its transponder. Which table would the third question of Section 6.3.3 then point to, and does that change your choice in (b)?
Write the relational schema of the two tables for your choice, with the foreign key referring to an identifier people read. What does that choice cost, and which rule of the association can the schema not enforce?



Exercise 6.7 Map the bins of Exercise 5.7, qualified by bin code within a warehouse. Give the table, and explain why bin_code must not be declared UNIQUE by itself.


Exercise 6.8 Map the generalization of Figure 6.12 to one table, as in Listing 6.17.

Explain how the two CHECK constraints enforce disjoint and complete.
Which rule of the bill of materials can the database no longer enforce, and why?
A manufactured part’s lot size is required. How does the single table enforce that, and how does the table-per-class mapping of Listing 6.15?



Exercise 6.9 The query of Table 6.10 finds parts that break disjoint or complete.

Explain each half of its condition, and say which rule each half checks.
Rewrite it as two queries, one for each rule, using INTERSECT for one and EXCEPT for the other (Section 3.9).



Exercise 6.10 HG Industries decides to record, for each machine, whether it is CNC or manual. A CNC machine has a controller model and a program memory in megabytes; a manual machine has neither. Certifications on CNC machines, and only on them, must record the controller version the operator was trained on. Record that version in a second association class, CncCertification, between Operator and the subclass for CNC machines; the association class Certification between Operator and Machine stays as it is.
Model the change as a generalization of Machine, choose a mapping, and justify the choice with Table 6.11. Give the resulting relational schema.


Exercise 6.11 The customer table stores each customer’s state as a two-letter code, and nothing stops a code such as ZZ.

Design a table of states with the code as its natural primary key, and change customer to refer to it. Give the relational schema.
Why is a natural key a sound choice here, when the book’s database uses surrogate keys everywhere else?
What does the new table give the business besides a check on the code?



Exercise 6.12 A plant’s access system records who opens which door. Each employee has an employee number, assigned at hiring and never reused, and carries a badge whose number is printed on it and recorded with the employee; a lost badge is replaced with a badge of a new number. Each employee belongs to a department, identified by a three-letter code such as MNT that the plant has used for twenty years. Each door has a number stenciled on it, such as D-14, and doors are never renumbered. Each entry in the access log records a badge reading at a door at a moment.

For each of the tables employee, department, door, and access_entry, choose a surrogate or a natural primary key, and justify each choice by the reasons of Section 6.6.
For each foreign key, say whether it should refer to a surrogate or to a natural key, and why.
Should access_entry record the badge number or the employee? What goes wrong with the other choice when a badge is replaced?



Exercise 6.13 HG Industries starts moving stock between its warehouses. A transfer moves a quantity of one product from one warehouse to another on a date.

Model the transfer, with its associations and multiplicities.
Map it to a table, naming its foreign keys by the rules of Section 6.6, and give the relational schema.
Add a constraint that stops a transfer from a warehouse to itself.



Exercise 6.14 Using Listing 6.18:

Suppose shipment SH-9004, made for order SO-5004, were given a line for line 1 of order SO-5001. Write the values the shipment line would need, and say which foreign key rejects it.
What does the natural-key design cost, compared with the surrogate keys of Listing 2.4? Name two costs.


The remaining exercises map the models of chapter 5’s exercises outside HG Industries. Each figure is the instructor’s model of that exercise, so that your mapping does not depend on your own answer to it. For each, give the relational schema of every table in the notation of Section 2.4, with its primary key, its alternate keys, and each foreign key with the table it refers to and whether it may be NULL; follow the book’s naming rules (Section 6.6); and say, for each foreign key, what happens when the row it refers to is deleted.

Exercise 6.15 Map the tool crib of Exercise 5.18, drawn in Figure 6.13.






Figure 6.13: The Tool Crib (Model for Exercise 5.18)




Give the relational schema of the three tables.
The note says a tool has at most one checkout without a return time. Can a UNIQUE constraint on tool_fk enforce it? What would it forbid?
PostgreSQL can enforce the rule with a unique index on tool_fk restricted to the rows WHERE returned_at IS NULL. Explain what that index allows and what it refuses.



Exercise 6.16 Map the gauges and calibrations of Exercise 5.19, drawn in Figure 6.14.






Figure 6.14: Gauge Calibration (Model for Exercise 5.19)




Give the relational schema.
What does the qualifier on certificateNumber become? Why must certificate_number not be UNIQUE by itself?
A laboratory loses its accreditation and is to be removed from the database. What should happen to its calibrations, and which delete response gives that?



Exercise 6.17 Map the kanban loop of Exercise 5.20, drawn in Figure 6.15.






Figure 6.15: The Kanban Loop (Model for Exercise 5.20)




Give the relational schema. For the association of Container and Card, say in which table the foreign key goes and why (Section 6.3.2).
Which multiplicity of the model can no table definition enforce? How would you check it with a query?



Exercise 6.18 Map the clinic of Exercise 5.21, drawn in Figure 6.16.






Figure 6.16: Clinic Appointments (Model for Exercise 5.21)




Give the relational schema.
Two associations join Provider and ExamRoom, one directly and one through Appointment. Name the foreign keys each produces, and explain why the home room’s needs a UNIQUE constraint and the appointment’s does not.
Write a CHECK constraint or explain why none can stop two appointments in the same room at overlapping times.



Exercise 6.19 Map the project network of Exercise 5.22, drawn in Figure 6.17.






Figure 6.17: The Project Network (Model for Exercise 5.22)




Give the relational schema with surrogate keys, as the book does.
The model requires a precedence to join two activities of the same project. Show that your schema does not enforce it, with two rows that break it.
Give a second schema in which activity has the natural key (project_fk, activity_id) and precedence refers to both activities through it, sharing one project_fk column. Explain why this schema enforces the rule, and what it costs (recall Exercise 6.14).



Exercise 6.20 Map both models of the plant locations of Exercise 5.23, drawn in Figure 6.18.






Figure 6.18: Plant Locations, Two Ways (Model for Exercise 5.23)




Give the relational schema of the fixed levels, with the delete responses the compositions call for.
Give the relational schema of the recursive class. Which foreign key may be NULL, and which rows have NULL in it?
In the recursive table, what stops a line from being made the parent of a site? Propose a check the database can make, or say why it cannot.



Exercise 6.21 Map the bike share of Exercise 5.24, drawn in Figure 6.19.






Figure 6.19: The Bike Share (Model for Exercise 5.24)




Give the relational schema.
The association of Dock and Bike is 0..1 at both ends. Where does the foreign key go, what constraint makes it one-to-one, and why may it be NULL?
Name the two foreign keys from ride to station, and say which may be NULL.



Exercise 6.22 Map the container yard of Exercise 5.25, drawn in Figure 6.20.






Figure 6.20: The Container Yard (Model for Exercise 5.25)




Give the relational schema. Watch the names of the slot’s columns: which of the model’s attribute names is a reserved word of the SQL standard?
Give the alternate key of slot, and explain why a key of three numbers alone would be wrong.



Exercise 6.23 Map the equipment rental of Exercise 5.27, drawn in Figure 6.21.






Figure 6.21: Equipment Rental (Model for Exercise 5.27)




Give the relational schema.
A rental refers to its unit and its rate period, not to a rate. Explain how a query finds the amount a rental is charged at, naming each table the joins pass through.
The yard raises its weekly rates. What happens to the charges of rentals already returned, and what would you change if past charges must not move?



Exercise 6.24 Map the fleet of Exercise 5.28, drawn in Figure 6.22.






Figure 6.22: The Fleet (Model for Exercise 5.28)




Give the relational schema for a table for each class (Section 6.5.1).
Give it for one table for the whole hierarchy (Section 6.5.3), with the CHECK constraints that keep each kind’s columns filled or empty.
Choose between them with Table 6.11, and say why.



Exercise 6.25 Map the route network of Exercise 5.30, drawn in Figure 6.23.






Figure 6.23: The Route Network (Model for Exercise 5.30)




Give the relational schema. Map the {ordered} end as this chapter describes.
Write a query that lists the points of route 7, in order, using only the segments.
The study this model comes from stored a sequence number on each point of a route as well as on each segment. What does that add, and what can go wrong?



Exercise 6.26 Map the cards, accounts, and trips of Exercise 5.34, drawn in Figure 6.24.






Figure 6.24: Cards, Accounts, and Trips (Model for Exercise 5.34)




Choose a mapping for the generalization of SmartCard, and justify it. Where does the foreign key of the association between Account and CreditCard go?
Give the relational schema of the rest: people, addresses, accounts, the authorizations, trips, and payments.
The study this exercise comes from mapped a generalization of transactions (fares and payments) to a table for each subclass only, repeating the common columns, so that a trip could refer to its fare directly. Explain what that mapping gives up.



Exercise 6.27 Reverse the mapping of this chapter on the Chinook database of Section C.11, loaded with the book’s loader (Section A.6): from its tables, recover the class model.

Draw the class diagram, with multiplicities, and no foreign keys or identifiers.

title: 7  Normalization
text:
7.1 The normalization procedure
Not every table an engineer meets was designed. Many began as a spreadsheet: an order log kept by a sales clerk, an inspection sheet filled in on the floor, a report exported from another system. Such a table puts everything about an event on one row, which is convenient to read and troublesome to keep. The same fact is written many times, and a change to it must be made everywhere at once. When it is not, the table contradicts itself.
This chapter presents normalization, a method for testing a table’s design and for repairing it by splitting the table into smaller ones. The test uses the table’s functional dependencies, the rules that say which columns decide the values of which others, and the repair produces tables in which each fact is recorded once. Chapter 6 arrived at well-designed tables from a class model; this chapter arrives at them from the other direction, from a table that already exists. The two routes meet: normalizing a flat report of HG Industries’ orders produces the tables that the mapping produced.
The chapter begins, as Chapter 6 did, with the whole procedure, and then illustrates each step on one running example.
This section presents the steps of normalizing a table, before the sections that illustrate each step.
A table is normalized in five steps:
Table 7.1 says where each step is illustrated.
The first step deserves a word of its own. Normalization is often taught as symbols, a list of dependencies manipulated by rules, and it goes wrong when the dependencies are guessed. Looking at rows first, real ones or made-up ones that obey the business’s rules, grounds each dependency in something concrete and shows the repeated facts that the method exists to remove. It is the same habit as the hand evaluations of Chapter 3: see a few rows before trusting a rule about all of them.

title: 7  Normalization
text:
Look at the data. Take a few rows of the table, or make up a few that obey the business’s rules, and find the facts that repeat.
State the functional dependencies. For each rule of the business that says one fact decides another, write the dependency, and draw them all in a dependency diagram.
Find the key. From the dependencies, find the smallest set of columns that decides every other column.
Name the normal form. Test the table against the normal forms, from the first up, and find the first one it fails.
Decompose. Split the table into tables that each pass, without losing any row and, where the normal form allows it, without losing any dependency, and repeat the test on each.

7.2 Anomalies in a poorly designed table
This section illustrates step 1: it looks at the rows of a flat table and at what goes wrong when the table is kept up to date.
Suppose that the sales department of HG Industries kept its orders in one table, a flat order report with a row for each order line: the order’s number, its customer’s number and name, the line’s number, its product’s number and description, and the quantity ordered. The book’s database does not store such a table, but a query can produce it, by joining the four tables of stage D3. We write the join once, as a common table expression named order_report (Section 3.10), and use it throughout the chapter as if it were a stored table. Its rows for the first six orders are:

The contradictions come in three kinds, called anomalies.

title: 7  Normalization
text:
7.3 Functional dependencies
This section illustrates steps 2 and 3: it states the rules that decide the values of columns, draws them, and finds the key.
A functional dependency holds between two sets of columns of a table when the values of the first set decide the values of the second: any two rows that agree on the first set also agree on the second. It is written with an arrow, order_number → customer_number, and read “order number determines customer number”. The set on the left is called the determinant. In words, the dependency says: whenever we see order SO-5001, we see customer C-1001, on every row of the order, now and in every future state of the table.
Functional dependencies come from the rules of the business, as candidate keys do (Section 2.2). For the order report, the rules are:

An order is placed by one customer: order_number → customer_number.
A customer has one name: customer_number → customer_name.
A line of an order is for one product, in one quantity: order_number, line_number → product_number, quantity.
A product has one description: product_number → description.

Notice the third rule’s determinant, two columns together. Neither the order nor the line number alone decides the product, since an order has several lines and every order has a line 1. The product does not identify a line either, since lines 1 and 3 of SO-5004 are both for the HT-100; the pair decides it.
A functional dependency diagram draws a table’s dependencies. Each column is an oval, and an arrow runs from each determinant to each column it determines. A determinant of several columns is a larger outline drawn around their ovals, and its arrows leave the outline, since only the columns together decide the value. The columns of the key are shaded and underlined. Figure 7.1 draws the four dependencies of the order report.






Figure 7.1: The Functional Dependencies of the Flat Order Report



Read Figure 7.1 one arrow at a time. The outline around order_number and line_number sends arrows to product_number and quantity: the pair decides them. A separate arrow leaves the order_number oval alone, inside the outline, for customer_number, which sends its own arrow on to customer_name. The last arrow runs from product_number to description. Thus each rule of the list above is drawn as the arrows from its determinant, one to each column it determines: the key’s outline sends two arrows for the third rule, and the figure draws four dependencies with five arrows.
A dependency is a rule, so the rows can refute it but never prove it, as with a candidate key. A query finds refutations: a dependency X → Y is broken whenever some value of X appears with two different values of Y. Grouping by X and counting the different values of Y (Section 4.2) checks it over the whole year of history:



Table 7.5: Customer Numbers with More Than One Name in the Report


WITH order_report AS (
  SELECT c.customer_number, c.name AS customer_name
  FROM distribution.customer_order AS o
  JOIN distribution.customer AS c
    ON c.customer_pk = o.customer_fk
  JOIN distribution.order_line AS l
    ON l.customer_order_fk = o.customer_order_pk
)
SELECT customer_number,
       COUNT(DISTINCT customer_name) AS names
FROM order_report
GROUP BY customer_number
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT customer_name) > 1;





customer_number


names












Table 7.5 is empty: no customer number appears with two names, so the data does not refute customer_number → customer_name. In a real flat table kept by hand, the same query is the quickest way to find the update anomalies that have already happened.
The dependencies also give step 3, the key. A set of columns is a key of the table when it determines every other column, directly or through a chain of dependencies, and no smaller set does. Follow the chains of Figure 7.1 from order_number and line_number. Together they determine product_number and quantity; order_number determines customer_number, which determines customer_name; and product_number determines description. Every column is reached, so the pair (order_number, line_number) is a key, and neither column alone is, since neither reaches product_number. Its two ovals are shaded and underlined in Figure 7.1.
Two kinds of dependency on a key matter for what follows. A dependency is partial when a column depends on only part of a composite key: customer_number depends on order_number alone, not on the whole key. A dependency is transitive when a column depends on the key only through another column that is not a key: customer_name depends on the key through customer_number. Both are visible in Figure 7.1. A partial dependency is an arrow that leaves one oval inside the key’s outline rather than the outline itself; a transitive one is a chain of arrows, the second leaving an unshaded oval.

title: 7  Normalization
text:
7.4 Normal forms
This section illustrates step 4: it defines the normal forms, from the first through Boyce-Codd, and tests the order report against each.
A normal form is a condition on a table’s dependencies that rules out one kind of repeated fact. The forms are nested: a table in a higher normal form is in every lower one. The first three are often summarized by one sentence, due to William Kent (Kent 1983): every column that is not part of a key depends on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key.
A table is in first normal form (1NF) when every value is atomic, a single value from its column’s domain (Section 2.1), and there are no repeating groups. Recall from Section 2.1.1 that the relational model already requires all three: atomic values are the first property of a relation, values from the domain are the second, and the ban on repeating groups is the companion of the first. Thus, 1NF is those rules stated as a test of a table. The order report is in 1NF, since each row holds one line. A version of the report with one row per order and the order’s products listed in a single cell is not:



Table 7.6: Orders with Their Products in One Cell, Not in 1NF


SELECT o.order_number,
       STRING_AGG(p.product_number, ', '
                  ORDER BY l.line_number) AS products
FROM distribution.customer_order AS o
JOIN distribution.order_line AS l
  ON l.customer_order_fk = o.customer_order_pk
JOIN distribution.product AS p
  ON p.product_pk = l.product_fk
WHERE o.order_number <= 'SO-5004'
GROUP BY o.order_number
ORDER BY o.order_number;





order_number


products






SO-5001


HT-100, GC-300




SO-5002


HT-200




SO-5003


HT-100, HT-200, GC-300




SO-5004


HT-100, GC-300, HT-100








STRING_AGG, PostgreSQL’s aggregate for the purpose (the SQL standard’s is LISTAGG), joins a group’s values into one string. The products column of Table 7.6 holds a list, not a value: no query can ask for the orders of the HT-200 without searching inside strings, and no foreign key can refer from one element of the list to the product table. Such a column belongs in a report, where it is read, and never in a stored table.
A table is in second normal form (2NF) when it is in 1NF and no column that is not part of a key depends on only part of a key; that is, it has no partial dependency. The order report fails. customer_number and customer_name depend on order_number alone, part of the key (order_number, line_number), and the failure is the cause of the repetition: an order’s customer is repeated on every line of the order because it depends on the order, not on the line. A table whose keys are all single columns cannot have a partial dependency, so it is in 2NF as soon as it is in 1NF.
A table is in third normal form (3NF) when it is in 2NF and no column that is not part of a key depends on another such column; that is, it has no transitive dependency on a key. The report fails here too, twice: customer_name depends on customer_number, and description on product_number, neither of which is a key. Each repeats a fact about a customer or a product on every row that mentions it. Thus, the order report is in 1NF, and it fails 2NF and 3NF; step 5 of the procedure must repair both.
The definitions of 2NF and 3NF speak of columns that are not part of a key, and that leaves a gap: a column that is part of a key may still depend on a column that is not. A table is in Boyce-Codd normal form (BCNF) when every determinant of a dependency is a candidate key. (Strictly, a determinant may also be a set of columns that contains a candidate key, called a superkey; the book states the rule with candidate keys because a determinant is taken to be as small as it can be.) BCNF is stricter than 3NF, and the difference shows up only in tables with overlapping composite keys. For example, suppose that HG Industries recorded which machine each operator runs in each work center, under two rules: an operator runs one machine in each work center, and each machine belongs to one work center. A few hypothetical rows illustrate:

In Figure 7.2, the arrow leaving the outline around operator and work_center is the first rule, operator, work_center → machine, and the arrow from machine back into the outline, onto work_center, is the second, machine → work_center. An arrow that points into the key from a column outside it, a column that is not itself a candidate key, is the mark of a table that is not in BCNF. The table has two candidate keys, (operator, work_center) and (operator, machine), since a machine decides its work center. Every column is part of a key, so no column “not part of a key” exists, and the table is in 3NF. But the determinant machine is not a candidate key, so the table is not in BCNF. The consequence is a repeated fact: that M-04 is in Welding is recorded on two rows of Table 7.7, and moving M-04 to another work center would need both changed. Exercise 7.6 asks for the repair.

In practice, a table in 3NF is nearly always in BCNF, and designers aim for BCNF and settle for 3NF only when BCNF would cost a dependency, as Section 7.5 shows. Higher normal forms exist, and Section 7.7 presents the fourth. The next section repairs the order report.

title: 7  Normalization
text:
7.5 Decomposition
This section illustrates step 5: it splits a table that fails a normal form into tables that pass, and checks that nothing is lost in the split.
A table that fails a normal form is repaired by decomposition: replacing it with two or more smaller tables whose columns, together, are the original columns. Each split follows one rule. Take a dependency X → Y that breaks the normal form; move X and Y into a new table, whose key is X; and remove Y from the original table, keeping X there to refer to the new table. Then test both tables again, and split again until every table passes.
Let’s decompose the order report. It fails 2NF through the partial dependency order_number → customer_number, and customer_name depends on customer_number, so it travels with it. The first split moves the three columns about the order into a table of their own:

customer_order (order_number, customer_number, customer_name), key order_number;
order_line (order_number, line_number, product_number, description, quantity), key (order_number, line_number).

Both are in 2NF, since customer_order has a single-column key and every column left in order_line depends on the whole of its key. Neither is in 3NF. In customer_order, customer_name depends on customer_number, which is not a key; in order_line, description depends on product_number. The second and third splits remove the two transitive dependencies in the same way, moving customer_number and customer_name into a customer table and product_number and description into a product table. Listing 7.1 writes the four resulting tables in the relational schema notation of Section 2.4.



Listing 7.1: The Order Report Decomposed, with Its Natural Keys (Hypothetical)


customer (customer_number, customer_name)
    primary key: customer_number

customer_order (order_number, customer_number)
    primary key: order_number
    customer_number references customer_number in customer,
        must not be NULL

order_line (order_number, line_number, product_number,
            quantity)
    primary key: (order_number, line_number)
    order_number references order_number in customer_order,
        must not be NULL
    product_number references product_number in product,
        must not be NULL

product (product_number, description)
    primary key: product_number



Notice that each split left a foreign key behind: the determinant that moved into the new table stays in the old one, and refers to the new table’s key. Figure 7.3 draws the dependencies of the four tables, each table in a dashed outline.






Figure 7.3: The Order Report Decomposed into Four Tables



Compare Figure 7.3 with Figure 7.1. Every arrow of the original diagram now lies inside one outline, and in every outline the arrows leave the key and nothing else. Thus each table is in BCNF: its only determinant is its key. The two transitive chains of Figure 7.1 have been cut at the middle column, which is now a foreign key in one table and the key of another.
The four tables are the four tables of stage D3 that Chapter 6 mapped from the class model (Listing 6.12). The database adds what normalization does not decide: a surrogate primary key for each table, with the natural key kept as an alternate key (Section 6.6), and the columns the report did not carry, such as order_date and unit_price. The dependencies are the same. Normalizing the report and mapping the class model are two routes to one design.

7.5.1 Lossless decomposition
A decomposition must not lose information. A decomposition is lossless when joining its tables gives back the original table’s rows, no fewer and no more. For a split on a functional dependency, the rule that guarantees it is simple: each split must join on columns that are a key of one of the two tables. Every split of the order report does, since the columns left behind (order_number, customer_number, product_number) are the keys of the new tables.
The order report itself is the evidence. Table 7.2 was produced by joining the four tables of stage D3 on their keys, so the join gives back every row the report holds. Over the year of history, the join gives one row for each order line, no more:



Table 7.9: Order Lines and Rows of the Joined Report, Stage G


WITH order_report AS (
  SELECT o.order_number, l.line_number
  FROM distribution.customer_order AS o
  JOIN distribution.customer AS c
    ON c.customer_pk = o.customer_fk
  JOIN distribution.order_line AS l
    ON l.customer_order_fk = o.customer_order_pk
  JOIN distribution.product AS p
    ON p.product_pk = l.product_fk
)
SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM distribution.order_line)
         AS order_lines,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM order_report) AS report_rows;

The check. The first three orders have six lines, and each of the three products appears on two of them with two quantities, so the join gives 2 × 2 = 4 rows per product, 12 in all. A lossy decomposition does not lose rows; it gains wrong ones, and the database cannot tell them apart from the right ones.


7.5.2 Preserving dependencies
A decomposition should also keep every dependency inside one table, where the table’s key enforces it. A decomposition is dependency preserving when each dependency of the original table lies wholly within one of the new tables. The decomposition of the order report is: each of its four dependencies is the key of one table of Listing 7.1 and the columns it determines, so the PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE constraints of Chapter 8 will enforce all four.
BCNF cannot always be reached without losing a dependency. The operator assignments of Table 7.7 are the standard case: any split that puts machine and work_center in a table keyed by machine leaves no table that holds operator, work_center, and machine together, so the rule “an operator runs one machine in each work center” has no key to enforce it (Exercise 7.6). You then choose between BCNF, with a rule that must be checked some other way, and 3NF, with a repeated fact. Most designers take BCNF when it preserves the dependencies and settle for 3NF when it does not. The example that follows normalizes a second report, this time from the quality department.

Example 7.1 (Normalizing an inspection sheet) HG Industries’ quality engineers inspect each lot of a part as it leaves production, and measure the part’s characteristics: the weld strength and coating thickness of a hand truck frame, the diameter and length of an axle. One engineer keeps the results in a spreadsheet, one row per measurement, with the lot, the characteristic, the part and its description, the inspector’s employee number and name, and the value measured. The example assumes stage Q.
The request. Normalize the inspection sheet: state its dependencies, find its key and normal form, decompose it into tables in BCNF, and compare the result with the quality schema of the book’s database.
The design. A query produces the sheet from the tables of stage Q. Its rows for the first four lots of the frame are:



Table 7.12: The Inspection Sheet, First Four Lots of FR-110


SELECT i.lot_number, c.name AS characteristic,
       p.part_number, p.description,
       o.employee_number, o.name AS operator_name,
       m.measured_value
FROM quality.measurement AS m
JOIN quality.inspection AS i
  ON i.inspection_pk = m.inspection_fk
JOIN quality.characteristic AS c
  ON c.characteristic_pk = m.characteristic_fk
JOIN production.part AS p ON p.part_pk = i.part_fk
JOIN production.operator AS o
  ON o.operator_pk = i.operator_fk
WHERE i.lot_number <= 'L7004-04'
ORDER BY i.lot_number, c.name;

The part and its description repeat on every row of Table 7.12, and each inspector’s number and name on both rows of each lot the inspector checked. The rules of the quality department give four dependencies:

A lot is of one part and, in this plant, is inspected once, by one inspector: lot_number → part_number, employee_number.
A part has one description: part_number → description.
An employee has one name: employee_number → operator_name.
A lot’s inspection measures each characteristic once: lot_number, characteristic → measured_value.

Figure 7.4 draws them.






Figure 7.4: The Functional Dependencies of the Inspection Sheet



In Figure 7.4, only the outline around lot_number and characteristic reaches measured_value, and the chains from lot_number reach every other column, so (lot_number, characteristic) is the key. The sheet is in 1NF. It fails 2NF, since the arrows to part_number and employee_number leave the lot_number oval alone; and it would fail 3NF through the two chains.
The first split moves the columns that depend on the lot into an inspection table keyed by lot_number, leaving measurement (lot_number, characteristic, measured_value). The new inspection table holds two transitive dependencies, and two more splits move them into part and operator tables. Figure 7.5 shows the four tables.






Figure 7.5: The Inspection Sheet Decomposed into Four Tables



Each outline of Figure 7.5 has arrows only from its key, so each table is in BCNF, and each dependency of Figure 7.4 lies inside one outline, so the decomposition preserves them. Listing 7.2 shows the corresponding tables of the book’s database.




Listing 7.2: The Tables of Stage Q That Hold the Inspection Sheet


part (part_pk, part_number, description, unit_of_measure,
      standard_cost)
    primary key: part_pk
    alternate key: part_number

    primary key: operator_pk
    alternate key: employee_number

            inspected_at, lot_number)
    primary key: inspection_pk
    part_fk references part_pk in part, must not be NULL
    operator_fk references operator_pk in operator,
        must not be NULL

measurement (measurement_pk, inspection_fk,
             characteristic_fk, measured_value)
    primary key: measurement_pk
    alternate key: (inspection_fk, characteristic_fk)
    inspection_fk references inspection_pk in inspection,
        must not be NULL
    characteristic_fk references characteristic_pk in
        characteristic, must not be NULL




The result. The four tables of Listing 7.2 match the four outlines of Figure 7.5, with surrogate keys added, with columns the sheet did not carry (such as inspected_at), and with measurement referring to a characteristic table, which records the specifications of each part’s characteristics (Exercise 7.8).
The check. The decomposition is lossless if the sheet has one row per measurement, since every join is on a key. Each of the first four lots has two measurements, and Table 7.12 has eight rows. Over the whole of stage Q:



Table 7.13: Measurements and Rows of the Inspection Sheet, Stage Q


WITH sheet AS (
  SELECT i.lot_number, c.name AS characteristic
  FROM quality.measurement AS m
  JOIN quality.inspection AS i
    ON i.inspection_pk = m.inspection_fk
  JOIN quality.characteristic AS c
    ON c.characteristic_pk = m.characteristic_fk
  JOIN production.part AS p ON p.part_pk = i.part_fk
  JOIN production.operator AS o
    ON o.operator_pk = i.operator_fk
)
SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM quality.measurement)
         AS measurements,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM sheet) AS sheet_rows;





measurements

Table 7.13 shows 34 of each.
Interpretation. The spreadsheet is a fine way to read the results, and a query produces it on demand. Stored as the spreadsheet, it would repeat each inspector’s name on every measurement the inspector took, could not record a new part until its first lot was inspected, and would lose an inspector who left along with the last row naming that inspector. The tables record each of those facts once.
Where it breaks. The design rests on the rule that a lot is inspected once. If a failed lot were reworked and inspected again, lot_number would no longer determine the inspector, and the key of inspection would need the inspection’s time as well. So would the key of measurement, since the lot’s characteristics would be measured twice, and (lot_number, characteristic) would no longer decide the value measured. The book’s database anticipates this: it identifies an inspection by its own surrogate key and does not declare lot_number unique, so a second inspection of a lot can be recorded. In stage Q, every lot happens to have been inspected once.

title: 7  Normalization
text:
7.6 Normalization and class modeling
This section connects normalization to the class modeling of Chapter 5 and the mapping of Chapter 6.
Recall that step 7 of the mapping (Section 6.1) checks the tables a class model produces, and reviews their normal form. The review seldom finds a problem, and the reason is worth stating. A class describes one kind of object, and its attributes describe that object: an order’s date, a product’s description. Mapped to a table, each attribute becomes a column that depends on the object’s identity, which is the table’s key, and on nothing else. That is the condition of BCNF. Thus, a class model in which every attribute describes the object of its own class maps to tables in BCNF.
The converse makes normalization a test of the model. A normal form violation in a mapped table points to a modeling mistake, and Table 7.14 pairs the most common ones.



Table 7.14: Normal Form Violations and the Modeling Mistakes Behind Them










The mapped table fails
Because the model
For example




1NF
stores several values in one attribute
the products of an order as one attribute of CustomerOrder


2NF
puts an attribute on a part that describes only its whole, or on an association class an attribute that describes only one end
orderDate as an attribute of OrderLine


3NF
puts an attribute on a class that describes another object
customerName as an attribute of CustomerOrder


BCNF
records as one association facts that belong to two
the operator assignments of Table 7.7






Each row of Table 7.14 has a repair in the model, not only in the tables. For example, customerName on CustomerOrder is a transitive dependency, order_number → customer_number → customer_name, and its repair is the class Customer of Figure 5.11, with the association that links an order to it. The operator assignments are two associations: the machine an operator is assigned to run, and the machine’s place in a work center. The assignment is not the certification of Figure 5.20. Stage P3 certifies Linda Nguyen on two machines of Welding, while the rule of Table 7.7 lets her run only one of them. The repaired model draws the assignment as an association of its own between operator and machine, beside the machine’s place in a work center. When the check of step 7 fails, the dashed arrow of Figure 6.1 sends you back to the class model, and the repair belongs there.
Normalization also judges what is not a repetition. The order line of stage D3 has a unit_price, and the product has a list_price, so the price of a product seems to be stored twice. It is not. Recall from Example 5.1 that order SO-5004 lists the HT-100 twice, at $89.00 and at $79.00. The unit price is the price of one line, determined by the line and not by the product, while the list price is the product’s current price. The two columns record different facts, and a design that dropped unit_price in favor of list_price would lose the price at which each line was actually sold.
Normalization governs the tables that store facts, not every table a database shows. A report such as the order report is produced by a query when it is needed, and a view (Section 9.1) can give such a query a name, so that the report reads like a table while its facts stay stored once. In addition, a designer sometimes stores a repeated fact on purpose, to make reading faster or simpler, and accepts the anomalies it brings. This is denormalization, and it is the usual design of a data warehouse, where the data is loaded in bulk and rarely updated (Section 11.2). A denormalized design is a decision made about a normalized one, and you should be able to say which dependencies it gives up.

title: 7  Normalization
section: 7.7 Multivalued dependencies and fourth normal form
text:
7.7 Multivalued dependencies and fourth normal form
This section presents one kind of repetition that BCNF does not catch, and the fourth normal form that removes it.
A table can be in BCNF and still repeat facts. Suppose that HG Industries kept, for each machine, the operators certified to run it and the routine maintenance tasks it needs, in one table with a row for each combination. The operators are real; stage P3 records the certifications of machine M-04:



Table 7.15: The Operators Certified on Machine M-04


SELECT m.machine_number, o.name AS operator
FROM production.certification AS c
JOIN production.machine AS m
  ON m.machine_pk = c.machine_fk
JOIN production.operator AS o
  ON o.operator_pk = c.operator_fk
WHERE m.machine_number = 'M-04'
ORDER BY o.name;





machine_number


operator






M-04


Linda Nguyen




M-04


Maria Lopez








The tasks are hypothetical, since the book’s database does not record maintenance: say that the welder needs its contact tip replaced, its wire feeder cleaned, and its gas flow checked. The rule of the business is that every certified operator performs every task on the machines they are certified on. The combined table must then hold each of the two operators of Table 7.15 with each of the three tasks:



Table 7.16: Operators and Maintenance Tasks of M-04 in One Table (Hypothetical)





Machine
Operator
Task




M-04
Linda Nguyen
Replace contact tip


M-04

Clean wire feeder


M-04

Check gas flow


M-04

M-04

No column of Table 7.16 determines another: a machine has several operators and several tasks, and an operator and a task each go with several machines. The key is all three columns, the only determinant is the key, and the table is in BCNF. Yet it repeats facts, and counting rows shows it. That Linda Nguyen is certified on M-04 is written three times, once per task, and that M-04 needs its gas flow checked is written twice, once per operator. Adding a fourth task to M-04 takes two new rows, one for each operator; certifying a third operator takes three, one for each task. Leaving one of those rows out does not record less; it records something false, that the operator skips that task.
The cause is a multivalued dependency. A multivalued dependency machine →→ operator holds when a machine determines a set of operators, and that set is the same whatever the other columns hold. The second half of the definition is the important one. A machine having many operators is only a one-to-many relationship; the multivalued dependency says, in addition, that the set of operators does not depend on the task, and so every operator must be paired with every task. Here machine →→ task holds as well, and the two sets vary independently of each other.
A table is in fourth normal form (4NF) when it is in BCNF and every multivalued dependency in it, other than one that covers all of the table’s columns, has a candidate key, or a superkey, as its determinant. Table 7.16 fails, since machine is not a key. The decomposition follows the same rule as before: move the dependency into a table of its own. The result is two tables, machine_operator (machine, operator) and machine_task (machine, task), with two rows and three rows for M-04 instead of six, and a new task or a new certification is one row. The first of the two is the certification table of stage P3.
The two tables join on machine, a key of neither, and yet the split loses nothing. The rule of Section 7.5.1 is the test for a split on a functional dependency; a split on a multivalued dependency is lossless for a different reason. Since every operator of a machine performs every task of the machine, joining the two tables pairs each operator with each task, and each of those pairings is a row the original table holds. For M-04, the join gives 2 × 3 = 6 rows, the six rows of Table 7.16 and no others.
Notice what the business rule decided. If the rule were instead that each task is assigned to particular operators, the three-way combination would be a fact of its own, and Table 7.16 would be a correct table recording a ternary association (Section 6.3.7). The test is the one of the counting argument: if deleting a single row would record something true, the combination is a fact, and the table stands; if it would record something false, the table hides two independent facts and belongs in 4NF.
Normal forms continue beyond the fourth. The fifth normal form concerns tables that can be rebuilt only by joining three or more smaller tables made from their columns, a situation rare enough in practice that this book names it and goes no further. A class model with two separate many-to-many associations, which is how Chapter 5 would model operators and tasks, maps to 4NF tables from the start.

title: 7  Normalization
text:
7.8 Summary
Normalization tests a table’s design against its dependencies and repairs it by decomposition. Its five steps look at the data, state the dependencies, find the key, name the normal form, and decompose.
A table that repeats facts invites anomalies. An update anomaly changes some copies of a fact and not others; a deletion anomaly loses a fact with an unrelated row; an insertion anomaly cannot record a fact until another exists. Queries find their symptoms and count the copies.
A functional dependency is a rule of the business that one set of columns decides another. Its determinant’s values decide its dependents’ values on every row, now and later; the data can refute a dependency but not prove it. A key is a smallest set of columns that determines every column, and a dependency on part of a key is partial, one through a column outside the key transitive.
Each normal form rules out one kind of repeated fact. 1NF requires atomic values; 2NF forbids partial dependencies, 3NF transitive ones; BCNF requires every determinant to be a candidate key. Every column outside a key must depend on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key.
Decomposition repairs a table by splitting it on a violating dependency. The determinant and the columns it decides move to a new table keyed by the determinant, and the determinant stays behind as a foreign key. Decomposing the order report produces the four tables of stage D3 that Chapter 6 mapped from the class model.
A decomposition must be lossless, and should preserve dependencies. Joining the tables must give back the original rows, which holds when each split joins on a key of one of its tables; a split on a column that is a key of neither can add rows that were never true. Each dependency should lie within one table, where a key enforces it, and when BCNF would lose one, 3NF is the usual compromise.
A sound class model maps to normalized tables. An attribute that describes the object of its own class depends on the key and nothing else, so a normal form violation in a mapped table points to a mistake in the model, and the repair belongs in the model. A report is a query, not a stored table, and denormalization is a deliberate decision about a normalized design.
A multivalued dependency repeats facts that BCNF allows. When a determinant fixes two sets of values that vary independently, one table must pair every member of one set with every member of the other, and counting the rows an insertion needs exposes it. Fourth normal form moves each set into a table of its own.

text:
7.9 Exercises

Exercise 7.1 Match each term on the left with the phrase on the right that defines it.

Exercise 7.2 Mark each statement true or false, and correct each false one.

If a query finds no customer number with two names, then customer_number → customer_name holds.
A table whose only key is a single column is in 2NF if it is in 1NF.
A table in 3NF is always in BCNF.
Normalization removes all repetition of values from a database.
The flat order report is in 1NF.



Exercise 7.3 The shipping department keeps a flat shipment report at stage D5 with the columns shipment_number, shipped_on, warehouse_code, warehouse_city, order_number, order_line_number, and quantity_shipped, one row per shipment line.

Produce the report with a query, and look at its first ten rows (step 1). Which facts repeat?
State its functional dependencies from the rules of stage D5, and draw them in the manner of Figure 7.1 (step 2).
Find its key (step 3).
Name the highest normal form it satisfies, and say why it fails the next (step 4).



Exercise 7.4 Using the flat order report at stage G, write a query that checks the dependency product_number → description, in the manner of Table 7.5. Then explain why an empty result does not prove the dependency, and what would.


Exercise 7.5 A warehouse manager keeps a table with one row per stock level and the columns warehouse_code, warehouse_city, product_number, description, quantity_on_hand, and reorder_point.

Give its dependencies and its key.
Test it against 1NF, 2NF, and 3NF, naming each dependency that causes a failure.
Describe an update anomaly, a deletion anomaly, and an insertion anomaly in this table, each with HG Industries’ data.



Exercise 7.6 Using Table 7.7 and Figure 7.2:

Explain, with the table’s rows, why the table is in 3NF.
Decompose it into two tables that are each in BCNF.
The rule “an operator runs one machine in each work center” was a dependency of the original table. Can either of your two tables enforce it with a key? What does that say about BCNF?



Exercise 7.7 Using the flat order report at stage D3, restricted to orders SO-5001 through SO-5006, consider splitting it into (order_number, line_number, quantity) and (order_number, product_number, description).

Is the split lossless? Name the rule you use.
Before running anything, predict the number of rows the join of the two parts on order_number returns. The lines of each order are in Table 7.2, and each part, being a table, holds no two identical rows.
Write a query, in the manner of Table 7.11, that builds the two parts and counts the rows of their join, and compare the count with your prediction.



Exercise 7.8 Suppose that the inspection sheet of Example 7.1 also carried each characteristic’s nominal value, the target the specification sets for it.

State the dependency that decides nominal, using the rules of the quality department: a part’s characteristic has one nominal value, and two parts may share a characteristic’s name with different nominal values.
Which normal form does the extended sheet fail because of it, and why?
Decompose the extended sheet into tables in BCNF, and compare the result with the quality.characteristic table of stage Q.



Exercise 7.9 A student models an order with a single class, Order, whose attributes are orderNumber, orderDate, customerNumber, customerName, and customerCity.

Map the class to a table, state its dependencies, and name its highest normal form.
Which row of Table 7.14 describes the mistake?
Repair the class model, and show that the repaired model maps to tables in BCNF.



Exercise 7.10 HG Industries offers each garden cart in several colors and with several wheel types. Assume that every color is offered with every wheel type, and consider the table cart_option (product_number, color, wheel_type), which holds a row for each combination. The GC-300 comes in green and red, with pneumatic or solid wheels.

List the rows the table holds for the GC-300. What is its key, and is it in BCNF?
How many rows must be added to offer the GC-300 in blue? How many to offer a third wheel type, first to the rows of part (a), and then once blue is offered?
State the multivalued dependencies, and decompose the table into 4NF.
Suppose instead that the solid wheels are not offered in red. Should the table still be decomposed as in part (c)? Explain with the counting test of Section 7.7.



Exercise 7.11 Each invoice of the Chinook database of Section C.11, loaded with the book’s loader (Section A.6) stores a billing address (billing_address, billing_city, and so on), and each customer an address.

Write a query that counts the invoices, and those whose billing address differs from their customer’s address.
The two agree on every invoice. Is the billing address then redundant, a copy the table should not keep (Section 7.2)? State the functional dependency that would make it redundant, and say whether it holds for the business.






Kent, William. 1983. “A Simple Guide to Five Normal Forms in Relational Database Theory.” Communications of the ACM 26 (2): 120–25. https://doi.org/10.1145/358024.358054.

title: 8  Defining and Populating Tables
text:
8.1 From a design to tables
The chapters so far have queried tables that already existed, and then shown where those tables come from: a class model (Chapter 5), mapped to a relational schema (Chapter 6), checked by normalization (Chapter 7). This chapter takes the last step. It turns a relational schema into tables that a database system holds, fills them with rows, and changes them as the business changes.
The statements that do this are the other half of SQL. The part of SQL that defines tables and their rules is called the data definition language (DDL): CREATE, ALTER, and DROP. The part that changes rows is called the data manipulation language (DML): INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE, together with the SELECT of the earlier chapters. A database is built with the first and kept current with the second.
The chapter builds the distribution schema of HG Industries, stages D1 to D3, from the relational schemas of Chapter 6. It does so by reading the scripts that build the book’s own database, one clause at a time, so that every statement in the chapter is one you can run and every table is one you have already queried.
This section presents the whole process of building a database from its design, before the sections that illustrate each step.
A relational schema says what tables a database holds and what rules they obey; it does not yet hold anything. Building the database from it takes five steps:
The steps are written down as a script, a file of SQL statements run in order, rather than typed once and forgotten. A script that builds a database from nothing is its most useful description: it can be read, kept under version control beside the code that uses the database, and run again to rebuild the database on another machine or after an experiment has spoiled it. The book’s database is kept this way. code/sql/reset.sql drops its four schemas, and each file of code/sql/load/ rebuilds them through one stage. Table 8.1 says where each step is illustrated.
The first step, for the distribution department, is one statement:
CREATE SCHEMA distribution;
A table in the schema is then named with the schema in front, distribution.customer, which is how the book has written table names in every query. PostgreSQL also keeps a search path, a list of schemas it looks in for a table named without one, so that SET search_path TO distribution; lets a session write customer alone. The book’s scripts always qualify the name, so that they work whatever the search path holds.
DataGrip and DBeaver can create schemas and tables through dialogs, without a statement being typed. The dialog is a convenience, not a different mechanism: it writes a CREATE statement and sends it to the server. Both tools will show the statement, and will also generate the DDL of any existing table (DataGrip’s SQL Scripts, Generate DDL to Query Console; DBeaver’s Generate SQL, DDL), which is how you capture a database that someone built by hand as a script. The rest of this chapter writes the statements directly, since a statement can be read, kept, and run again, and a sequence of clicks cannot.

title: 8  Defining and Populating Tables
text:
Create a place for the tables. A PostgreSQL server holds databases, and a database holds schemas, each a named group of tables. HG Industries’ tables live in one database, dbconcepts in the book’s setup (Appendix A), with a schema per department.
Choose a data type for each column. The type implements the column’s domain, as far as a type can; a CHECK constraint narrows it further.
Create each table with its constraints. One CREATE TABLE statement per table of the relational schema declares its columns, its primary key, its alternate keys, its foreign keys with their delete rules, and its checks. A table is created after every table it refers to.
Put rows into the tables. Rows are inserted by statements or loaded from files, in the same order as the tables were created, so that a foreign key always refers to a row that exists.
Check the result. Queries count the rows and look for what the constraints cannot catch, as the hand check of each worked example has done.





Table 8.1: The Steps of Building a Database and Where They Are Illustrated





Step
Illustrated in




1: a place for the tables
this section


2: data types
Section 8.2


3: tables and constraints
Section 8.3

Section 8.4 and Section 8.5


5: checking
each section’s queries, and Section 8.5

title: 8  Defining and Populating Tables
text:
8.2 Data types
This section illustrates step 2: choosing the data type of each column.
Recall from Section 6.2 that a column’s type is chosen in two steps: first the domain is stated in words, and then an SQL type and constraints implement it (Table 6.2). A data type is the set of values a column can hold, as the database system knows it, together with the operations it allows on them. The type decides more than storage: it decides how values compare, sort, and add, and whether a value that does not belong is refused or silently changed. The book’s database uses few types, and the query below counts the columns of each across all four schemas:



Table 8.2: The Data Types of the Book’s Database


SELECT data_type, COUNT(*) AS columns
FROM information_schema.columns
WHERE table_schema IN ('distribution', 'production',
                       'quality', 'sales')
GROUP BY data_type
ORDER BY columns DESC, data_type;





data_type


columns

36

Recall from Section 2.5 that the information_schema of Table 8.2 is the standard’s set of views of the catalog, the database’s description of its own tables and columns. Its type names are the standard’s long spellings: character varying is VARCHAR, and character is CHAR. The types fall into five kinds.
Whole numbers. INTEGER holds whole numbers up to about two billion, which covers every key and count in the book. SMALLINT and BIGINT hold smaller and larger ranges. The surrogate keys are INTEGER columns whose values the database generates, declared GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY, the standard form since PostgreSQL 10. Older scripts write SERIAL for the same purpose, a PostgreSQL shorthand that you will still meet.
Numbers with fractions. NUMERIC(p, s) holds exact decimal numbers with p digits in all, s of them after the decimal point: a price is NUMERIC(10,2), a measured diameter NUMERIC(10,4). The alternative, REAL or DOUBLE PRECISION, holds binary floating-point numbers, which are fast and compact but cannot represent most decimal fractions exactly. The difference is easy to show:



Table 8.3: Adding 0.1 and 0.2 as Floating-Point and as Exact Numbers


SELECT 0.1::DOUBLE PRECISION + 0.2 AS double_sum,
       0.1::NUMERIC + 0.2 AS numeric_sum,
       0.1::DOUBLE PRECISION + 0.2 = 0.3 AS double_equal,
       0.1::NUMERIC + 0.2 = 0.3 AS numeric_equal;





double_sum


numeric_sum


double_equal


numeric_equal






0.30000000000000004


0.3


false


true








The :: of Table 8.3 is PostgreSQL’s shorthand for converting a value to a type, the standard’s CAST(0.1 AS DOUBLE PRECISION). The floating-point sum is not 0.3, and a comparison with 0.3 is false.
The error does not always show. PostgreSQL prints a REAL or DOUBLE PRECISION value as the shortest decimal that reads back to the same stored value, so a stored value that is not exact can print as if it were:



Table 8.4: A REAL Value as Printed and as Stored


SELECT 32.38::REAL AS real_value,
       32.38::REAL::DOUBLE PRECISION AS stored_value;





real_value


stored_value






32.38


32.380001068115234








The REAL of Table 8.4 prints as 32.38, but the value stored is 32.380001068115234, which converting it to DOUBLE PRECISION reveals. Thus, a column of floating-point prices can look right and still not add up to the cent. For money, and for any measurement recorded to a known number of decimal places, use NUMERIC; a sum of prices that is off by a fraction of a cent fails every reconciliation. Keep floating point for quantities that are computed rather than recorded, such as the output of a simulation. PostgreSQL also has a MONEY type; avoid it, since it is PostgreSQL’s own, and how it reads and prints values depends on the server’s locale settings.
Text. VARCHAR(n) holds text of up to n characters, and refuses a longer value. CHAR(n) holds exactly n, padding a shorter value with spaces, which suits a code that always has the same length, such as a two-letter state, and little else. TEXT holds text of any length; it is PostgreSQL’s (the standard has no TEXT), and suits notes and descriptions with no natural limit. A length limit in VARCHAR(n) is a small domain rule: an order number of 40 characters is a mistake, and the limit refuses it.
A code that is written with digits is still text, and belongs in a text column. Part numbers, employee numbers, and postal codes are identifiers, not quantities: nobody adds them, and a leading zero is part of the code. Stored as a number, the zero is lost:



Table 8.5: A Postal Code Stored as a Number and as Text


SELECT '07201'::INTEGER AS as_integer,
       '07201'::VARCHAR(5) AS as_text;





as_integer


as_text






7201


07201








Dates and times. DATE holds a calendar date, TIMESTAMP a date and a time of day. The book writes date values in the ISO form '2026-01-05', which PostgreSQL reads the same way whatever its settings, and the standard’s typed literal DATE '2026-01-05', used since Section 3.2. A TIMESTAMP records a time without saying where; inspected_at is one, since HG Industries inspects in one plant. A business spread across time zones uses TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE, which records an instant and displays it in the reader’s zone.
True or false. BOOLEAN holds true, false, or NULL, as the results of Table 8.3 show. The sales schema’s date dimension marks weekends with one.
A domain narrower than its type is finished with a CHECK constraint, as Section 6.2 described: list_price > 0, level BETWEEN 1 AND 3. A domain that is a short list of values, an enumeration, can be implemented in two ways (Blaha and Premerlani 1998). The list can be written into the table as a check, CHECK (unit_of_measure IN ('EA', 'FT')); or the values can be rows of a table of their own, a lookup table, which the column refers to with a foreign key. The quality schema’s defect_type table is a lookup table: each defect code is a row, with its description. The check is simpler; the lookup table lets the list grow by inserting a row instead of changing a table’s definition, and gives each value a place for its description. You should choose the lookup table when the list will change or its values need more than a name. Table 8.6 collects the choices.
