Every “not” of Table 8.6 is a type that accepts the value and then misbehaves: a date stored as text sorts '10/2/2026' before '9/2/2026', and a price stored as text cannot be summed. The next section writes the types into tables.

title: 8  Defining and Populating Tables
text:
8.3 Creating tables and constraints
This section illustrates step 3: writing a CREATE TABLE statement for each table of a relational schema, with its constraints.
Recall the complete relational schema of the customer table from Listing 6.1: five columns with their types and NULL rules, a primary key, and an alternate key. The stage D1 script turns it into one statement:

CREATE TABLE distribution.customer (
    customer_pk     INTEGER GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY
                    PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_number VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    name            VARCHAR(60) NOT NULL,
    city            VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL,
    state           CHAR(2)     NOT NULL
);

Each line inside the parentheses declares one column: its name, its type, and its column constraints, the rules that concern that column alone. Read them against Listing 6.1. customer_pk is INTEGER, filled by the database (GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY), and the primary key (PRIMARY KEY), which also makes it NOT NULL and unique. customer_number must be present (NOT NULL) and may not repeat (UNIQUE), the alternate key. The other three columns must be present. Nothing in the listing is left out, and nothing is added.
A rule that concerns several columns is written after the columns, as a table constraint. The customer_order table of stage D2 has two, a foreign key and a check that compares two dates:

CREATE TABLE distribution.customer_order (
    customer_order_pk   INTEGER GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY
                        PRIMARY KEY,
    order_number        VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    order_date          DATE        NOT NULL,
    requested_ship_date DATE,
    customer_fk         INTEGER     NOT NULL
        REFERENCES distribution.customer (customer_pk),
    CHECK (requested_ship_date >= order_date)
);

requested_ship_date has no NOT NULL, so it may be missing, as the attribute requestedShipDate [0..1] allows. customer_fk is a foreign key: REFERENCES distribution.customer (customer_pk) says that every value must be the key of an existing customer. It is written here as a column constraint, which is allowed because it concerns one column; FOREIGN KEY (customer_fk) REFERENCES distribution.customer (customer_pk) after the columns says the same thing as a table constraint, and is the only form for a foreign key of several columns. The last line is a check that involves two columns, so it is written as a table constraint. The standard requires that form for a check of several columns; PostgreSQL also accepts such a check written on one of its columns, but the table constraint is the portable form, and it says what the rule concerns.
Notice that a check passes when its condition is true or unknown. An order with no requested ship date makes requested_ship_date >= order_date unknown (Section 3.3), and the order is accepted, as it should be. A check such as this one therefore passes a NULL and does not make a column required; NOT NULL is how a column is made required. (A check written to test for NULL, such as CHECK (state IS NOT NULL), does refuse one, and NOT NULL says the same thing more plainly.)
The database gives every constraint a name, and names it in every message that reports a violation. A constraint left unnamed, as in the book’s scripts, is named by PostgreSQL from its table and columns: the check of customer_order becomes customer_order_check, the alternate key customer_order_order_number_key. A constraint can be named explicitly by writing CONSTRAINT order_ship_after_order CHECK (...), which you should do when the generated name would not tell a reader which rule was broken.

Example 8.1 (Creating the order line table) The sales department of HG Industries wants to record what each order is for: the products, the quantity of each, and the price charged, which may differ from the list price. Chapter 6 mapped the order line, composed in its order, to the complete relational schema of Listing 6.10. The example assumes stage D2, with customer_order in place, and a product table already created by the first statement of the stage D3 script.
The request. Write the CREATE TABLE statement for order_line from Listing 6.10, and confirm that the database holds every constraint the listing names.
The design. The columns come first, each line of the listing becoming one column declaration:

CREATE TABLE distribution.order_line (
    order_line_pk     INTEGER GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY
                      PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_order_fk INTEGER NOT NULL
        REFERENCES distribution.customer_order
            (customer_order_pk)
        ON DELETE CASCADE,
    line_number       INTEGER NOT NULL
                      CHECK (line_number > 0),
    product_fk        INTEGER NOT NULL
        REFERENCES distribution.product (product_pk),
    quantity          INTEGER NOT NULL
                      CHECK (quantity > 0),
    unit_price        NUMERIC(10,2) NOT NULL
                      CHECK (unit_price > 0),
    UNIQUE (customer_order_fk, line_number)
);

The two foreign keys differ in one clause. customer_order_fk adds ON DELETE CASCADE: deleting an order deletes its lines, as the composition of Section 6.3.6 requires. product_fk has no ON DELETE clause, so it takes the default, NO ACTION, and a product that has been ordered cannot be deleted. Each positive quantity, price, and line number of the listing is a CHECK on its column. The alternate key (customer_order_fk, line_number) spans two columns, so it is a table constraint, the last line.
The result. The standard view information_schema.table_constraints lists the constraints the database holds for the table:



Table 8.7: The Constraints of the Order Line Table


SELECT constraint_name, constraint_type
FROM information_schema.table_constraints
WHERE table_schema = 'distribution'
  AND table_name = 'order_line'
  AND constraint_name NOT LIKE '%not_null'
ORDER BY constraint_type, constraint_name;





constraint_name


constraint_type






order_line_line_number_check


CHECK




order_line_quantity_check


CHECK




order_line_unit_price_check


CHECK




order_line_customer_order_fk_fkey


FOREIGN KEY




order_line_product_fk_fkey


FOREIGN KEY




order_line_pkey


PRIMARY KEY




order_line_customer_order_fk_line_number_key


UNIQUE








The last condition of the query leaves out the six NOT NULL rules, which PostgreSQL’s version of the view lists as checks whose names end in not_null.
The check. Listing 6.10 names one primary key, one alternate key, two foreign keys, and three checks: seven constraints, and Table 8.7 has seven rows, one of each kind named.
Interpretation. The table now enforces the business’s rules about order lines without any program’s help. A line cannot be recorded for an order or a product that does not exist, with a zero quantity or a zero price, or with a line number its order already uses; and an order cannot be removed while leaving its lines behind.
Where it breaks. The constraints check each line alone. Nothing requires an order to have at least one line, which the multiplicity 1..* of the class model says it must; an order with no lines is accepted, and a query such as those of Section 3.7 must find it. Nor does anything tie unit_price to the product’s list_price, deliberately, since the business sells below list.

The constraints are the database’s defense, and they are worth seeing at work. A statement that breaks one is refused, with a message that names the constraint. For example, a second customer with an existing customer number breaks the alternate key:

INSERT INTO distribution.customer
    (customer_number, name, city, state)
VALUES ('C-1001', 'Riverside Supply', 'Rogers', 'AR');
ERROR:  duplicate key value violates unique constraint "customer_customer_number_key"
DETAIL:  Key (customer_number)=(C-1001) already exists.

An order line for a product that does not exist breaks a foreign key, and one with a quantity of zero breaks a check:

INSERT INTO distribution.order_line
    (customer_order_fk, line_number, product_fk,
     quantity, unit_price)
VALUES (12, 3, 9, 5, 89.00);
ERROR:  insert or update on table "order_line" violates foreign key constraint "order_line_product_fk_fkey"
DETAIL:  Key (product_fk)=(9) is not present in table "product".


INSERT INTO distribution.order_line
    (customer_order_fk, line_number, product_fk,
     quantity, unit_price)
VALUES (12, 3, 1, 0, 89.00);
ERROR:  new row for relation "order_line" violates check constraint "order_line_quantity_check"
DETAIL:  Failing row contains (23, 12, 3, 1, 0, 89.00).

Each message names the table, the constraint, and for a key the offending value, which is usually enough to find the bad row in a long script. An identity column declared GENERATED ALWAYS refuses a value supplied for it, so that the database alone numbers its rows; the message’s hint names the override that a script copying rows from another database, keys and all, would use:

INSERT INTO distribution.customer
    (customer_pk, customer_number, name, city, state)
VALUES (9, 'C-1009', 'Rogers Farm Supply', 'Rogers', 'AR');
ERROR:  cannot insert a non-DEFAULT value into column "customer_pk"
DETAIL:  Column "customer_pk" is an identity column defined as GENERATED ALWAYS.
HINT:  Use OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE to override.

The order of the statements in a script follows from the foreign keys. A table can be created only after every table it refers to, so the stage scripts create customer, then customer_order, then product and order_line. Removing tables runs the other way: DROP TABLE removes a table and its rows, and it refuses to remove a table that another table refers to:

DROP TABLE distribution.customer;
ERROR:  cannot drop table distribution.customer because other objects depend on it
DETAIL:  constraint customer_order_customer_fk_fkey on table distribution.customer_order depends on table distribution.customer
HINT:  Use DROP ... CASCADE to drop the dependent objects too.

As the message’s hint says, DROP TABLE distribution.customer CASCADE would remove the foreign key constraints that depend on customer and then the table; the tables that referred to it would remain, without their foreign keys. DROP SCHEMA distribution CASCADE, which code/sql/reset.sql runs, removes the schema with every table in it. Once kept, neither can be undone, and you should keep them in scripts that rebuild what they remove. (A change can be tried without being kept, inside a transaction, as Section 8.4 shows.) The tables now exist, and the next section changes their rows.

title: 8  Defining and Populating Tables
text:
8.4 Inserting, updating, and deleting rows
This section illustrates step 4: putting rows into tables, and then changing and removing them as the business changes.
INSERT adds rows to a table. Its usual form names the table, lists the columns it supplies, and gives a row of values for each row to add, in the same order as the columns:

INSERT INTO distribution.customer
    (customer_number, name, city, state)
VALUES ('C-1009', 'Rogers Farm Supply', 'Rogers', 'AR'),
       ('C-1029', 'Crowley''s Ridge Hardware',
        'Jonesboro', 'AR');

The statement adds two customers. A column left out of the list, such as customer_pk, takes its default: the next identity value for a key, and NULL for a column with no default. You should always write the column list. Without it, the values are matched to the table’s columns in the order the table declared them, and a script written that way breaks, or worse loads values into the wrong columns, when a column is added. Notice the second name: a quote inside a text value is written twice, 'Crowley''s Ridge Hardware', which is how SQL tells the quote in the value from the quote that ends it.






TipTrying a change without keeping it



DataGrip and DBeaver keep each statement’s change the moment it runs (auto-commit). A change run that way alters your copy of the stage for good, and the examples and exercises that assume the stage as loaded no longer give the book’s results. To try a change without keeping it, run BEGIN before it and ROLLBACK after it:
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO distribution.customer
    (customer_number, name, city, state)
VALUES ('C-1009', 'Rogers Farm Supply', 'Rogers', 'AR');
SELECT * FROM distribution.customer;
ROLLBACK;
The statements between the two form a transaction, and ROLLBACK discards everything it changed, as if it had never run. After a statement is refused, PostgreSQL refuses every later statement of the transaction until the ROLLBACK, so try each change that may be refused in a transaction of its own. Chapter 9 presents transactions. Try the insert above, and every change of this chapter’s examples and exercises, this way: Example 8.2 and Example 8.3 assume stage D3 as loaded, and both add C-1009 themselves. A change kept by mistake is undone by reloading the stage with its script in code/sql/load/.


A foreign key column needs the key of the row it refers to, and a generated key is not something you know in advance. The stage scripts can write the keys as numbers, since they insert into empty tables in a fixed order (code/sql/README.md explains). A statement that records a new order for an existing customer instead looks the key up by the customer’s number, with a scalar subquery (Section 3.8) in place of the value. The example below records a whole order this way.

Example 8.2 (Recording a new customer’s first order) On April 2, 2026, Rogers Farm Supply of Rogers, Arkansas, placed its first order with HG Industries: eight GC-300 steel garden carts at $119.00, twelve HT-100 hand trucks at $89.00, and ten HT-200 convertible hand trucks at $139.00, to ship by April 9. The sales department gave it customer number C-1009 and the order the number SO-5018. The example assumes stage D3.
The request. Record the customer, the order, and its three lines, referring to the customer and the products by their business numbers.
The design. The customer comes first, since the order refers to it:

INSERT INTO distribution.customer
    (customer_number, name, city, state)
VALUES ('C-1009', 'Rogers Farm Supply', 'Rogers', 'AR');

The order’s customer_fk is found by a subquery on customer_number:

INSERT INTO distribution.customer_order
    (order_number, order_date, requested_ship_date,
     customer_fk)
VALUES ('SO-5018', DATE '2026-04-02', DATE '2026-04-09',
        (SELECT customer_pk
         FROM distribution.customer
         WHERE customer_number = 'C-1009'));

Each line looks up its order by order_number and its product by product_number in the same way:

INSERT INTO distribution.order_line
    (customer_order_fk, line_number, product_fk,
     quantity, unit_price)
VALUES
  ((SELECT customer_order_pk
    FROM distribution.customer_order
    WHERE order_number = 'SO-5018'), 1,
   (SELECT product_pk FROM distribution.product
    WHERE product_number = 'GC-300'), 8, 119.00),
  ((SELECT customer_order_pk
    FROM distribution.customer_order
    WHERE order_number = 'SO-5018'), 2,
   (SELECT product_pk FROM distribution.product
    WHERE product_number = 'HT-100'), 12, 89.00),
  ((SELECT customer_order_pk
    FROM distribution.customer_order
    WHERE order_number = 'SO-5018'), 3,
   (SELECT product_pk FROM distribution.product
    WHERE product_number = 'HT-200'), 10, 139.00);

The result. After the three statements, a query joins the new rows back together:



Table 8.8: Order SO-5018 After the Three Inserts


SELECT c.customer_pk, o.customer_order_pk,
       l.line_number, p.product_number, l.quantity,
       l.unit_price, l.quantity * l.unit_price AS value
FROM distribution.customer AS c
JOIN distribution.customer_order AS o
  ON o.customer_fk = c.customer_pk
JOIN distribution.order_line AS l
  ON l.customer_order_fk = o.customer_order_pk
JOIN distribution.product AS p
  ON p.product_pk = l.product_fk
WHERE c.customer_number = 'C-1009'
ORDER BY l.line_number;

The check. A generated key comes from the column’s identity counter, not from a count of the rows. On a freshly loaded stage D3 the counters of customer and customer_order stand at 8 and 12, the last keys the load used, so the new customer’s key is 9 and the new order’s is 13, as Table 8.8 shows. An insert takes the next value even when it is refused or rolled back, and the value is never given back; in a copy of the stage where inserts have been tried, the keys are higher and the rows are otherwise the same. The three line values are 8 × 119.00 = 952.00, 12 × 89.00 = 1,068.00, and 10 × 139.00 = 1,390.00, and the order is worth $3,410.00.
Interpretation. Rogers Farm Supply is now a customer with one open order, and every query of the earlier chapters counts it: it appears in the order report, in the sales of each product, and among the orders due to ship on April 9.
Where it breaks. A subquery that finds no row returns NULL. A mistyped product number, 'HT-210', makes product_fk NULL, and the NOT NULL of the column refuses the line:

INSERT INTO distribution.order_line
    (customer_order_fk, line_number, product_fk,
     quantity, unit_price)
VALUES
  ((SELECT customer_order_pk
    FROM distribution.customer_order
    WHERE order_number = 'SO-5018'), 3,
   (SELECT product_pk FROM distribution.product
    WHERE product_number = 'HT-210'), 10, 139.00);
ERROR:  null value in column "product_fk" of relation "order_line" violates not-null constraint
DETAIL:  Failing row contains (23, 13, 3, null, 10, 139.00).

The refusal protects the order. Had product_fk allowed NULL, the line would have been recorded for no product at all.

INSERT can also take its rows from a query, INSERT INTO t (columns) SELECT ..., which adds every row the query returns. It is the form used to copy or transform rows already in the database, and Section 8.5 uses it to move loaded rows into their table. It has one danger the VALUES form lacks: a query that finds no rows inserts nothing, and reports success.
UPDATE changes values in existing rows. It names the table, sets one or more columns to new values, and chooses the rows with a WHERE clause, as a query does. Suppose that HG Industries raises the list prices of its garden carts by 5 percent, rounded to the cent. Before changing anything, preview the change with a query that selects the same rows and computes the new values:



Table 8.9: The Garden Carts’ Prices, Before and After a 5 Percent Increase


SELECT product_number, list_price,
       ROUND(list_price * 1.05, 2) AS new_price
FROM distribution.product
WHERE product_number LIKE 'GC-%'
ORDER BY product_number;





product_number

Table 8.9 shows the two rows the update will touch and what they will become. The update itself reuses the preview’s WHERE clause and its expression:

UPDATE distribution.product
SET list_price = ROUND(list_price * 1.05, 2)
WHERE product_number LIKE 'GC-%';




Table 8.10: The Product List After the Price Increase


SELECT product_number, description, list_price
FROM distribution.product
ORDER BY product_number;

The two carts in Table 8.10 have the prices the preview promised, $124.95 and $156.45, and the hand trucks are unchanged. The preview is a habit worth keeping. An UPDATE without a WHERE clause changes every row of the table, and the database will not ask whether you meant it; the preview shows the rows before they change. Notice also that the new prices apply to future orders only. The lines already recorded keep their unit_price, which is why Section 7.6 kept the price of a line apart from the product’s.
An update must leave every row within its constraints, or it is refused as an insert would be. Moving an order’s requested ship date before its order date breaks the check of customer_order:

UPDATE distribution.customer_order
SET requested_ship_date = DATE '2026-01-01'
WHERE order_number = 'SO-5001';
ERROR:  new row for relation "customer_order" violates check constraint "customer_order_check"
DETAIL:  Failing row contains (1, SO-5001, 2026-01-05, 2026-01-01, 1).

DELETE removes rows, chosen by a WHERE clause. The foreign keys decide what happens to the rows that refer to them. Recall from Section 6.3.6 that an order line is composed in its order, so that deleting an order deletes its lines; Chapter 6 promised to show it, at stage D5, with order SO-5012, which has two lines and has not shipped. Before the deletion, the last two orders have these lines:



Table 8.11: The Last Two Orders and Their Lines, Before the Deletion


SELECT o.order_number,
       COUNT(l.order_line_pk) AS lines
FROM distribution.customer_order AS o
LEFT JOIN distribution.order_line AS l
  ON l.customer_order_fk = o.customer_order_pk
WHERE o.order_number >= 'SO-5011'
GROUP BY o.order_number
ORDER BY o.order_number;





order_number


lines






SO-5011


2




SO-5012


2








The deletion names only the order:

DELETE FROM distribution.customer_order
WHERE order_number = 'SO-5012';




Table 8.12: Order Lines Remaining After SO-5012 Is Deleted


SELECT COUNT(*) AS order_lines,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE customer_order_fk = 12)
         AS lines_of_so5012
FROM distribution.order_line;





order_lines


lines_of_so5012






20


0








Stage D5 holds 22 order lines, and Table 8.12 shows 20, none of them SO-5012’s: the database deleted the two lines itself, because of the ON DELETE CASCADE of customer_order_fk. (FILTER limits one aggregate to some rows; it is standard SQL, and PostgreSQL supports it.) A foreign key without the cascade refuses instead. Order SO-5001 has shipped, and its shipment refers to it:

DELETE FROM distribution.customer_order
WHERE order_number = 'SO-5001';
ERROR:  update or delete on table "customer_order" violates foreign key constraint "shipment_customer_order_fk_fkey" on table "shipment"
DETAIL:  Key (customer_order_pk)=(1) is still referenced from table "shipment".

The refusal is the design working. The shipment is a record of goods that left the warehouse, and the database will not let the order it fulfilled disappear from under it. In the same way, a product that has been ordered cannot be deleted, since order lines refer to it:

DELETE FROM distribution.product
WHERE product_number = 'HT-100';
ERROR:  update or delete on table "product" violates foreign key constraint "order_line_product_fk_fkey" on table "order_line"
DETAIL:  Key (product_pk)=(1) is still referenced from table "order_line".

A DELETE without a WHERE clause removes every row and keeps the table. TRUNCATE, standard since SQL:2008, also empties a table, faster, without examining the rows one at a time, but it is not the same. A DELETE follows each foreign key’s delete rule, so at stage D3 deleting every order deletes every order line with it; TRUNCATE refuses a table that another table refers to, unless the tables that refer to it are truncated with it:

TRUNCATE distribution.customer_order;
ERROR:  cannot truncate a table referenced in a foreign key constraint
DETAIL:  Table "order_line" references "customer_order".
HINT:  Truncate table "order_line" at the same time, or use TRUNCATE ... CASCADE.

Neither statement removes the table; DROP TABLE does (Section 8.3). The three are easy to confuse, and they differ in what remains: rows and table, table only, or nothing.
Under auto-commit, each statement of this section changes the database as soon as it runs, and each is complete in itself; inside a BEGIN and ROLLBACK, as in the callout of Section 8.4, its change is not kept. Chapter 9 shows how several statements, such as the three inserts of Example 8.2, can be made to succeed or fail together. The next section adds rows in bulk, from files.

title: 8  Defining and Populating Tables
text:
8.5 Loading data from files
This section illustrates step 4 again, for rows that arrive as files, and step 5, checking them before they enter the database.
Data often reaches a database as a file. A colleague exports a list from another system or a spreadsheet, and the rows must be loaded into tables that someone else designed. The usual form is a CSV file (comma-separated values): plain text, one row per line, the values separated by commas, and usually a first line of column names. A value that contains a comma or a quote is enclosed in double quotes. The file carries no types, no keys, and no rules; everything in it is text, and nothing in it has been checked.
PostgreSQL offers two ways to load such a file, and the tools add a third:

COPY table FROM 'file' is an SQL statement that the server runs. It reads a file on the server’s own machine, so it needs a server-side path, and PostgreSQL allows it only to superusers and to roles granted pg_read_server_files.
\copy table FROM 'file' is a psql command (Appendix A) that reads a file on your machine and sends its rows to the server. It takes the same options as COPY, needs no special privilege, and is the form the book uses.
The import wizards of DataGrip and DBeaver read a file on your machine, show its first rows, and map its columns to a table’s columns. They are convenient for a single load, and they do what \copy does.

Whichever you use, do not load a file straight into its final table. If one row breaks a constraint, the whole load is refused, and you learn only about the first bad row; and a value that is wrong but legal, such as a city misspelled, goes in unnoticed. Load the file instead into a staging table, a table with the file’s columns, all of type TEXT and without constraints, which accepts anything. Then examine the staged rows with queries, and move them into the real table with INSERT ... SELECT, cleaning them on the way.

Example 8.3 (Loading new customers from a file) HG Industries is expanding into Oklahoma, Kansas, and Texas, and the sales department has signed 22 new customers. A sales assistant exported them from the contact list to code/data/new-customers-raw.csv, one customer per line with a header line: the customer number, name, city, and state. The first lines of the file are:
customer_number,name,city,state
C-1009,Rogers Farm Supply,Rogers,AR
C-1010,Boston Mountain Hardware,Harrison,AR
C-1011,Riverbend Home and Garden,Conway,AR
The example assumes stage D3, which holds the eight customers of stage D1.
The request. Load the new customers into distribution.customer, after finding and repairing whatever is wrong with the file.
The design. The staging table has the file’s four columns, as text:

CREATE TABLE distribution.customer_staging (
    customer_number TEXT,
    name            TEXT,
    city            TEXT,
    state           TEXT
);

The file is loaded with psql, started in the companion code’s folder. The options say that the file is CSV and that its first line is a header:

\copy distribution.customer_staging FROM 'data/new-customers-raw.csv' WITH (FORMAT csv, HEADER true)

A \copy command is one line, however long, and ends without a semicolon. psql answers COPY 23: the file holds 23 rows, although the sales department signed 22 customers. The staged rows are now examined with queries. The first looks for customer numbers that appear more than once:



Table 8.13: Customer Numbers That Appear More Than Once in the File


SELECT customer_number, COUNT(*) AS copies,
       COUNT(DISTINCT name || city || state)
         AS different_versions
FROM distribution.customer_staging
GROUP BY customer_number
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

C-1015 appears twice, and both copies are the same, so one can be dropped. The second query looks for states that are not two capital letters, with the state shown between brackets so that a space is visible:



Table 8.14: Staged Customers Whose State Is Not Two Capital Letters


SELECT customer_number, city,
       '[' || state || ']' AS state_as_loaded
FROM distribution.customer_staging
WHERE state <> UPPER(state) OR LENGTH(state) <> 2;

Norman’s state was typed as ok with a trailing space. The CHAR(2) column would not refuse it: PostgreSQL drops extra characters that are spaces, and would store ok in lower case, where a query grouping by state would count it apart from every OK. The third query looks for customers that the database already holds, which the alternate key would refuse:



Table 8.15: Staged Customers Already in the Database


SELECT s.customer_number, s.name
FROM distribution.customer_staging AS s
JOIN distribution.customer AS c
  ON c.customer_number = s.customer_number;





customer_number


name












Table 8.15 is empty, as it should be. The move into customer repairs the two problems found: DISTINCT keeps one copy of each identical row, and UPPER(TRIM(state)) removes the space and capitalizes the state. The staging table is then dropped:

INSERT INTO distribution.customer
    (customer_number, name, city, state)
SELECT DISTINCT customer_number, name, city,
       UPPER(TRIM(state))
FROM distribution.customer_staging;

DROP TABLE distribution.customer_staging;

The result. The customers by state, after the load:



Table 8.16: Customers by State After the Load


SELECT state, COUNT(*) AS customers
FROM distribution.customer
GROUP BY state
ORDER BY state;





state

The check. The file has 24 lines: a header and 23 rows. One row is a duplicate, so 22 customers are new, and with the 8 of stage D1 the table should hold 30. The counts of Table 8.16 add up to 30, and Norman is counted under OK, not in a group of its own.
Interpretation. HG Industries now has customers in five states, and eleven of its twelve customers outside Arkansas and Missouri are new; before the load, Cedar Creek Home Center of Tulsa was the only one. Every query of the earlier chapters sees the new customers as if they had been entered one at a time.
Where it breaks. DISTINCT removes only rows that are identical in every column. Had the two copies of C-1015 differed, say in the spelling of the city, DISTINCT would have kept both, and the alternate key would have refused the whole INSERT, naming C-1015. The different_versions column of Table 8.13 checks for this case before the move, and a duplicate with two versions needs a person to decide which is right.

The staging pattern of Example 8.3 is the heart of every load: land the data where nothing can refuse it, look at it with queries, and move it with a query that repairs what the looking found. Chapter 11 builds on it, as extract, transform, and load. Two problems that files commonly carry did not occur in this one. A code written with digits loses its leading zeros if the file passed through a spreadsheet that took the code for a number (Table 8.5), and nothing in the database can restore them. Dates arrive in more than one form: 2026-04-13 and 4/13/2026 are the same day, and a staging query must find which form each row uses before converting it, as Exercise 8.8 asks. The next section changes the tables themselves.

title: 8  Defining and Populating Tables
text:
8.6 Changing a table’s definition
This section changes the definition of tables that already hold rows.
A design changes after the database is built: the business records something new, a rule is discovered, or two departments’ data must be connected. Dropping and recreating a table would lose its rows, so SQL changes a table in place with ALTER TABLE. Table 8.17 lists the changes the book uses.



Table 8.17: The Changes ALTER TABLE Makes





To
Write




add a column
ALTER TABLE t ADD COLUMN c type


remove a column
ALTER TABLE t DROP COLUMN c


require a value
ALTER TABLE t ALTER COLUMN c SET NOT NULL


allow NULL again
ALTER TABLE t ALTER COLUMN c DROP NOT NULL


change a column’s type
ALTER TABLE t ALTER COLUMN c TYPE type


add a constraint
ALTER TABLE t ADD CONSTRAINT name ...


remove a constraint
ALTER TABLE t DROP CONSTRAINT name


rename a column
ALTER TABLE t RENAME COLUMN c TO d






A change must hold for the rows already there, and the database checks them before it accepts the change. Requiring a requested ship date on every order is refused at stage D3, since two orders have none:

ALTER TABLE distribution.customer_order
    ALTER COLUMN requested_ship_date SET NOT NULL;
ERROR:  column "requested_ship_date" of relation "customer_order" contains null values

A constraint added to a table applies to every later change. The customer load of Example 8.3 repaired a lower-case state in its INSERT ... SELECT; a check makes the database refuse one. Its name is chosen so that a message names the rule:

ALTER TABLE distribution.customer
    ADD CONSTRAINT customer_state_in_capitals
    CHECK (state = UPPER(state));


INSERT INTO distribution.customer
    (customer_number, name, city, state)
VALUES ('C-1017', 'Canadian River Home Center',
        'Norman', 'ok');
ERROR:  new row for relation "customer" violates check constraint "customer_state_in_capitals"
DETAIL:  Failing row contains (9, C-1017, Canadian River Home Center, Norman, ok).

The most common change adds a column to connect data that were designed apart. Stage P1 adds the production department’s parts, and each product that distribution sells is a manufactured part: the HT-100 hand truck is part HT-100. The P1 script, code/sql/production/p1-part.sql, connects them in three steps, which is the pattern for adding a required column to a table that already has rows. First, the column is added, allowing NULL, since the existing products have no value for it yet:

ALTER TABLE distribution.product
    ADD COLUMN manufactured_part_fk INTEGER
        REFERENCES production.manufactured_part (part_fk);

Second, an UPDATE fills it for every product, finding each product’s part by its number. The standard form sets the column to a correlated subquery (Section 3.8):

UPDATE distribution.product
SET manufactured_part_fk =
    (SELECT part_pk
     FROM production.part
     WHERE part.part_number = product.product_number);

The P1 script writes the same update in PostgreSQL’s own form, UPDATE ... FROM production.part WHERE ..., which joins the table being updated to another; both give the same result here. Third, once every product has its part, the column is required:

ALTER TABLE distribution.product
    ALTER COLUMN manufactured_part_fk SET NOT NULL;

The stage P1 database holds the result, and a join through the new column finds each product’s part:



Table 8.18: Each Product and Its Manufactured Part, Stage P1


SELECT p.product_number, p.manufactured_part_fk,
       pt.part_number, pt.standard_cost
FROM distribution.product AS p
JOIN production.part AS pt
  ON pt.part_pk = p.manufactured_part_fk
ORDER BY p.product_number;

Each product of Table 8.18 has found the part with its own number, so the update matched all four. Had one product had no part of the same number, its column would have stayed NULL, and the third step would have been refused, as the ship-date change was: the order of the three steps turns a silent gap into a refusal. The same pattern, create bare, fill, then constrain, is how a large load is often done: the tables are created without their keys, loaded, and the keys added with ALTER TABLE ... ADD CONSTRAINT, so that each constraint checks all the rows once.
A change made with ALTER TABLE must also be made to the scripts that build the database, or the next rebuild will lose it. The book’s database does this by adding each change as a stage script that runs after the scripts before it, as p1-part.sql runs after the distribution stages. You should keep your own databases the same way: the scripts, not the running database, are the definition.

title: 8  Defining and Populating Tables
text:
8.7 Summary
A database is built from its relational schema by a script. The script creates a schema, then each table after the tables it refers to, then the rows in the same order; kept and run again, it is the database’s most useful description.
A data type implements a domain, and the wrong type distorts values. Use INTEGER for keys and counts, NUMERIC for money and recorded measurements, text for every code even one written in digits, and DATE or TIMESTAMP for dates. Floating point cannot hold most decimal fractions exactly, and a number drops a code’s leading zero.
Constraints make the database enforce the business’s rules. PRIMARY KEY, UNIQUE, NOT NULL, REFERENCES, and CHECK implement a relational schema’s keys, NULL rules, foreign keys, and domains, and a statement that breaks one is refused with a message naming it. A rule about one column can be a column constraint; a rule about several is a table constraint, as the standard requires (PostgreSQL also accepts a check of several columns on one column).
INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE change rows, and the constraints judge every change. Write the column list of every INSERT, look up a generated key by its business number with a subquery, and preview every UPDATE and DELETE with a query that selects the same rows. A foreign key decides what a deletion does to the rows that refer to it: ON DELETE CASCADE deletes them with it, and the default refuses the deletion.
A file is loaded into a staging table, examined, and then moved. Load it with psql’s \copy or a tool’s import wizard into a table of text columns with no constraints; find duplicates, malformed values, and existing keys with queries; and move the rows with an INSERT ... SELECT that repairs what the queries found. Count the rows at each step.
ALTER TABLE changes a table that holds rows, and the rows must satisfy the change. A new required column is added in three steps: add it allowing NULL, fill it with an UPDATE, and then require it. Every change to a running database belongs in the scripts that rebuild it.

text:
8.8 Exercises

Exercise 8.1 Match each term on the left with the phrase on the right that defines it.







Term
Definition




a. DDL

b. DML

e. lookup table
5. statements that change the rows of tables





Exercise 8.2 Mark each statement true or false, and correct each false one.

A CHECK (quantity > 0) constraint refuses a row whose quantity is NULL.
DOUBLE PRECISION is a good type for the unit price of an order line, since it holds more digits than NUMERIC(10,2).
An employee number such as 0412 should be stored in an INTEGER column, since it is made of digits.
A foreign key of two columns must be written as a table constraint.
DROP TABLE removes a table’s rows but keeps its definition.



Exercise 8.3 HG Industries wants to record the maintenance done on its machines, one row per job: the machine’s number (such as M-04), the date of the job, the time the machine was stopped and restarted, the technician’s employee number (such as E-0204), the labor hours to the nearest quarter hour, the cost of parts in dollars and cents, whether the job was planned or a breakdown, and a technician’s note of any length.

State the domain of each attribute in words, in the manner of Table 6.2.
Choose a PostgreSQL type and constraints for each, and justify each choice that Table 8.6 does not settle.
Would you record “planned or breakdown” as a BOOLEAN, a check, or a lookup table? Give a reason for your choice.



Exercise 8.4 Stage D4 adds warehouses and the stock level of each product in each warehouse. Its relational schema is Listing 6.7; in addition, a warehouse code is at most 10 characters, a city at most 40, a state two letters, and a quantity on hand and a reorder point are whole numbers that are never negative.

Write the CREATE TABLE statements for warehouse and stock_level, in the order a script must run them.
Compare your statements with code/sql/distribution/d4-warehouse-stock-level.sql and explain any difference.
How many constraints, other than NOT NULL, does stock_level have? Check your answer with a query in the manner of Table 8.7, at stage D4.



Exercise 8.5 For each statement below, run at stage D3 in a transaction of its own that you roll back (Section 8.4), say whether the database accepts it, and if not, which constraint refuses it and why.

An order requested to ship before it was placed:
INSERT INTO distribution.customer_order
    (order_number, order_date, requested_ship_date,
     customer_fk)
VALUES ('SO-5013', DATE '2026-03-20',
        DATE '2026-03-18', 2);

INSERT INTO distribution.customer_order
    (order_number, order_date, customer_fk)
VALUES ('SO-5013', DATE '2026-03-20', 2);

    (customer_order_fk, line_number, product_fk,
     quantity, unit_price)
VALUES (12, 1, 2, 3, 139.00);
A product given away:
INSERT INTO distribution.product
    (product_number, description, list_price)
VALUES ('GC-500', 'Folding garden cart', 0);
A customer with a three-letter state:
INSERT INTO distribution.customer
    (customer_number, name, city, state)
VALUES ('C-1009', 'Rogers Farm Supply', 'Rogers', 'ARK');



Exercise 8.6 HG Industries raises the list prices of its two hand trucks, the HT-100 and the HT-200, by 3 percent, rounded to the cent. Use stage D3.

Compute the two new prices by hand.
Write a query that previews the change, in the manner of Table 8.9, and compare its result with your answer to a.
Write the UPDATE statement. If you run it, run it inside a transaction you roll back (Section 8.4).
What would your UPDATE do if its WHERE clause were left out, and how would the preview have warned you?



Exercise 8.7 For each statement below, run at stage D5 in a transaction of its own that you roll back (Section 8.4), say whether the database accepts it and what it removes, or which constraint refuses it.

DELETE FROM distribution.customer_order WHERE order_number = 'SO-5011';
DELETE FROM distribution.customer_order WHERE order_number = 'SO-5004';
DELETE FROM distribution.product WHERE product_number = 'GC-400';
DELETE FROM distribution.customer WHERE customer_number = 'C-1008';



Exercise 8.8 The new customers of Example 8.3 placed 40 orders in April 2026, which the sales assistant exported to code/data/april-orders-raw.csv, with the columns order_number, customer_number, order_date, and requested_ship_date. Assume stage D3 with the customers of Example 8.3 loaded. If you run your statements, run them in one transaction that you roll back at the end (Section 8.4), loading the customers as Example 8.3 does and then the orders.

Write the statements that create a staging table for the file and load it with \copy.
Write a query that finds the rows whose dates are not in the ISO form YYYY-MM-DD. How many are there, and what form do they use?
Write the INSERT ... SELECT that moves the orders into distribution.customer_order, converting both dates and finding each order’s customer_fk from its customer number. An empty requested ship date in the file must become NULL.
How many orders should the insert add, and how many of them should have no requested ship date? Check your answer with a query of stage G, which holds the same orders among those of all its customers: count the April 2026 orders of the new customers, C-1009 to C-1030.



Exercise 8.9 The sales department divides its customers into two territories: East for customers in Arkansas and Missouri, West for Oklahoma, Kansas, and Texas. Every customer must have a territory, and no other territory exists.

Write the statements that add a required column territory to distribution.customer, fill it, and restrict it to the two values, in the order the database requires. If you run them at stage G, run them inside a transaction you roll back (Section 8.4).
Write a query of stage G that previews the change by counting the customers each territory will hold.
Explain why adding the column as NOT NULL in one step would be refused at stage G, but accepted in a database with no customers yet.



Exercise 8.10 Northwind’s orders.freight has the type REAL, a floating-point number. Using the Northwind database of Section C.11, loaded with the book’s loader (Section A.6):

Compare the sum of freight as it is with the sum of each value rounded to cents (freight::NUMERIC(10, 2)), and count the values whose stored value is not a whole number of cents, by comparing each REAL value with its rounding (freight <> freight::NUMERIC(10, 2)).
Explain the difference, with Section 8.2, and explain why the values nevertheless look like whole numbers of cents when PostgreSQL prints them. Give the type you would use instead.



Exercise 8.11 The meat_poultry_egg_establishments table of the Practical SQL database of Section C.11 was loaded from the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s directory. Some ZIP codes are shorter than five characters.

Count them by state, with an example of each, and explain how they lost their digits (Section 8.5).
Write the UPDATE statements that repair them, and say what you would check before and after running them inside a transaction you roll back (Section 8.4).

title: 9  Views, Transactions, and Concurrency
text:
9.1 Views
The chapters so far have treated a database as if one person used it at a time, and as if every statement stood alone. Neither is true in a working plant. Sales, shipping, and quality use the same tables at once, and a single piece of work, such as shipping an order, takes several statements that make sense only together. This chapter presents the database’s answers: views, which give each user the queries they need under a name; transactions, which make several statements succeed or fail as one; isolation, which keeps concurrent users from spoiling each other’s work; and privileges, which decide who may do what.
The chapter is brief, and it shows each idea once, mostly on HG Industries’ distribution schema at stages D3 to D5, and for privileges on the production schema of stage P1. The ideas matter to an engineer less as theory than as explanations: of why a report run twice gives two answers, why a statement waits, and why a program must sometimes try a change again.
This section presents views: queries that the database keeps under a name.
A view is a named query stored in the database, which can be used in other queries as if it were a table. It stores no rows. Each time a query uses the view, the database runs the view’s query and uses its result, so a view always reflects the tables as they are at that moment. Recall the flat order report of Section 7.2: normalization split it into four tables, and Section 7.6 observed that the report itself belongs in a query. A view gives that query a name:
CREATE VIEW distribution.order_report AS
SELECT o.order_number, c.customer_number,
       c.name AS customer_name, l.line_number,
       p.product_number, p.description, l.quantity
FROM distribution.customer_order AS o
JOIN distribution.customer AS c
  ON c.customer_pk = o.customer_fk
JOIN distribution.order_line AS l
  ON l.customer_order_fk = o.customer_order_pk
JOIN distribution.product AS p
  ON p.product_pk = l.product_fk;
The view is queried as a table is. A user who wants the lines of SO-5004 no longer writes the joins:
Table 9.1: The Lines of SO-5004, from the Order Report View


SELECT order_number, customer_name, line_number,
       product_number, description, quantity
FROM distribution.order_report
WHERE order_number = 'SO-5004'
ORDER BY line_number;

Because the view stores no rows, the anomalies of Section 7.2 cannot arise in it. A change to a product’s description is made once, in product, and every row of the report shows it at once:
UPDATE distribution.product
SET description = 'Two-wheel steel hand truck'

Both HT-100 lines of Table 9.2 show the new description, from the one row that changed. A view serves three purposes. It simplifies: a join or a calculation written once is used by name. It insulates: if the tables behind it are later split or renamed, the view can be redefined so that the queries built on it keep working. And it restricts: a user can be allowed to query a view without being allowed to query the tables behind it, which Section 9.4 takes up. A view that answers a standing question of the business is worth its name. For example, the warehouse manager’s question “what needs reordering?” becomes, at stage D4:
CREATE VIEW distribution.stock_to_reorder AS
SELECT w.warehouse_code, p.product_number,
       s.quantity_on_hand, s.reorder_point
FROM distribution.stock_level AS s
JOIN distribution.warehouse AS w
  ON w.warehouse_pk = s.warehouse_fk
JOIN distribution.product AS p
  ON p.product_pk = s.product_fk
WHERE s.quantity_on_hand < s.reorder_point;

Can a view be changed, as a table can? A view is updatable when each of its rows comes from one row of one table, so that the database knows which row an INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE on the view must change. In PostgreSQL, a view is updatable automatically when it selects from a single table and has none of DISTINCT, GROUP BY, HAVING, aggregates, window functions, LIMIT or OFFSET, a WITH clause, or set operations such as UNION. Even then, only the view’s columns that are plain columns of the table can be changed through it. The order report joins four tables, and is not updatable:
DELETE FROM distribution.order_report
WHERE order_number = 'SO-5004';
ERROR:  cannot delete from view "order_report"
DETAIL:  Views that do not select from a single table or view are not automatically updatable.
HINT:  To enable deleting from the view, provide an INSTEAD OF DELETE trigger or an unconditional ON DELETE DO INSTEAD rule.
A single-table view is updatable, and it raises a question of its own. The view below shows the customers in Oklahoma, and a clerk who works only with that territory could add customers through it. Nothing yet stops the clerk from adding, through the view, a customer in Arkansas, a row the view itself would never show. The clause WITH CHECK OPTION makes the view refuse such a row:
CREATE VIEW distribution.oklahoma_customer AS
SELECT customer_number, name, city, state
FROM distribution.customer
WHERE state = 'OK'
WITH CHECK OPTION;
INSERT INTO distribution.oklahoma_customer
    (customer_number, name, city, state)
VALUES ('C-1009', 'Rogers Farm Supply', 'Rogers', 'AR');
ERROR:  new row violates check option for view "oklahoma_customer"
DETAIL:  Failing row contains (9, C-1009, Rogers Farm Supply, Rogers, AR).
A view stores no rows: its query runs, as part of the query that uses it, every time it is used, which is what keeps it current. A query of a view therefore costs about what the same query would cost written out with the view’s joins: PostgreSQL merges the view’s query into the query that uses it, so that a condition such as order_number = 'SO-5004' is applied inside the joins. PostgreSQL also offers a materialized view, which stores its result and is brought up to date only when told to (REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW); it trades currency for speed, as the summary tables of Chapter 11 do. The next section turns from naming queries to grouping changes.

title: 9  Views, Transactions, and Concurrency
text:
9.2 Transactions and the ACID properties
This section presents transactions: groups of statements that succeed or fail as one.
Shipping an order at HG Industries is several changes. The clerk records a shipment, a shipment line for each order line shipped, and a smaller quantity on hand for each product that left the warehouse. For order SO-5011 at stage D5, 30 HT-100 hand trucks and 12 GC-300 carts leaving Fayetteville, the changes are four statements; the stock levels of the two products in Fayetteville have keys 1 and 3 (stock_level_pk), and the order’s lines have keys 19 and 20 (order_line_pk):

INSERT INTO distribution.shipment
    (shipment_number, shipped_on, carrier,
     customer_order_fk, warehouse_fk)
VALUES ('SH-9012', DATE '2026-03-10',
        'Boston Mountain Freight', 11, 1);

INSERT INTO distribution.shipment_line
    (shipment_fk, order_line_fk, quantity)
SELECT shipment_pk, 19, 30 FROM distribution.shipment
WHERE shipment_number = 'SH-9012'
UNION ALL
SELECT shipment_pk, 20, 12 FROM distribution.shipment
WHERE shipment_number = 'SH-9012';

UPDATE distribution.stock_level
SET quantity_on_hand = quantity_on_hand - 30
WHERE stock_level_pk = 1;

UPDATE distribution.stock_level
SET quantity_on_hand = quantity_on_hand - 12
WHERE stock_level_pk = 3;

The four statements belong together. A shipment recorded without its stock decrease overstates the stock; a stock decrease without its shipment loses carts from the books. Suppose that the clerk, not noticing that SO-5011 has already shipped, runs the four statements again, as shipment SH-9013. The warehouse had 18 GC-300 carts and now has 6, so the last statement drives the quantity below zero, and the check of stock_level refuses it. Run one at a time, as the tools run statements by default, the first three have already taken effect:



Table 9.4: Shipping SO-5011 a Second Time, Statement by Statement




 
  
    Step 
    Session 
    Statement 
    Result 
  
 

  
    1 
    A 
    INSERT INTO shipment (shipment_number, shipped_on, carrier, customer_order_fk, warehouse_fk) VALUES ('SH-9013', DATE '2026-03-11', 'Boston Mountain Freight', 11, 1); 
    1 row inserted 
  
  
    2 
    A 
    INSERT INTO shipment_line (shipment_fk, order_line_fk, quantity) SELECT shipment_pk, 19, 30 FROM shipment WHERE shipment_number = 'SH-9013' UNION ALL SELECT shipment_pk, 20, 12 FROM shipment WHERE shipment_number = 'SH-9013'; 
    2 rows inserted 
  
  
    3 
    A 
    UPDATE stock_level SET quantity_on_hand = quantity_on_hand - 30 WHERE stock_level_pk = 1; 
    1 row updated 
  
  
    4 
    A 
    UPDATE stock_level SET quantity_on_hand = quantity_on_hand - 12 WHERE stock_level_pk = 3; 
    ERROR:  new row for relation "stock_level" violates check constraint "stock_level_quantity_on_hand_check" 
  
  
    5 
    A 
    SELECT COUNT(*) FROM shipment WHERE customer_order_fk = 11; 
    2 
  
  
    6 
    A 
    SELECT quantity_on_hand FROM stock_level WHERE stock_level_pk IN (1, 3) ORDER BY stock_level_pk; 
    60; 6 
  






The database of Table 9.4 now contradicts itself. It records two shipments of SO-5011, and a second 30 hand trucks gone from Fayetteville (90 became 60), but the 12 carts of the second shipment never left the stock (6 remain). Someone must find and repair the damage by hand.
A transaction is a sequence of statements that the database treats as one unit: either every change it makes takes effect, or none does. BEGIN (or the standard START TRANSACTION) opens a transaction; COMMIT ends it and makes its changes permanent; ROLLBACK ends it and discards them. In PostgreSQL, a statement that fails inside a transaction makes the whole transaction fail: the database refuses every later statement until the transaction ends, and a COMMIT then rolls it back. (The SQL standard, and several other systems, undo only the failed statement and let the transaction go on.) The same mistake, made inside a transaction, leaves no trace:



Table 9.5: Shipping SO-5011 a Second Time, Inside a Transaction




 
  
    Step 
    Session 
    Statement 
    Result 
  
 

  
    1 
    A 
    BEGIN; 
    transaction begun 
  
  
    2 
    A 
    INSERT INTO shipment (shipment_number, shipped_on, carrier, customer_order_fk, warehouse_fk) VALUES ('SH-9013', DATE '2026-03-11', 'Boston Mountain Freight', 11, 1); 
    1 row inserted 
  
  
    3 
    A 
    INSERT INTO shipment_line (shipment_fk, order_line_fk, quantity) SELECT shipment_pk, 19, 30 FROM shipment WHERE shipment_number = 'SH-9013' UNION ALL SELECT shipment_pk, 20, 12 FROM shipment WHERE shipment_number = 'SH-9013'; 
    2 rows inserted 
  
  
    4 
    A 
    UPDATE stock_level SET quantity_on_hand = quantity_on_hand - 30 WHERE stock_level_pk = 1; 
    1 row updated 
  
  
    5 
    A 
    UPDATE stock_level SET quantity_on_hand = quantity_on_hand - 12 WHERE stock_level_pk = 3; 
    ERROR:  new row for relation "stock_level" violates check constraint "stock_level_quantity_on_hand_check" 
  
  
    6 
    A 
    SELECT COUNT(*) FROM shipment WHERE customer_order_fk = 11; 
    ERROR:  current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of transaction block 
  
  
    7 
    A 
    COMMIT; 
    rolled back: the transaction had failed 
  
  
    8 
    A 
    SELECT COUNT(*) FROM shipment WHERE customer_order_fk = 11; 
    1 
  
  
    9 
    A 
    SELECT quantity_on_hand FROM stock_level WHERE stock_level_pk IN (1, 3) ORDER BY stock_level_pk; 
    90; 6 
  






Read Table 9.5 step by step. The first three changes succeed, as before, but inside the transaction. The fourth is refused, and from then on the transaction has failed: even the harmless count of step 6 is refused, and the COMMIT of step 7 rolls everything back. Afterward SO-5011 has one shipment, and the stock stands at 90 and 6, as the first shipment left it. The database is as it was before the clerk’s mistake, and the clerk has an error message to act on.
An error typed in a console has the same effect on an open transaction. Until you type ROLLBACK (or COMMIT, which then rolls back), PostgreSQL refuses every statement with the message that the current transaction is aborted. The ROLLBACK undoes all of the transaction’s work, not only the failed statement, and with it any setting made by SET inside the transaction, such as a search path or a role (Section 9.4). When a statement may fail and the work before it should survive, mark the point before it with a savepoint. Suppose that, after the first shipment of SO-5011, a clerk ships 30 more hand trucks from Fayetteville for another order, and 12 carts with them if the stock allows:
BEGIN;
UPDATE distribution.stock_level
SET quantity_on_hand = quantity_on_hand - 30
WHERE stock_level_pk = 1;
SAVEPOINT before_carts;
UPDATE distribution.stock_level
SET quantity_on_hand = quantity_on_hand - 12
WHERE stock_level_pk = 3;
ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT before_carts;
The second UPDATE is refused, since only 6 carts remain, and ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT before_carts undoes it alone. The transaction is usable again, with the hand trucks’ decrease still in it. The clerk can ship the 6 carts that remain and commit, or end with ROLLBACK and undo everything.
The guarantees a transaction gives are summarized by four properties, known by their initials as ACID:

Atomicity: the transaction’s changes take effect all together or not at all, as Table 9.5 showed.
Consistency: a transaction takes the database from a state that satisfies every rule to another that does: the constraints the database declares, and the business’s rules that the transaction’s statements carry out together. Each statement is checked against the declared constraints as it runs, and a transaction that cannot finish consistent is rolled back.
Isolation: transactions running at the same time do not see each other’s unfinished changes, and do not spoil each other’s work, to the degree the isolation level promises (Section 9.3).
Durability: once COMMIT returns, the changes survive a crash of the server or of the machine.

The first three properties can be seen in a schedule. Durability is the one you trust: PostgreSQL writes every change first to a write-ahead log, a file of changes in the order they were made, and, under its default settings, does not report a commit until the log records it, so that after a crash it can replay the log and recover every committed transaction. Durability does not protect against a mistaken DELETE that was committed, a failed disk, or a lost machine. For those you need a backup, a copy of the database made on purpose and kept elsewhere. PostgreSQL’s pg_dump program writes a database to a single file, and pg_restore (or psql, for a plain SQL dump) rebuilds it, into a new database if need be; a backup that has never been restored should not be trusted.
A transaction also changes when some constraints are checked. Recall from Section 2.3 that PostgreSQL’s NO ACTION and RESTRICT both refuse a deletion that would leave a foreign key pointing nowhere. The SQL standard has RESTRICT check at once and NO ACTION at the end of the statement. In PostgreSQL the difference that matters is another. A NO ACTION foreign key can be declared DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED, and its check then waits until COMMIT, which lets a transaction pass through an inconsistent state on its way to a consistent one. A RESTRICT check is never deferred.
Two practical points follow. First, DataGrip and DBeaver run each statement in its own transaction, committed at once (auto-commit). Both tools can switch a console to manual transactions, but this book keeps the consoles in auto-commit and types BEGIN where it wants a transaction. A DELETE typed in a console is therefore permanent the moment it runs; to experiment safely, type BEGIN first, and end with ROLLBACK. Second, the three inserts that recorded a new customer’s order in Example 8.2 belong in one transaction, between BEGIN and COMMIT, for the reason this section has shown. The next section considers transactions that run at the same time.

title: 9  Views, Transactions, and Concurrency
text:
9.3 Concurrency and isolation levels
This section considers transactions that run at the same time, and the isolation that keeps them from spoiling each other’s work.
A database serves many sessions at once, and their transactions interleave: one clerk’s statements run between another’s. Most of the time they touch different rows and nothing goes wrong. Trouble comes when two transactions read and change the same rows, and the classic case is the lost update: two transactions read a value, each computes a new value from what it read, and the second to write overwrites the first, whose change is lost.
At stage D5 the Fayetteville warehouse holds 18 GC-300 carts (stock level 3). Clerk A ships the 12 carts of SO-5011, and at the same moment clerk B ships 10 carts for another order. Each reads the quantity on hand, subtracts, and writes the result back:



Table 9.6: Two Clerks Ship GC-300 Carts at Once, Reading Before Writing




 
  
    Step 
    Session 
    Statement 
    Result 
  
 

  
    1 
    A 
    BEGIN; 
    transaction begun 
  
  
    2 
    B 
    BEGIN; 
    transaction begun 
  
  
    3 
    A 
    SELECT quantity_on_hand FROM stock_level WHERE stock_level_pk = 3; 
    18 
  
  
    4 
    B 
    SELECT quantity_on_hand FROM stock_level WHERE stock_level_pk = 3; 
    18 
  
  
    5 
    A 
    UPDATE stock_level SET quantity_on_hand = 6 WHERE stock_level_pk = 3; 
    1 row updated 
  
  
    6 
    B 
    UPDATE stock_level SET quantity_on_hand = 8 WHERE stock_level_pk = 3; 
    waits: session A holds a lock on the row 
  
  
    7 
    A 
    COMMIT; 
    committed 
  
  
    8 
    B 
    (step 6 completes) 
    1 row updated 
  
  
    9 
    B 
    COMMIT; 
    committed 
  
  
    10 
    A 
    SELECT quantity_on_hand FROM stock_level WHERE stock_level_pk = 3; 
    8 
  






Both clerks read 18 (steps 3 and 4). Clerk A writes 6, which is 18 − 12. Clerk B’s write must wait (step 6), because A’s uncommitted change locks the row; when A commits, B’s write goes ahead and sets 8, which is 18 − 10. The books now say 8 carts remain, after 22 carts were shipped from 18. A’s update is lost, and nothing refused anything: each statement was legal on its own.
Notice step 6. A transaction that changes a row holds a lock on it until the transaction ends, and another transaction that wants to change the same row waits. The lock did not prevent the lost update, because B’s mistake was made earlier, when it read 18 and decided on 8. The repair is to let the database do the arithmetic, in a single statement that reads and writes the row while holding its lock, and to state the condition under which the change is allowed:



Table 9.7: The Same Two Shipments, Letting the Database Subtract




 
  
    Step 
    Session 
    Statement 
    Result 
  
 

  
    1 
    A 
    BEGIN; 
    transaction begun 
  
  
    2 
    B 
    BEGIN; 
    transaction begun 
  
  
    3 
    A 
    UPDATE stock_level SET quantity_on_hand = quantity_on_hand - 12 WHERE stock_level_pk = 3 AND quantity_on_hand >= 12; 
    1 row updated 
  
  
    4 
    B 
    UPDATE stock_level SET quantity_on_hand = quantity_on_hand - 10 WHERE stock_level_pk = 3 AND quantity_on_hand >= 10; 
    waits: session A holds a lock on the row 
  
  
    5 
    A 
    COMMIT; 
    committed 
  
  
    6 
    B 
    (step 4 completes) 
    0 rows updated 
  
  
    7 
    B 
    ROLLBACK; 
    rolled back 
  
  
    8 
    A 
    SELECT quantity_on_hand FROM stock_level WHERE stock_level_pk = 3; 
    6 
  






B’s update waits for A’s lock, as before (step 4), and when A commits it reads the row again, as A left it: 6 carts, fewer than 10, so its condition fails and it updates no row (step 6). Clerk B’s program learns that the stock is short, rolls back, and can offer a partial shipment or a backorder. The stock ends at 6, which is right. When a program must read a value and decide before it writes, as when it shows the quantity to a clerk, it can take the lock at the read with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE; a second transaction’s SELECT ... FOR UPDATE of the same row then waits until the first ends.
The lost update is one of several ways concurrent transactions can interfere. The SQL standard names three more, which concern what a transaction reads:

A dirty read reads a change that another transaction has made but not committed, and may yet roll back.
A nonrepeatable read reads a row twice and gets two values, because another transaction changed and committed the row in between.
A phantom read runs the same query twice and finds rows the second time that were not there the first, because another transaction inserted them.

One more interference involves no row that both transactions change. In a write skew, two transactions read the same rows, and each then changes a different row on the strength of what it read, so that the two changes together break a rule that each alone keeps. Table 9.11 shows one.
The isolation level of a transaction says which of these it is protected from. The standard defines four levels, and Table 9.8 gives what each allows, with PostgreSQL’s behavior where it is stricter than the standard requires.



Table 9.8: The Standard’s Isolation Levels and the Anomalies Each Allows












Isolation level
Dirty read
Nonrepeatable read
Phantom read
Write skew




READ UNCOMMITTED
allowed (never in PostgreSQL)
allowed
allowed
allowed


READ COMMITTED
prevented
allowed
allowed
allowed

prevented
prevented
allowed (never in PostgreSQL)
allowed


SERIALIZABLE
