title: 12  Databases for Simulation and Analytics
text:
12.6 Exercises

Exercise 12.1 Match each term on the left with the phrase on the right that defines it.







Term
Definition




a. replication
1. starting each scenario from the same random numbers


b. warm-up period
2. a tree stored with a left and a right number for each node


c. common random numbers
3. one run of the model, with its own random numbers


d. nested set
4. the start of each replication, whose statistics are discarded


e. experiment
5. one scenario of a model, run for a number of replications





Exercise 12.2 Besides the routing, list three facts in HG Industries’ database, at stage Q or stage G, that a model of the frame line could read instead of assuming, and name the table and columns each comes from. For one of them, say what the model of Figure 12.1 assumes in its place.


Exercise 12.3 Suppose that HG Industries buys a second powder coat booth and certifies an operator on it, while welding keeps its two staffed welders.

Compute the utilization of each work center by hand, as Table 12.2 does.
Which work center is then the busiest?
Which change to the database of stage Q would the model’s query of Table 12.1 see, so that the scenario needs no change to the model?



Exercise 12.4 Using stage K:

Write a query that lists every model element below the paint station, PNT, in experiment 2, with each element’s name, class name, and nested set numbers, in the manner of Table 12.4.
Before running it, predict the number of rows from the station’s own left and right numbers, and say how you obtained them.
Explain why the right number of an element is always one more than its left number when the element has no children.



Exercise 12.5 Using stage K, write a query that counts the model elements below each of the three stations, SAW, WLD, and PNT, in experiment 1, using the nested set numbers alone and a single GROUP BY. Why should the three counts be equal?


Exercise 12.6 True or false? Explain each answer in a sentence or two.

If a 95 percent confidence interval for the difference between two scenarios excludes zero, the difference is large enough to justify the change.
The average of a_minus_b over the replications in pw_diff_within_rep_view equals the difference between the two scenarios’ averages over the replications.
Since PostgreSQL has no function for the t distribution, a confidence interval cannot be computed in SQL.
Had the two experiments of stage K not used common random numbers, the half-width in Table 12.12 would be expected to be larger.
A table the KSL creates from a DbTableData data class refuses a row whose key names a test case that no other table records.



Exercise 12.7 Using stage K, write a query on ksl_db.within_rep_view that gives, for the response WorkInProcess in each experiment, the number of replications, the average, the standard deviation, and the half-width of a 95 percent confidence interval, each rounded to 3 decimal places, in the manner of Table 12.8. Compare your half-widths with those the KSL stored in Table 12.7.


Exercise 12.8 Using stage K, write a query on ksl_db.across_rep_view that returns one row per queue, the responses whose names end in :Q:TimeInQ, with three columns: the response name, its average under TwoWelders, and its average under ThreeWelders, the averages rounded to 1 decimal place. Use FILTER (Section 4.4), and order the rows by the response name. Which work center’s queue changes least, and why?


Exercise 12.9 Using stage K:

Write a query that gives the paired difference, ThreeWelders minus TwoWelders, in the response LotsCompleted: the number of pairs, the average difference, and the half-width of a 95 percent confidence interval, each rounded to 3 decimal places.
Does the interval include zero? Explain in terms of the frame line why a third welder should change the number of lots completed so little.



Exercise 12.10 Using stage K:

Before writing any query, predict how many rows ksl_db.within_rep_view holds for the responses SAW:Q:TimeInQ, WLD:Q:TimeInQ, and PNT:Q:TimeInQ in the experiment ThreeWelders, and how many rows and columns the same values occupy in a wide table with a row per replication.
Write a query that returns that wide table for the first five replications of ThreeWelders: the replication number and the three queue times, each rounded to 1 decimal place, in replication order.
Add a column giving the total of the three queue times, in minutes. Why is the total easier to compute in the wide shape than in the long one?



Exercise 12.11 Using stage K, write a query on ksl_db.within_rep_view, without using pw_diff_within_rep_view, that returns for the response TimeInShop one row per replication with the value under TwoWelders, the value under ThreeWelders, and ThreeWelders minus TwoWelders, each rounded to 3 decimal places, for the first five replications. Compare your result with Table 12.9, and say what counts as the observation and what as the variables in your table.


Exercise 12.12 An engineer keeps the results of a study in a spreadsheet with one row per scenario and the columns scenario, tis_rep1, tis_rep2, …, tis_rep30, wip_rep1, …, wip_rep30, the time in shop and the work in process of each replication, 61 columns in all.

Name the observations and the variables of the study, and say what is wrong with the spreadsheet’s shape, in the terms of Section 12.4.2.
Give two tidy designs for a table holding the same values, one long and one wide, as CREATE TABLE statements, and say how many rows each holds for two scenarios.
For each of your designs, say what changes when the engineer runs 10 more replications, and when the engineer adds a third response, the number of lots completed.


The remaining exercises are mini-projects. Each asks for a design, the SQL that builds and queries it, and a short written justification, in the manner of Section 12.4.

Exercise 12.13 (Mini-project: a staffing study for the frame line) After Example 12.1, HG Industries’ plant manager asks for a comparison of three options for the frame line: TwoWelders, the line as it is staffed (one staffed machine at SAW, two at WLD, one at PNT); ThreeWelders, with an operator certified on M-07 (three at WLD); and SecondBooth, with a second powder coat booth, installed and staffed (two at PNT). Training the M-07 operator costs $2,400 once, and installing the booth $45,000 once. The cost per hour of running the line is the sum, over the work centers, of the staffed machines times the work center’s hourly_rate in production.work_center. The results of TwoWelders and ThreeWelders are the experiments of those names in stage K; SecondBooth has not been simulated.

Draw a class model of what the study adds, with the classes of the production schema and of ksl_db that it links to.
Map it to tables in a schema study, and write the CREATE statements, following the book’s conventions for keys and names. A scenario must be recordable before it has been simulated.
Write the statements that load the three scenarios and their staffing.
Write a query that returns, for each scenario, its name, its one-time cost, its cost per hour, and the average and half-width of its time in shop from ksl_db.across_rep_stat, keeping the scenarios not yet simulated. Run parts (b) to (d) at stage K in one transaction, ending with ROLLBACK, and state the result.
Explain how your design links a scenario to its experiment, and why it is not a foreign key to ksl_db.experiment.
The manager then asks for scenarios with lots of 50 frames instead of 100. Assuming the study covers only the frame, FR-110, say where the lot size belongs in your class model and give the change to your tables as SQL. How would the answer change if the study also covered the cart frame, CF-310, each part with its own lot size in each scenario?



Exercise 12.14 (Mini-project: a database for benchmarking optimization solvers) A benchmark study runs solver configurations on test problems. A solver configuration has a label, such as SA-slow, the name of the solver algorithm it uses, and its parameter settings by name, such as an initial temperature of 100; different algorithms have different parameters. A test problem has a name, whether it is minimized or maximized, its input variables, each with a name and lower and upper bounds, and, for some problems, the known optimal objective value. Every configuration is run on every problem for a number of macro-replications, each run under the same budget of simulation replications. A run records its random number stream, its starting point and the best point it found (a value for each input variable), the best objective value, the number of replications it used, its status (completed or failed), and, when the optimum is known, its gap, the absolute difference between its best objective value and the optimum divided by the absolute value of the optimum. A run may also record a trace: for each iteration, the replications used so far and the best objective value so far.
The study must answer: (Q1) for each problem and configuration, the proportion of completed runs with a gap of at most 0.01; (Q2) the average number of replications used, by configuration; and (Q3) a given run’s trace, in iteration order.

Draw a class model of the study, and say which classes of Figure 12.3 each of yours corresponds to.
Map it to PostgreSQL tables in a schema benchmark, and write the CREATE statements with their keys, foreign keys, and CHECK constraints.
The points (starting and best) have one value per input variable, and the number of variables differs from problem to problem. Compare storing a point as rows (one per variable) with storing it as a single text value (for example JSON), and choose.
Write Q1, Q2, and Q3 as queries against your tables.
The KSL’s own benchmark database is defined by the data classes in KSLCore/src/main/kotlin/ksl/simopt/benchmark/io/BenchmarkDbData.kt of the KSL source (https://github.com/rossetti/KSL). Read it and name two decisions its designers made differently from yours. For each, say what it gains and what it costs.



Exercise 12.15 (Mini-project: a database for testing distribution fitting) A study tests a distribution-fitting procedure by fitting samples from known distributions. Each test case is a true distribution: a family, such as gamma, and its parameter values by name, such as a shape of 2 and a scale of 5. For each case and each sample size in a set, such as 25, 50, 100, and 200, the study generates a number of samples, the same number for every size, and records each sample’s average, standard deviation, skewness, minimum, and maximum. It fits each candidate family to each sample and records, for each fitted family, its parameter estimates by name, its score under each of several scoring models (such as the chi-squared, Kolmogorov-Smirnov, and Anderson-Darling statistics), its rank under each scoring model used alone, and its overall rank, where rank 1 is the family the procedure recommends.
The study must answer: (Q1) for each case and sample size, the proportion of samples for which the true family has overall rank 1; (Q2) for each scoring model, the proportion of samples for which it alone would rank the true family first; and (Q3) for each case and sample size, the average relative error of each parameter’s estimate when the true family is fitted.

Draw a class model of the study.
Map it to PostgreSQL tables in a schema fitting, and write the CREATE statements.
Scores, ranks, and parameter estimates can each be stored long (a row per named value) or wide (a column per value). Decide for each, and justify the decision against the study’s questions.
Write Q1 and Q3 as queries against your tables.
The KSL’s examples hold a database for such a study, defined in KSLExamples/src/main/kotlin/ksl/examples/general/utilities/fitting/ResultsDb.kt of the KSL source. Find in it (1) a table with columns whose values can be computed from its other columns, and (2) a table whose single value column holds several kinds of result. For each, say what the choice costs and why its authors might have made it.



Exercise 12.16 (Mini-project: quick tables and a designed schema) Take the run table of your design for Exercise 12.14, or, if you have not done that exercise, the class SolverRun of Section 12.4 with a result table of your own.

Write DbTableData data classes for the run table and for one table that refers to it, and print the CREATE TABLE statement the KSL generates for each, as QuickTable.kt does.
List every rule of your designed tables that the generated statements do not state: keys, foreign keys, UNIQUE and CHECK constraints, types, and names.
Run one generated statement at any stage of the book’s database, in a transaction ended by ROLLBACK, and explain what PostgreSQL reports.
Write a paragraph advising a colleague when the quick tables will do for a study and when the designed schema is worth its time.



Exercise 12.17 (Mini-project: a database for your own analysis) Choose an analysis question about HG Industries’ operations that the book’s database can support, for example the capacity of the garden cart line, the effect of inspection on the time in shop, or the reorder points of the Fayetteville warehouse.

State the questions the study must answer, as requests in words.
List the data each question needs, and for each, the schema it comes from or that it belongs in.
Draw a class model of what the study adds, with the classes it links to, and compare it with Figure 12.3.
Map it to a schema of the study’s own, as SQL, and load realistic data, enough that some rows do not contribute to each question’s answer.
Write each question as a query, and state its result.
Write down your assumptions, grouped as (1) about the classes and their attributes, (2) about the associations, and (3) about everything else, and keep a log of your work: the date, what you did, and why.






Celko, Joe. 2012. Joe Celko’s Trees and Hierarchies in SQL for Smarties. 2nd ed. Morgan Kaufmann.


Rossetti, Manuel D. 2025. Simulation Modeling Using the Kotlin Simulation Library (KSL). Https://rossetti.github.io/KSLBook/.


Wickham, Hadley. 2014. “Tidy Data.” Journal of Statistical Software 59 (10): 1–23. https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v059.i10.

title: Appendix A — Installing PostgreSQL and Its Tools
text:
A.1 Installing the PostgreSQL server
This appendix sets up what the book’s examples need: a PostgreSQL server on your own computer, DataGrip or DBeaver to work with it, and the book’s database loaded into it. It also introduces psql and pgAdmin, which come with PostgreSQL, so that you recognize them. The steps take under an hour, most of it waiting for downloads.
The book’s results were produced with PostgreSQL 18. Later releases give the same query results, but the order of the rows in a result without ORDER BY, what a result shows of the database’s own catalog, and the wording of an error message can differ from one release to the next. PostgreSQL publishes a new major release about once a year, and supports each for five years. Install the current one unless your course or employer asks for another.
PostgreSQL runs as a server, a program that starts with your computer and waits for connections (Section 1.3). Installing it creates the server, a first database named postgres, and a first user, a superuser who may do anything. The installers differ by operating system.
To check the installation, open a terminal and ask psql for its version:
If the command is not found, the tools are not on your path; add them as the step for your system describes. The rest of this appendix assumes the server runs on your own computer (localhost) at port 5432.
The superuser is all you need for the book: you create and load your own databases on your own computer. On a shared server, you would instead be given a role with only the privileges your work needs, as Section 9.4 describes.

title: Appendix A — Installing PostgreSQL and Its Tools
text:
macOS. Postgres.app (postgresapp.com) is the simplest: move it to the Applications folder, open it, and choose Initialize. The server then runs whenever the app does, and its first user has your macOS login name and no password. To use psql and the other command-line tools from a terminal, add them to your path once, as the app’s site describes:
sudo mkdir -p /etc/paths.d &&
echo /Applications/Postgres.app/Contents/Versions/latest/bin |
sudo tee /etc/paths.d/postgresapp
Homebrew (brew install postgresql@18) and the EDB installer below also work on macOS.
Windows. Download the interactive installer by EDB from the Windows page of postgresql.org/download. Keep the default components (the server, pgAdmin 4, and the command-line tools); Stack Builder is not needed. The installer asks for a password for the superuser, named postgres: choose one you will remember, since every tool asks for it. Keep the default port,

The server then starts with Windows. The installer does not put the command-line tools on your path: search the Start menu for Edit environment variables for your account, select Path, choose Edit, then New, enter the folder C:\Program Files\PostgreSQL\18\bin, choose OK in both windows, and open a new terminal. A terminal inside an application that was already open, such as IntelliJ IDEA’s, keeps the old path until the application restarts. The Start menu’s SQL Shell (psql) also opens psql, and asks for each connection setting in turn, showing its default in brackets; press Enter to accept it.

Linux. Install the server from your distribution’s packages, or from the PostgreSQL project’s own repository for a newer release, as the Linux page of postgresql.org/download explains. The superuser is postgres, reached with sudo -u postgres psql.


psql --version

title: Appendix A — Installing PostgreSQL and Its Tools
text:
A.2 Connecting with DataGrip
DataGrip, by JetBrains, is a database tool for many DBMSs, and the one this book’s steps assume. It is free for non-commercial use, including learning, from version 2025.2.4, and free to students with a JetBrains student license; choose Non-commercial use when it first starts.
To connect to your server:

Choose File, New, Data Source, PostgreSQL.
Enter the host localhost, the port 5432, your user (your login name with Postgres.app, postgres otherwise) and its password, and the database postgres for now.
If DataGrip offers to download the PostgreSQL driver, accept.
Choose Test Connection, then OK.

DataGrip lists the new data source in its Database Explorer. By default it shows only some of a database’s schemas; open the data source’s properties and, on its Schemas tab, select All schemas, or the book’s schemas will seem to be missing after you load them.
Two ways of running SQL cover everything the book asks. A query console (right-click the data source, New, Query Console) holds statements you type; place the cursor in one and press Ctrl+Enter (Cmd+Enter on macOS) to run it. A script file (File, Open, then choose the data source to run it against) runs whole: right-click in it and choose Run. The book’s load files are script files.

title: Appendix A — Installing PostgreSQL and Its Tools
text:
A.3 Connecting with DBeaver
DBeaver is a database tool for many DBMSs whose Community Edition is free and open source (dbeaver.io). The book’s steps work in it as well as in DataGrip.

Choose Database, New Database Connection, PostgreSQL.
Enter the host localhost, the port 5432, the database postgres, and your user and password, as for DataGrip.
On the PostgreSQL tab, select Show all databases, so that the databases you create later appear.
Accept the offer to download the driver, choose Test Connection, then Finish.

Open an SQL editor on the connection (SQL Editor, New SQL script). Press Ctrl+Enter to run the statement under the cursor, and Alt+X to run the whole script. The book’s load files are run with Alt+X.

title: Appendix A — Installing PostgreSQL and Its Tools
text:
A.4 psql and pgAdmin
Two tools come with PostgreSQL itself. The book does not build on either, but you will meet both.
psql is PostgreSQL’s command-line client. It connects to a database, runs SQL typed at its prompt or read from a file, and adds its own commands, which begin with a backslash. Run from a terminal, psql -d dbconcepts connects to the book’s database; \dn lists its schemas, \dt distribution.* the tables of one schema, \d distribution.customer one table’s columns, keys, and constraints, \i file.sql runs a script, and \q quits. On Windows, psql connects as your Windows login name, which is not a role on the server, so name the superuser, psql -U postgres -d dbconcepts, and give the password you chose at installation. In the Command Prompt, psql may also warn that the console code page differs from the Windows code page. The warning concerns only how accented letters show in that window, such as those in some names of the public sample databases, and DataGrip and DBeaver are not affected. On Linux, run psql as the superuser, sudo -u postgres psql -d dbconcepts. Listing the schemas of the book’s database, loaded through stage S, gives:
         List of schemas
     Name     |       Owner
--------------+-------------------
 distribution | rossetti
 production   | rossetti
 public       | pg_database_owner
 quality      | rossetti
 sales        | rossetti
(5 rows)
The owner is the user who loaded the database, here the author’s login name. psql is the quickest way to run a script from a terminal, and the book’s own tooling uses it for that.
pgAdmin is a graphical administration tool, installed with the Windows installer and available separately for macOS and Linux. It shows a server’s databases, schemas, tables, roles, and settings, and has a query tool. It suits administration (Section 1.3); for the work of this book, DataGrip or DBeaver is the better fit.
crumbs: A  Installing PostgreSQL and Its Tools

title: Appendix A — Installing PostgreSQL and Its Tools
text:
A.5 Creating the book’s databases
The book’s database lives in a database of its own, named dbconcepts. Create it once, connected to the postgres database, in a DataGrip or DBeaver console:
CREATE DATABASE dbconcepts;
or from a terminal with createdb dbconcepts (on Windows, createdb -U postgres dbconcepts). Then change your data source to the dbconcepts database (in DataGrip, edit the data source’s Database field; in DBeaver, select it under the connection) and check the connection by running the companion script code/sql/setup/check-connection.sql. It reports the server’s version and which database and user you are connected as; its second result should read:
 current_database | current_user
------------------+--------------
 dbconcepts       | rossetti
(1 row)
with your own user name in place of the author’s. Now load the database: open code/sql/load/through-s.sql, from the book’s companion code (https://github.com/rossetti/DbConceptsBookCode), and run it as a script. It builds every schema through the last stage in a few seconds. Section C.2 explains the stages and how to load the database as it stands at any one of them, which is how you reproduce a chapter’s examples exactly.
Millbrook Transit, the exercise database of Section C.10, goes in a database of its own: create dbconcepts_transit as above and run code/sql/transit/t-schema.sql and then code/sql/transit/t-data.sql. The public sample databases, next, have a loader of their own.

title: Appendix A — Installing PostgreSQL and Its Tools
text:
A.6 Loading public sample databases
The public sample databases of Section C.11 are not distributed with the book. The companion code’s code/sql/public/ holds what is needed to fetch and load them: manifest.tsv, which gives each file’s address at a fixed release or commit of its source, its size, its license, and its SHA-256 checksum; load-public.sh, which does the work; and practical-schema.sql, which defines the tables for the Practical SQL files.
On macOS or Linux, or in Git Bash on Windows, with PostgreSQL running and psql on the path, run the loader with the database’s name. In Git Bash, first name the superuser and its password, so that each of the loader’s psql commands can connect:
export PGUSER=postgres
export PGPASSWORD='your-password'
The two settings last until the window closes. Do not save the password in a script or in any file you share. Then run:
code/sql/public/load-public.sh chinook
code/sql/public/load-public.sh northwind
code/sql/public/load-public.sh practical
code/sql/public/load-public.sh employees
Each command downloads the files once, into ~/.cache/dbconcepts-public, refuses any file whose checksum differs from the manifest’s, creates the database dbconcepts_<name>, and loads it. The employees database downloads about 172 MB and takes a minute or so to load; the others take seconds. A second argument names a different database, and --replace drops and rebuilds a database that exists; without it, the loader stops rather than overwrite anything.
Without a shell, the same can be done by hand. Create the database in DataGrip or DBeaver, download each file listed for it in manifest.tsv, and run it: Chinook’s script after deleting its first lines, which create and connect to a database of its own; Northwind’s as it is; for Practical SQL, practical-schema.sql followed by an import of each CSV file into its table (Section 8.5); and for employees, the schema script employees.sql, less its database lines, followed by the eight load_*.dump files after removing the MySQL backquotes (`) they contain. The loader’s comments give each step exactly.

title: Appendix B — Kotlin and KSL Setup
text:
B.1 Installing a JDK and IntelliJ IDEA
Most of this book needs only PostgreSQL and a database tool (Appendix A). Two chapters also run programs: Chapter 10, which connects Kotlin programs to the database, and Chapter 12, which reads a simulation model’s inputs from the database and analyzes its results. Their programs are written in Kotlin and use the Kotlin Simulation Library, the KSL, whose database utilities wrap JDBC (Rossetti 2025). This appendix sets up what those programs need: a Java Development Kit, an editor, the companion code project, and its connection to your database.
Kotlin programs run on the Java Virtual Machine, so they need a Java Development Kit (JDK). The companion project asks for version 21, the version the KSL is built for, and you need not install it yourself: the project’s build is configured to download a JDK 21 the first time it runs on a machine that has none. If you prefer to install one, any JDK 21 distribution works, such as Eclipse Temurin from adoptium.net.
The book uses IntelliJ IDEA, JetBrains’ editor for Kotlin and Java, from jetbrains.com/idea. Since release 2025.3 it is one download whose free features include everything the companion code needs; a subscription adds features the book does not use. IntelliJ IDEA can also download a JDK for you, from File, Project Structure, SDKs.
If you use the KSL in a simulation course, you may already have both. The KSL’s own textbook has an appendix on the same setup (Rossetti 2025), and the companion project here is an ordinary Gradle project like its examples.

title: Appendix B — Kotlin and KSL Setup
section: B.2 Opening the companion code project
text:
B.2 Opening the companion code project
The companion code is the public repository https://github.com/rossetti/DbConceptsBookCode. Download it from there (Code, then Download ZIP) and unzip it, or clone it with Git. The book calls the folder that holds it, the one that contains build.gradle.kts, the code folder. It holds the SQL scripts the chapters refer to and the Kotlin programs, and it is a Gradle project: build.gradle.kts declares what the programs depend on, the KSL among them, and the Gradle wrapper (gradlew, or gradlew.bat on Windows) downloads Gradle and those dependencies the first time the project is built.
To open it, start IntelliJ IDEA, choose File, Open, and select the code folder, the one that contains build.gradle.kts. IntelliJ IDEA recognizes the Gradle project and imports it, downloading the dependencies from Maven Central; the first import takes a few minutes, and later ones seconds. The project’s README.md describes its layout. The programs are under src/main/kotlin/dbconcepts/, one package for each subject: connecting for the connection itself, programming for the programs of Chapter 10, and simulation for those of Chapter 12.

title: Appendix B — Kotlin and KSL Setup
text:
B.3 Configuring the database connection
The programs read their connection settings from a file, db.properties, in the code folder, so that no password is written into a program (Section 10.2 explains why that matters). The project provides a template, db.properties.example; copy it to db.properties and fill it in:
host=localhost
port=5432
database=dbconcepts
user=postgres
password=
Give the user and password you connect with in DataGrip or DBeaver (Section A.1): with Postgres.app, your login name and an empty password; with the Windows installer, postgres and the password you chose. The database is dbconcepts, created and loaded as Section A.5 describes. The programs of Chapter 10 expect it loaded through stage Q; load code/sql/load/through-q.sql (or any later stage) before running them.
Keep db.properties to yourself. It holds a password, so it is excluded from the project’s version control, and you should not e-mail it or copy it into a report. Every program opens the database the same way, through the object BookDatabase in the connecting package, which reads the file.

title: Appendix B — Kotlin and KSL Setup
text:
B.4 Running your first program
The first program to run is CheckConnection.kt, in the connecting package. It connects with your settings, asks the server for its version, and lists the tables of each of the book’s schemas:

val rs = db.fetchCachedRowSet("SELECT current_setting('server_version')")
if (rs != null && rs.next()) {
    println("Connected to PostgreSQL ${rs.getString(1)}")
} else {
    println("Could not query the server. Check the settings in db.properties.")
    return
}
for (schema in listOf("distribution", "production", "quality")) {
    val tables = db.tableNames(schema).sorted()
    if (tables.isEmpty()) {
        println("$schema: (not loaded)")
    } else {
        println("$schema:")
        tables.chunked(4).forEach { println("    " + it.joinToString(", ")) }
    }
}

In IntelliJ IDEA, open the file and click the green arrow beside fun main(). From a terminal in the code folder, the Gradle wrapper runs it:
./gradlew run
In the Windows Command Prompt, the command is gradlew run. With the database loaded through stage Q, it prints:

Connected to PostgreSQL 18.6 (Postgres.app)
distribution:
    customer, customer_order, order_line, product
    shipment, shipment_line, stock_level, warehouse
production:
    bom_line, certification, machine, manufactured_part
    operation, operator, part, purchased_part
    work_center, work_order
quality:
    characteristic, defect_count, defect_type, inspection
    measurement

The first line gives your server’s version, which may differ from the book’s; the words in parentheses appear only with Postgres.app. If the program stops instead, its message says why. No connection settings means db.properties is missing from the code folder. A failed password means the user or password in the file is not the one the server expects. A refused connection means the server is not running, or is not at the host and port in the file. A database that does not exist means dbconcepts has not been created yet. A schema reported as (not loaded) means the database exists but the load file has not been run.
Every other program runs the same way: from IntelliJ IDEA, with the green arrow beside its main, or from a terminal by naming its class, the file’s name followed by Kt:
./gradlew run -PmainClass=dbconcepts.programming.LotMeasurementsKt
The simulation of Section 12.1, RunFrameLine.kt in the simulation package, writes the KSL’s output schema, ksl_db, into the database it connects to. Run on dbconcepts loaded through stage Q, it reproduces stage K of Section 12.2, with the same statistics, since the model’s random number streams are fixed. The KSL also writes its reports and any files a program creates under kslOutput in the code folder.




Rossetti, Manuel D. 2025. Simulation Modeling Using the Kotlin Simulation Library (KSL). Https://rossetti.github.io/KSLBook/.

title: Appendix C — The Book’s Databases
text:
C.1 HG Industries
The examples and exercises in this book use one database, built for the book. It records the business of HG Industries, a small manufacturer of hand trucks and garden carts, as its distribution, production, and quality departments see it. The chapters introduce the database a few tables at a time, as each new idea needs them. This appendix shows it whole: what it contains, how to load it, how its tables and columns are named, and what each table holds.
HG Industries makes four products: two hand trucks and two garden carts. It sells them to hardware stores, farm stores, and distributors from two warehouses, one at the plant in Fayetteville, Arkansas, and one in Tulsa, Oklahoma. The products are simple enough to picture and still have the structure of real manufactured goods. For example, both hand trucks and both carts roll on the same wheel assembly, which is itself built from purchased tires, rims, and bearings and from an axle the plant machines from bar stock.
Each department keeps its own data, and each department’s data is a separate schema, a named group of tables within one database. Table C.1 lists them. The sales schema is not a department’s working data. It is built from the other schemas for analysis, and Chapter 11 explains why a company keeps its data twice in this way.
The schemas refer to one another where the business connects. A product that distribution sells is one of the parts production makes, and an inspection in quality examines one of production’s parts and is performed by one of production’s operators. Thus, a query can join tables across departments, as the company’s own reports must.

text:
Table C.1: Schemas of the Book’s Database

title: Appendix C — The Book’s Databases
text:
C.2 Loading the database
The database is built by SQL scripts that come with the book, in the sql folder of the companion code project (https://github.com/rossetti/DbConceptsBookCode) and as downloads from the book’s site. Appendix A explains how to install PostgreSQL and connect to it with DataGrip or DBeaver. You then create an empty database once; the book calls it dbconcepts.
The scripts build the database in stages, each adding one idea’s tables and rows to the stages before it. Table C.2 lists them in the order they load. The chapters say which stage their examples assume. For example, the single-table queries of Chapter 3 need only stage D1, while the analytical queries of Chapter 4 need the year of history in stage G.



Table C.2: Stages of the Book’s Database










Stage
Adds
The new idea




D1
customer
One table: rows, columns, and a key


D2
customer_order
A one-to-many association and its foreign key


D3
product, order_line
A many-to-many association resolved by a table with its own data


D4
warehouse, stock_level
A second association class


D5
shipment, shipment_line
Optional participation


P1
part, manufactured_part, purchased_part
Generalization; connecting distribution to production


P2
bom_line
A recursive association, the bill of materials


P3
work_center, machine, operator, certification, operation, work_order
Qualified associations and aggregation


Q
the quality schema
Measurements over time


G
a year of history
Enough data to analyze


S
the sales schema
A star schema






Each load file, in the sql/load folder, is named for its stage (through-d1.sql, through-d2.sql, and so on to through-s.sql) and rebuilds the database as it stands at that stage. It first deletes the four schemas of Table C.1, then runs every stage script up to its own. Thus, you can run a load file at any time to return the database to a known state, and one file is all you ever need to open. A load file touches no schema other than these four.
In DataGrip or DBeaver, open the load file, choose the dbconcepts connection, and run the whole script. From a terminal, psql does the same:
psql -d dbconcepts -f sql/load/through-s.sql
The stage scripts themselves are in sql/distribution, sql/production, sql/quality, sql/history, and sql/sales, one file per stage. They are worth reading, since each is a short, complete example of defining and populating tables. Run them only through a load file, though. Each assumes the stages before it were loaded into a freshly reset database, because its rows refer to earlier rows by their key numbers.

title: Appendix C — The Book’s Databases
text:
C.3 Naming and keys
Every table follows the same rules, and knowing them makes any table readable at a glance. Chapter 2 and Chapter 6 explain the reasoning behind them.

Table names are singular nouns in lower case with underscores (customer, order_line), like the class each table implements. No table or column is named with a word reserved in the SQL standard. That is why an order is a customer_order (ORDER is reserved) and a date column is full_date rather than date.
Primary keys are named for their table with the suffix _pk (customer.customer_pk). They are surrogate keys: integers that PostgreSQL generates, which carry no business meaning.
Business identifiers, the numbers people use (customer_number, part_number, order_number), are separate columns declared UNIQUE. Where a row is identified by two columns together, such as an order line by its order and its line number, the pair is declared UNIQUE.
Foreign keys are named for the table they refer to with the suffix _fk (customer_order.customer_fk). Where a table refers to the same table more than once, each column is named for its role: a bill of materials line has an assembly_fk and a component_fk, both referring to part.

title: Appendix C — The Book’s Databases
text:
C.4 The distribution schema
Figure C.1 shows the class model of the distribution schema. A customer places orders, and each order is made of order lines, numbered within the order, that name a product and a quantity. Notice that the order line is drawn with a qualifier, lineNumber: an order and a line number together identify at most one line. The stock of each product in each warehouse is an association class, StockLevel, because a quantity on hand belongs to neither the warehouse nor the product alone. An order may have any number of shipments, including none, and each shipment line ships some quantity of one order line.






Figure C.1: Distribution Schema Class Model



Table C.3 lists the tables that implement the model. The foreign key from product to production.manufactured_part is added in stage P1, when the production schema exists to refer to.




Table C.3: Tables of the Distribution Schema









Table
Columns, in order, and their keys




customer
customer_pk (primary key), customer_number (unique), name, city, state


customer_order
customer_order_pk (primary key), order_number (unique), order_date, requested_ship_date (optional), customer_fk (refers to customer)


product
product_pk (primary key), product_number (unique), description, list_price, manufactured_part_fk (refers to production.manufactured_part)


order_line
order_line_pk (primary key), customer_order_fk (refers to customer_order), line_number, product_fk (refers to product), quantity, unit_price; (customer_order_fk, line_number) is unique


warehouse
warehouse_pk (primary key), warehouse_code (unique), city, state


stock_level
stock_level_pk (primary key), warehouse_fk (refers to warehouse), product_fk (refers to product), quantity_on_hand, reorder_point; (warehouse_fk, product_fk) is unique


shipment
shipment_pk (primary key), shipment_number (unique), shipped_on, carrier, customer_order_fk (refers to customer_order), warehouse_fk (refers to warehouse)


shipment_line
shipment_line_pk (primary key), shipment_fk (refers to shipment), order_line_fk (refers to order_line), quantity; (shipment_fk, order_line_fk) is unique







The base data (stages D1 to D5) covers January through March 2026 and is small enough to print whole. It was written to contain the situations the chapters’ queries must handle:

One customer, C-1008 Northgate Hardware, has never ordered, and one product, the GC-400 poly garden cart, has never been ordered.
Two orders have no requested ship date, so the column holds NULL.
Order SO-5004 lists the HT-100 on two lines at two prices, which is why an order line is a class of its own rather than a simple pairing of an order and a product (Chapter 5).
Order SO-5004 shipped in two shipments. Three order lines shipped only in part, leaving backorders, and orders SO-5011 and SO-5012 have not shipped at all.
Two stock levels are below their reorder points, and the GC-400 in Tulsa has none on hand.

title: Appendix C — The Book’s Databases
text:
C.5 The production schema
Figure C.2 shows the class model of the production schema. Every part is either purchased or manufactured, never both, and there is no third kind; the generalization is {disjoint, complete}. A manufactured part is an assembly of components through the bill of materials, where the quantity of each component per assembly is the association class BomLine. Notice that a component may itself be an assembly, which makes the association recursive. Each manufactured part has a routing: operations numbered within the part, each performed at a work center. Work centers aggregate machines, operators hold certifications on machines, and work orders release a quantity of a manufactured part to the plant floor.






Figure C.2: Production Schema Class Model



Table C.4 lists the tables. Notice that manufactured_part and purchased_part have no surrogate key of their own: each row’s primary key, part_fk, is also its reference to the part it is.




Table C.4: Tables of the Production Schema









Table
Columns, in order, and their keys




part
part_pk (primary key), part_number (unique), description, unit_of_measure, standard_cost


manufactured_part
part_fk (primary key, refers to part), lot_size


purchased_part
part_fk (primary key, refers to part), lead_time_days


bom_line
bom_line_pk (primary key), assembly_fk (refers to manufactured_part), component_fk (refers to part), quantity_per; (assembly_fk, component_fk) is unique


work_center
work_center_pk (primary key), work_center_code (unique), name, hourly_rate


machine
machine_pk (primary key), machine_number (unique), model, installed_on, work_center_fk (refers to work_center)


operator
operator_pk (primary key), employee_number (unique), name, hire_date


certification
certification_pk (primary key), operator_fk (refers to operator), machine_fk (refers to machine), certified_on, level; (operator_fk, machine_fk) is unique


operation
operation_pk (primary key), manufactured_part_fk (refers to manufactured_part), operation_number, description, setup_minutes, run_minutes_per_unit, work_center_fk (refers to work_center); (manufactured_part_fk, operation_number) is unique


work_order
work_order_pk (primary key), work_order_number (unique), manufactured_part_fk (refers to manufactured_part), quantity, released_on, due_on, completed_on (optional)







The eighteen parts form a bill of materials up to four levels deep. The HT-100 hand truck contains the WA-10 wheel assembly, which contains the AX-10 axle, which is machined from BS-075 bar stock. The wheel assembly is used in all four products. Tubing and bar stock are bought by the foot, so their quantities per assembly are not whole numbers. In addition, the data holds:

a work center, Assembly, with no machines;
a machine, the M-07 robotic welder, on which no one is certified yet;
an operator, Tom Becker, hired in January 2026, with no certification;
ten work orders, of which three are still open (no completion date) and two finished after their due dates.

title: Appendix C — The Book’s Databases
text:
C.6 The quality schema
Figure C.3 shows the class model of the quality schema. Each characteristic, such as an axle’s diameter, belongs to a part and carries its nominal value and specification limits. An inspection examines a lot of one part, is performed by one of production’s operators, and records a measurement of each of the part’s characteristics and a count of each kind of defect it finds. Measurements and defect counts are both association classes.






Figure C.3: Quality Schema Class Model







Table C.5: Tables of the Quality Schema









Table
Columns, in order, and their keys




characteristic
characteristic_pk (primary key), part_fk (refers to production.part), name, nominal, lower_spec_limit (optional), upper_spec_limit (optional), unit; (part_fk, name) is unique


defect_type
defect_type_pk (primary key), defect_code (unique), description


inspection
inspection_pk (primary key), part_fk (refers to production.part), operator_fk (refers to production.operator), inspected_at, lot_number


measurement
measurement_pk (primary key), inspection_fk (refers to inspection), characteristic_fk (refers to characteristic), measured_value; (inspection_fk, characteristic_fk) is unique


defect_count
defect_count_pk (primary key), inspection_fk (refers to inspection), defect_type_fk (refers to defect_type), quantity; (inspection_fk, defect_type_fk) is unique







The base data holds twenty inspections of axles, hand truck frames, and cart frames in January and February 2026. Weld strength has a lower specification limit and no upper one, since a stronger weld is never a defect, so its upper limit is NULL. The data was built to show:

an axle diameter that rises at every inspection and ends above its upper specification limit;
five measurements outside their specification limits in all;
one inspector, Linda Nguyen, whose coating thickness readings run consistently lower than Robert Hayes’s readings of the same parts;
paint runs outnumbering every other defect combined, and one defect type, cracks, that has never been found.

title: Appendix C — The Book’s Databases
text:
C.7 The year of history
The base data is small by design, and some questions need more. Stage G adds a year of business to the distribution and quality schemas:

22 more customers, for 30 in all, in Arkansas, Oklahoma, Missouri, Kansas, and Texas;
602 orders from April 2026 through March 2027, with 1,043 order lines, 641 shipments, and 1,078 shipment lines;
236 inspections from April through September 2026, with 419 measurements and 101 defect counts.

The history follows patterns that the analytical chapters look for. Garden carts sell mainly in the spring: the GC-300 sells 1.75 times as many units from April to June as from October to December. Hand trucks rise toward the end of the year. The GC-400 is sold from its launch on 1 September 2026, and large customers and large order lines receive discounts. On the plant floor, the axle diameter creeps upward as the lathe’s cutting tool wears and drops back at each of five tool changes.
The history was generated by a program, GenerateHistory, in the companion code project, which draws its random choices from seeded random number streams of the KSL. Thus, the program writes the same history on every run, and every reader’s queries return the same results. Chapter 10 discusses programs that work with databases in this way.

title: Appendix C — The Book’s Databases
text:
C.8 The sales star schema
Stage S builds the sales schema of Figure C.4, a star schema for analyzing sales. The fact table, order_line_fact, has one row for every order line. Its measures (quantity, sales, discount from list price, and standard cost) can be added up along any of the three dimensions around it: the date of the order, the customer, and the product. The dimensions carry attributes the operational tables do not, such as each customer’s sales region and each product’s product line.






Figure C.4: Sales Star Schema



Notice that the diagram shows the tables’ key columns, unlike the class models above. A star schema is a design for tables, not a model of the business, and Chapter 11 develops it at that level.




Table C.6: Tables of the Sales Schema









Table
Columns, in order, and their keys




date_dim
date_dim_pk (primary key), full_date (unique), calendar_year, calendar_quarter, calendar_month, month_name, day_of_month, day_of_week, day_name, is_weekend


customer_dim
customer_dim_pk (primary key), customer_number (unique), name, city, state, sales_region


product_dim
product_dim_pk (primary key), product_number (unique), description, product_line, list_price, standard_cost


order_line_fact
order_line_fact_pk (primary key), order_date_fk (refers to date_dim), customer_dim_fk (refers to customer_dim), product_dim_fk (refers to product_dim), order_number, line_number, quantity, sales_amount, discount_amount, cost_amount; (order_number, line_number) is unique







The stage S script is itself an extract, transform, and load process written in SQL. It reads the distribution and production schemas, derives the new attributes, and loads the fact table by looking up each dimension’s key from the business identifiers. Chapter 11 walks through it.

title: Appendix C — The Book’s Databases
text:

title: Appendix C — The Book’s Databases
text:
C.10 Millbrook Transit
A second, smaller database gives the query exercises of chapters 3 and 4 a setting outside HG Industries. It records one week of service, Monday 2 March to Sunday 8 March 2026, of Millbrook Transit, a fictional town’s bus agency. Its design is adapted from the class model of the transit exercises of chapter 5, which come from a Transportation Research Board study of transit monitoring (Rossetti 1999), and mapped to tables as chapter 6 teaches. It differs from the exercises’ model in a few places. Every person has a rider category. An account has an opening date and no balance. A smart card names the person who carries it (person_fk, NULL for an anonymous card), an association the model does not have. A trip refers to the point traversals where it boarded and alighted, not to an origin and a destination point, and records no times of its own. A driver has an employee number and a hire date, not a license number. An assignment has no comments. A route traversal refers to an assignment, not to a vehicle and a route; the assignment names both. A schedule adds the times of its first and last departures (first_departure, last_departure), and a schedule line holds the minutes after the bus’s departure, not an arrival and a departure time. An access point’s block location may also be off street. Finally, the database has no tables for authorizations, points of interest, or link traversals.
The agency runs three loop routes, each starting and ending at the Transit Center: the Plant Loop (route 1), the Campus Loop (route 2), and the Hospital Loop (route 3). Buses leave every 30 minutes on weekdays, from 6:00 to 19:30, and every hour on Saturday, from 8:00 to 17:00; there is no service on Sunday. The tables fall into four groups.

The network. route, point, and segment: each route is its ordered segments, each segment joining a start point to an end point. Points are specialized into access_point, where passengers board and alight, and scheduled_point, which appears on the timetables, mapped to a table for each class (Section 6.5.1).
Schedules. schedule, with its days (schedule_day, day_of_week) and its lines (schedule_line), each giving the minutes from departure to a scheduled point.
Operations. vehicle, driver, and assignment, which puts a driver on a vehicle on a route for a shift; route_traversal, one run of a route under an assignment; and point_traversal, each point the bus reached on a run, with the passengers boarding and alighting there.
Riders. person, mailing_address, account, smart_card, trip, and payment. Smart cards are debit or credit cards, a generalization mapped to one table with card_kind (Section 6.5.3). Each trip made with a card refers to the point traversals where it boarded and alighted. Riders who pay cash are counted in the boardings and alightings but recorded as no trip.

Listing C.1 gives the tables in the notation of Section 2.4.

C.11 Public sample databases for further practice
HG Industries’ data is small so that every result can be checked. For practice at a larger scale, several public sample databases can be loaded into the same PostgreSQL server, each into a database of its own. They are not distributed with the book: Section A.6 explains how to fetch each one from its source, where its license is stated.
Table C.9 lists the four the book’s exercises use. Each is openly licensed; the license travels with the data, not with this book, and you should read it before you reuse the data in work of your own.

Each is useful for something the book’s own data is too small or too clean to show. Chinook and Northwind are ordinary business databases designed by other people, with their own naming conventions (customer_id rather than customer_fk, plural table names in Northwind), which is practice in reading a schema you did not write. The Practical SQL data are real public records, with the inconsistencies real records have. Employees is large enough that a careless query is slow, and it records history with dates rather than replacing rows.
Load each with the book’s loader, code/sql/public/load-public.sh, as Section A.6 describes. It fetches the files from their original sources at the versions in the table, checks each against a recorded checksum, and loads them into a database of their own, dbconcepts_chinook, dbconcepts_northwind, dbconcepts_practical, and dbconcepts_employees. Exercises that use them name the database, and their answers assume these versions.

title: Appendix D — Translating Between Crow’s Foot and UML
text:
D.1 Why two notations
This book draws its data models as UML class diagrams. Other books, many courses, and most database tools draw them as entity-relationship diagrams in the crow’s foot notation. Section 5.10 showed how to read the crow’s foot marks; this appendix translates every construct in both directions, says what is lost on the way, and ends with a procedure for translating a whole model and a worked example.
The examples come from HG Industries’ production and distribution schemas, drawn both ways, so that each crow’s foot diagram can be set beside a class diagram the book has already explained.
The entity-relationship model was introduced by Peter Chen as a way to describe data independently of how it is stored (Chen 1976). Chen’s diagrams drew relationships as diamonds; the crow’s foot notation, which draws a relationship as a line with marks at its ends, dates from the same decade and spread with the Information Engineering method and the design tools built on it. UML came later, in the 1990s, from object-oriented software design, and its class diagrams are a standard of the Object Management Group.
The two notations describe the same things: kinds of objects, their facts, and the associations among them, with how many of each may be linked. They differ in emphasis. A crow’s foot diagram is usually drawn close to the tables it will become, with identifiers marked and foreign keys often shown, while a UML class diagram describes the business and leaves keys to the mapping of Chapter 6. That is why this book models in UML and maps afterwards. You will still meet crow’s foot diagrams in other textbooks, in DataGrip’s and DBeaver’s generated diagrams, and in design documents at work, and you should be able to read one as a class model and draw one when asked.
crumbs: D  Translating Between Crow's Foot and UML

title: Appendix D — Translating Between Crow’s Foot and UML
text:
D.2 Entities and classes
An entity type is the ERD’s name for a class: a kind of thing the business records, drawn as a box with its name above its attributes. An entity, or entity instance, is one object of it. Crow’s foot diagrams conventionally write entity names in upper case with underscores (WORK_CENTER), the style of the tables they become, where UML writes class names in upper camel case (WorkCenter); Figure 5.21 kept the class names only so that it could be set beside its class diagram. The difference is one of spelling only: an entity type translates to a class with the same meaning, and a class to an entity type.
Recall from Section 5.3 that the book distinguishes a class from the table it maps to; in a crow’s foot diagram that distinction is often blurred, and the box is read as both. Translating to UML restores it: the class describes the business, and Chapter 6 decides the table.
crumbs: D  Translating Between Crow's Foot and UML

title: Appendix D — Translating Between Crow’s Foot and UML
text:
D.3 Attributes and keys
Figure D.1 draws work centers and their machines as a design tool draws them. Each entity lists its identifier above the line, marked with an asterisk, and its other attributes below. MACHINE also lists work_center_code, marked (FK): the foreign key by which each machine refers to its work center.






Figure D.1: Work Centers and Machines, with Identifiers and a Foreign Key



Three rules translate these boxes to classes.

An identifier that the business uses becomes an attribute. Work center codes and machine numbers are business identifiers, so workCenterCode and machineNumber are attributes of WorkCenter and Machine, as in Figure 5.16. The class description records that each is unique (Section 5.3).
An artificial identifier is dropped. A column such as checkout_id that exists only to number rows has no place in a class model; the mapping of Section 6.6 adds a surrogate key to every table in any case.
A foreign key is dropped, and the line carries its meaning. work_center_code (FK) in MACHINE repeats what the relationship line already says, that each machine belongs to a work center. A class model shows the association and no foreign key attribute (1).

Some ERD styles mark other kinds of attribute: a multivalued attribute, such as an employee’s several phone numbers, and a derived attribute, such as an age computed from a birth date. A multivalued attribute translates to a class of its own with a one-to-many association, since a table’s column holds one value (Section 2.1); a derived attribute is left out of the class model, or noted in the class description, since it is computed rather than recorded.
crumbs: D  Translating Between Crow's Foot and UML

title: Appendix D — Translating Between Crow’s Foot and UML
text:
D.4 Relationships and multiplicity
A relationship is the ERD’s association, drawn as a line between two entity types. Recall Table 5.8: the mark nearer the box gives the maximum (a bar for one, the crow’s foot for many) and the mark farther from the box the minimum (a bar for one, a circle for zero). The marks sit at the same ends as UML’s numbers, so each end translates on its own:



Table D.1: Translating the Four Crow’s Foot Ends





Crow’s foot end
UML multiplicity




bar, bar
1


circle, bar
0..1


circle, crow’s foot
0..*


bar, crow’s foot
1..*






In Figure D.1, the line has two bars at WORK_CENTER and a circle with a crow’s foot at MACHINE. The UML association of Figure 5.16 has 1 at the work center and 0..* at the machine: each machine belongs to exactly one work center, and a work center has zero or more machines.
The translation is exact for the four ends of Table D.1 and no further. Crow’s foot has no mark for a count other than zero, one, and many, so a UML multiplicity such as 2..* or 1..3 becomes the nearest end (1..*) and a note. A relationship’s name, often a verb phrase written on the line (“performs”, “is assigned to”), translates to a UML association name or, when it names what one end is to the other, to a role name. A relationship between an entity type and itself, a unary or recursive relationship, translates to a recursive association with role names (1).
crumbs: D  Translating Between Crow's Foot and UML

title: Appendix D — Translating Between Crow’s Foot and UML
section: D.5 Associative entities and association classes
text:
D.5 Associative entities and association classes
Crow’s foot draws only lines between two boxes. A many-to-many relationship with facts of its own, or a relationship among three entity types, is therefore drawn as an associative entity: an entity type in the middle, with a one-to-many line to each of the entity types it connects. Figure D.2 draws the stock levels of stage D4 this way.






Figure D.2: Stage D4’s Stock Levels in Crow’s Foot Notation



Read each line of Figure D.2 on its own: a warehouse has zero or more stock levels, each stock level is of exactly one warehouse, and the same for products. Its identifier is the pair of foreign keys. In UML the same facts are the association class StockLevel of Figure 5.7: an association between Warehouse and Product, 0..* at both ends, with quantityOnHand and reorderPoint on the association class.
An associative entity does not always become an association class. Recall the decision of Section 5.5 about order lines: an association class allows at most one link per pair of objects, so it is right only when the pair identifies the associative entity. The test in translation is the identifier:

Identified by the pair of foreign keys, as STOCK_LEVEL is: an association class.
Identified by something else, a number of its own or the pair plus another attribute, because the same pair may occur more than once: a class with two associations. The order line of Figure 5.11, drawn as OrderLine in Figure 5.21, is one; so is a checkout of a tool (Exercise 5.18).

The same test applies to an associative entity with three lines, the crow’s foot form of a ternary association (Section 5.5.1): identified by the three foreign keys, it is a ternary association with an association class; otherwise, a class with three binary associations.
crumbs: D  Translating Between Crow's Foot and UML

title: Appendix D — Translating Between Crow’s Foot and UML
text:
D.6 Identifying relationships and composition
Crow’s foot distinguishes two kinds of relationship line. An identifying relationship, drawn as a solid line, is one whose parent’s identifier is part of the child’s identifier: the child cannot be identified, and so cannot exist, without its parent. A non-identifying relationship, drawn as a dashed line, only refers to the parent. A child entity type with an identifying relationship is often called a weak entity, and the part of its identifier that it adds is its partial identifier. Figure D.3 shows both kinds.






Figure D.3: Stage P3’s Routing in Crow’s Foot Notation



An operation of Figure D.3 is identified by its part’s number and its own operation number, so its line to MANUFACTURED_PART is identifying, solid: operation 20 means nothing without the part it belongs to. Its line to WORK_CENTER is dashed: the work center is a fact about the operation, not part of its name.
Now compare Figure 5.16. The identifying relationship with a partial identifier is the qualified composition ManufacturedPart [operationNumber] "1" *-- "0..1" Operation: the partial identifier operation_number becomes the qualifier, and the dependence of the operation on its part becomes the filled diamond. The non-identifying relationship is an ordinary association. The translation rules are:

Identifying, with a partial identifier: a qualified association, usually a composition (Section 5.6).
Identifying, with no partial identifier (the child’s identifier is the parent’s alone): a one-to-one association, often a composition, or, if the child is a kind of the parent, a generalization (the next section).
Non-identifying: an ordinary association or an aggregation.

The translation back is looser, because UML distinguishes what crow’s foot does not. A UML composition says that the part cannot exist without its whole and is deleted with it, which Section 6.3.6 maps to on delete cascade; an identifying relationship says only how the child is named. An aggregation, such as a work center’s machines in Figure 5.16, has no crow’s foot mark at all: it becomes a non-identifying line, and the diamond is lost.
crumbs: D  Translating Between Crow's Foot and UML

title: Appendix D — Translating Between Crow’s Foot and UML
text:
D.7 Subtypes and generalization
ERDs record kinds of an entity type as supertypes and subtypes, drawn in many styles: a subtype box inside its supertype, a circle joining the lines, or, as design tools and Figure D.4 draw it, a one-to-zero-or-one line from the supertype to each subtype, with the subtype sharing the supertype’s identifier.






Figure D.4: Stage P1’s Parts as a Supertype and Two Subtypes



Each line of Figure D.4 says that a part may have one row of manufactured-part facts and one of purchased-part facts. The note adds what the lines cannot: a subtype discriminator, part_kind, whose value says which subtype a part belongs to, and two constraints. Exclusive (also called disjoint) means a part belongs to at most one subtype; total (also called complete) means every part belongs to one. Their opposites are overlapping and partial.
The translation is the generalization of Figure 5.17: Part is the superclass, ManufacturedPart and PurchasedPart its subclasses, and the constraints translate word for word: exclusive to {disjoint} and total to {complete}, and their opposites, overlapping and partial, to {overlapping} and {incomplete}. A total supertype has no objects of its own, so it becomes an abstract class, its name in italics, as Part is in Figure 5.17. The discriminator is dropped from the class model, since in UML an object’s class says its kind; it returns in the mapping, as the part_kind column of the single-table mapping of Section 6.5.3. The subtypes’ copies of part_number, marked (FK), are dropped as foreign keys are.
Reading a diagram drawn with plain one-to-zero-or-one lines and no note, you cannot tell a subtype from an ordinary optional one-to-one relationship. The test is the one of Section 5.7: is every manufactured part a part, with all of a part’s facts? If so, it is a subtype.
crumbs: D  Translating Between Crow's Foot and UML

title: Appendix D — Translating Between Crow’s Foot and UML
text:
D.8 What does not translate
Most of a model survives translation in either direction. What does not is worth knowing before you translate, so that the losses are recorded in a note rather than silently dropped.



Table D.2: What Is Lost Translating UML to Crow’s Foot










UML construct
In crow’s foot
What is lost




Multiplicity other than 0, 1, many (2..*)
nearest end (1..*)
the exact count; keep it in a note


Qualifier
partial identifier of a weak entity
nothing, if the relationship is drawn as identifying


Composition
identifying relationship
that the part is deleted with its whole


Aggregation
ordinary relationship
the whole-part meaning


Association class
associative entity
nothing, but the reverse translation needs the identifier test


{ordered}
a sequence-number attribute
the constraint becomes data


{disjoint, complete} and their opposites
a note or a style-specific symbol
the constraint, where the style has no symbol


Operations of a class
nothing
not used in data models






In the other direction, a crow’s foot diagram carries facts that a class model leaves to the mapping: identifiers, foreign keys, and sometimes types and lengths. None of these is lost in translation, since Chapter 6 recreates them, but you should record in the class descriptions any business identifier and any rule the ERD states through its keys, such as the uniqueness of an operation number within its part.
crumbs: D  Translating Between Crow's Foot and UML

title: Appendix D — Translating Between Crow’s Foot and UML
section: D.9 Translating a model, step by step
text:
D.9 Translating a model, step by step
The sections above translate one construct at a time. A whole model is translated in a fixed order, so that each decision rests on the ones before it. From crow’s foot to UML:

Entity types to classes. Rename each to upper camel case. Set aside the associative entities and the subtypes for steps 4 and 5.
Attributes. Keep each business attribute and business identifier; drop artificial identifiers and every attribute marked as a foreign key.
Relationships to associations. Translate each end with Table D.1. Turn relationship names into association names or role names; give role names to every recursive relationship and to every second relationship between the same pair.
Associative entities. Apply the identifier test of Section D.5: an association class if the foreign keys alone identify it, a class of its own otherwise.
Identifying relationships and subtypes. A partial identifier becomes a qualifier; decide whether the dependence is a composition. Subtypes become a generalization with the constraints of the note.
Read the result both ways. Read every association as two sentences

and review the model with Table 5.6.


From UML to crow’s foot, the steps run in the same order: classes to entity types; attributes, adding the identifiers the class descriptions name; associations to relationships by Table D.1; association classes to associative entities; qualifiers to partial identifiers on identifying relationships; generalizations to subtypes with a discriminator; and every loss of Table D.2 to a note.

Example D.1 (Translating a production model from crow’s foot to UML) A consultant’s report on HG Industries’ production floor includes Figure D.5, drawn in crow’s foot notation with a design tool. The plant’s engineers maintain their models in UML.






Figure D.5: Part of HG Industries’ Production Model in Crow’s Foot Notation



The request. Translate Figure D.5 into a UML class diagram, and check it against the class model of Figure 5.20.
The translation. We follow the procedure.

Classes. WORK_CENTER, MACHINE, OPERATOR, OPERATION, and MANUFACTURED_PART become WorkCenter, Machine, Operator, Operation, and ManufacturedPart. CERTIFICATION is associative and waits for step 4.
Attributes. The business identifiers stay as attributes: workCenterCode, machineNumber, employeeNumber, partNumber. Every (FK) attribute is dropped: work_center_code from MACHINE and OPERATION, and the foreign keys of CERTIFICATION and OPERATION. operation_number is not a foreign key; it waits for step 5.
Associations. WORK_CENTER ||..o{ MACHINE becomes 1 at the work center and 0..* at the machine; WORK_CENTER ||..o{ OPERATION becomes 1 and 0..*.
The associative entity. CERTIFICATION is identified by the pair (employee_number, machine_number), its two foreign keys alone, so it is the association class Certification (certifiedOn, level) of an association between Operator and Machine, 0..* at both ends. Each end’s multiplicity comes from the crow’s foot at the associative entity: an operator has zero or more certifications, so zero or more machines.
The identifying relationship. OPERATION is identified by its part’s number and operation_number, through a solid line: operationNumber becomes a qualifier, and since an operation cannot exist without its part’s routing, the association is a composition, ManufacturedPart [operationNumber] "1" *-- "0..1" Operation. The crow’s foot 1..* at OPERATION (every manufactured part has at least one operation) is not visible through the qualifier and goes into the class description.

The check. The result is the part of Figure 5.20 that Figure D.5 covers, with one difference: the diagram draws the work center’s machines with an ordinary line, and the class model with an aggregation. The crow’s foot diagram cannot state the whole-part meaning, so the translation cannot recover it; whether a work center is an assembly of its machines is a question for the engineers, not for the notation. Reading each association both ways confirms the rest: each operation is performed at exactly one work center; a work center performs zero or more operations.
Where it breaks. Had CERTIFICATION carried an identifier of its own, a certification number, the identifier test would have made it a class with two associations, allowing an operator to be certified twice on one machine. The diagram alone cannot say which the business intends; Exercise 5.5 asks the question the business must answer.

title: Appendix E — Tools for Drawing UML and ER Diagrams
text:
E.1 Two jobs, two kinds of tool
Students of this course ask, every term, what software to use for their diagrams. The answer depends on the job. Drawing a class model of a business before any table exists is a design job, and needs a tool that draws what you tell it to. Drawing a picture of a database that already exists is a documentation job, and a database tool can do it from the database itself. This appendix describes both kinds of tool, starting with the approach every diagram in this book was drawn with: diagrams written as text.
The tools change quickly, and their prices and licenses change with them. The descriptions here were checked against each tool’s own documentation in September 2026; check again before you depend on one.
A design diagram states what a business records, in UML (Chapter 5) or in crow’s foot notation (Appendix D), before any table exists. It shows classes, associations with their multiplicities, association classes, qualifiers, and generalization, and it shows no foreign keys, since keys are decided later, in the mapping of Chapter 6. Any tool that lets you place and connect these elements will do.
A generated diagram is drawn by a database tool from a database’s catalog (Section 2.5): each table as a box with its columns, and a line for each foreign key. It is exact, since it is read from the database, and it stays current with one click. It is also a picture of the implementation, not of the business. Recall stage D4’s stock levels: the class model of Figure 5.7 draws them as an association class of warehouses and products, while a generated diagram draws a table, stock_level, with two foreign keys, and nothing on it says that a warehouse and a product may have at most one stock level between them, except a UNIQUE constraint the diagram may not show.
Thus, you need both. A design tool for the models you hand in and discuss, and your database tool for checking what you built. The next section describes the design approach this book uses.

title: Appendix E — Tools for Drawing UML and ER Diagrams
section: E.3 Diagrams from a database: DataGrip, DBeaver, and pgAdmin
text:
E.3 Diagrams from a database: DataGrip, DBeaver, and pgAdmin
The database tools of Appendix A each draw a diagram of a database that exists, from its catalog.

DataGrip. Select a schema or some tables in the Database Explorer, right-click, and choose Diagrams, Show Diagram. Each table is a box with its columns, keys marked, and an arrow for each foreign key. The diagram can be saved as an image, and exported as PlantUML, a text file you can then edit and keep beside your model.
DBeaver. Open a schema or a table and choose its ER Diagram tab. Right- clicking the diagram’s background offers a choice of Notation, crow’s foot among them (IDEF1X is the default). The diagram can be saved as an image, PNG among the free edition’s formats, or as GraphML for other diagram tools.
pgAdmin. Right-click a database and choose ERD For Database. pgAdmin’s ERD tool draws the tables, and it also works the other way: you can draw new tables in it and choose Generate SQL, which writes the CREATE TABLE statements for the design and opens them in the query tool.

Each of these shows what Figure 2.2, the book’s generated diagram of the distribution schema, shows: tables, columns, types, keys, and references. None shows an association class as such, a composition’s diamond, or a generalization, since the catalog holds only tables and constraints. Use a generated diagram to check that the database you built matches your design, and to learn an unfamiliar database quickly, as the public databases of Section C.11 invite.

title: Appendix E — Tools for Drawing UML and ER Diagrams
text:
E.5 Choosing a tool
For a homework design or a project model, any of the tools above will do; pick one that draws association classes and qualifiers, which rules out Mermaid and some web tools. For a model you will revise over weeks, or keep with the code and SQL of a project, write it as text in PlantUML, since a text file records its own history and never needs redrawing. For seeing what a database holds, use your database tool’s diagram, and never draw by hand what the database can draw for you. Whatever you use, a diagram you hand in is a class model in the notation of Chapter 5, or a crow’s foot diagram translated as Appendix D describes.

title: Appendix F — SQL Quick Reference
text:
F.1 Defining tables
This appendix collects, in one place, the SQL this book teaches: the statements that define tables, the statements that change data, the clauses of a query, and the data types and functions the chapters use. It is a reminder, not a tutorial. Each entry names the section that teaches it, where the examples and the reasons are.
The skeletons follow three conventions. Words in upper case are SQL; words in lower case stand for names or values you supply. Square brackets enclose what may be left out, and ... means the previous item may repeat. PostgreSQL is the reference system (Section 1.3); a feature marked (PostgreSQL) is PostgreSQL’s own, not standard SQL, and may be written differently in another DBMS.
A table is created with its columns and its rules together. The skeleton gives the parts the book’s tables use:
A table’s definition changes with ALTER TABLE, and the other statements that define things follow the same pattern:

title: Appendix F — SQL Quick Reference
text:

    table_pk INTEGER GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY
        PRIMARY KEY,
    column_name type [NOT NULL] [DEFAULT value]
        [UNIQUE] [CHECK (condition)],
    other_fk INTEGER [NOT NULL]
        REFERENCES schema_name.other_table
        [ON DELETE action] [ON UPDATE action],
    ...
    [UNIQUE (column_name, ...)],
    [CHECK (condition)]
);

title: Appendix F — SQL Quick Reference
text:
F.3 Queries
A query’s clauses are written in one order and evaluated in another. The skeleton gives the written order; the database evaluates FROM and its joins first, then WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, the window functions, the SELECT list, DISTINCT, ORDER BY, and finally LIMIT. That is why a WHERE clause cannot name a column alias from the SELECT list, and why it runs before the grouping that HAVING filters.
[WITH [RECURSIVE] name AS (query), ...]
SELECT [DISTINCT] expression [AS alias], ...
FROM table [AS alias]
    [[LEFT | RIGHT | FULL] JOIN table [AS alias]
        ON condition] ...
[WHERE condition]
[GROUP BY expression, ...]
[HAVING condition]
[ORDER BY expression [ASC | DESC], ...]
[LIMIT n];
