title: Appendix G — Embedded Databases: SQLite and DuckDB
text:
G.1 What an embedded database is
This book’s databases run on a PostgreSQL server, which programs and tools connect to over the network. An embedded database runs instead inside the program that uses it, with its data in a file. This appendix explains what an embedded database is and when you should use one, introduces two of them, SQLite, which holds the KSL’s simulation output, and DuckDB, which is built for analysis, and shows how a Kotlin program creates and queries one.
PostgreSQL is a client-server database. The server is a program of its own, always running; DataGrip, psql, and the book’s Kotlin programs are clients that connect to it, sign in as a user, and send it SQL (Appendix A). The server holds the data, enforces the constraints, and lets many clients work at once.
An embedded database has no server. Its database engine is a library that runs inside the program that opens it, and its data is an ordinary file, or a directory of files, on the program’s own disk. There is nothing to install and start, no user to create, and no password; opening the database means opening the file. When the program ends, so does the engine. The same SQL creates tables and queries them, with differences this appendix points out.
Thus, an embedded database trades the server’s services for simplicity. It cannot serve many users at once as a server does, and whoever can read the file can read the data. It needs no administration at all.
crumbs: G  Embedded Databases: SQLite and DuckDB

title: Appendix G — Embedded Databases: SQLite and DuckDB
text:
G.2 When to use one
An embedded database suits data that belongs to one program or one person.

A study’s own results. The quick tables of Section 12.4, written by one program and read by one analyst, need no server. The KSL writes its simulation output to an embedded SQLite database unless it is given another.
Data that travels with a program or a report. A file can be copied, e-mailed, or archived with the study it belongs to, and opened years later with any tool that reads its format.
A tool on one desktop, a test that needs a fresh database each time it runs, or a device with no network.

A client-server database suits data that is shared: many people or programs writing at once, users with different privileges (Section 9.4), data that must be backed up and kept available by someone whose job it is. HG Industries’ order and production databases are shared, which is why the book runs them on PostgreSQL. A study that starts in an embedded file and becomes shared should move to a server; the SQL mostly moves with it.
crumbs: G  Embedded Databases: SQLite and DuckDB

title: Appendix G — Embedded Databases: SQLite and DuckDB
text:
G.3 SQLite
SQLite is the most widely used embedded database. It is in the public domain, keeps a whole database in one file, and is built into phones, web browsers, and many desktop programs. Its command-line shell, sqlite3, comes with macOS and Linux and is a small download for Windows; DataGrip and DBeaver open a SQLite file directly, as a data source of type SQLite.
The companion scripts in code/sql/embedded/ build the warehouses and stock levels of stage D4 in a SQLite file. The first creates two tables, loads a few rows, and queries them. Run with sqlite3 -echo stock.db < sqlite-stock-create.sql, the shell creates stock.db if it does not exist, echoes each statement, and prints each result:
.headers on
.mode column
CREATE TABLE warehouse (
    warehouse_pk INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    warehouse_code TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    city TEXT NOT NULL,
    state TEXT NOT NULL
);
CREATE TABLE stock_level (
    stock_level_pk INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    warehouse_fk INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES warehouse,
    product_number TEXT NOT NULL,
    quantity_on_hand INTEGER NOT NULL
        CHECK (quantity_on_hand >= 0),
    UNIQUE (warehouse_fk, product_number)
);
INSERT INTO warehouse (warehouse_code, city, state)
VALUES ('W-FAY', 'Fayetteville', 'AR'), ('W-TUL', 'Tulsa', 'OK');
INSERT INTO stock_level
    (warehouse_fk, product_number, quantity_on_hand)
VALUES (1, 'HT-100', 120), (1, 'GC-300', 18), (2, 'HT-100', 60);
SELECT w.warehouse_code, s.product_number, s.quantity_on_hand
FROM stock_level AS s
JOIN warehouse AS w ON w.warehouse_pk = s.warehouse_fk
ORDER BY w.warehouse_code, s.product_number;
warehouse_code  product_number  quantity_on_hand
--------------  --------------  ----------------
W-FAY           GC-300                        18
W-FAY           HT-100                       120
W-TUL           HT-100                        60
The statements are the book’s own, with three changes that SQLite’s rules call for. The types are SQLite’s (TEXT for strings); a key column declared INTEGER PRIMARY KEY is numbered by SQLite itself, the role an identity column plays in PostgreSQL; and .headers and .mode are commands of the shell, not SQL, which format the output.
SQLite departs from PostgreSQL, and from the standard, in two ways that matter to a designer. The first is its types. A column’s declared type is a preference, called its type affinity, not a rule, so SQLite stores a value of another type rather than refuse it. The second script inserts the text forty into quantity_on_hand:
.headers on
.mode column
INSERT INTO stock_level
    (warehouse_fk, product_number, quantity_on_hand)
VALUES (2, 'GC-300', 'forty');
SELECT product_number, quantity_on_hand,
       typeof(quantity_on_hand) AS stored_as
FROM stock_level
WHERE warehouse_fk = 2;
product_number  quantity_on_hand  stored_as
--------------  ----------------  ---------
GC-300          forty             text
HT-100                        60  integer
CREATE TABLE stock_count (
    product_number TEXT NOT NULL,
    counted INTEGER NOT NULL
) STRICT;
INSERT INTO stock_count VALUES ('GC-300', 'forty');
Error near line 15: cannot store TEXT value in INTEGER column stock_count.counted
The insert succeeded, and typeof shows that the column now holds a text value in one row and an integer in another. Even the CHECK constraint passed, since SQLite compares any text as greater than any number. A strict table, declared with the word STRICT after its definition (SQLite 3.37 and later), enforces the declared types, and the last statement shows it refusing the same value. You should declare a SQLite table STRICT whenever its data will be analyzed, since a wrong type is otherwise stored silently.
The second departure is foreign keys. SQLite parses a REFERENCES clause but, for compatibility with old databases, enforces it only on a connection that asks, with PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON:
.headers on
.mode column
INSERT INTO stock_level
    (warehouse_fk, product_number, quantity_on_hand)
VALUES (9, 'HT-200', 5);
PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;
INSERT INTO stock_level
    (warehouse_fk, product_number, quantity_on_hand)
VALUES (9, 'GC-400', 7);
Error near line 9: FOREIGN KEY constraint failed
SELECT stock_level_pk, warehouse_fk, product_number
FROM stock_level
WHERE warehouse_fk NOT IN (SELECT warehouse_pk FROM warehouse);
stock_level_pk  warehouse_fk  product_number
--------------  ------------  --------------
             5             9  HT-200
The first insert referred to warehouse 9, which does not exist, and SQLite accepted it: the shell’s connection had not asked. After the PRAGMA, the same kind of insert was refused. The orphan row remains, and the last query finds it with an anti-join (Section 3.7), written with NOT IN. The setting lasts only as long as the connection, so every program and tool that writes the file must turn it on; the KSL’s SQLite connections do (Section G.5).
A few other differences are worth knowing before you design for SQLite:

No date type. Dates and times are stored as text in the ISO form (2026-09-29 14:30:00), as numbers, or as both, and SQLite’s date functions work on any of them.
One writer at a time. Many connections may read at once, but a write locks the whole file briefly. That suits one program, not a busy system.
Limited ALTER TABLE. A table can be renamed and columns added, renamed, or dropped. Recent versions (3.53 and later; this book used 3.54) can also set or drop a column’s NOT NULL and add or drop a CHECK constraint, but a foreign key or a UNIQUE constraint still cannot be added to an existing table; the table is rebuilt instead.
No schemas. A file is one database with one set of tables. ATTACH opens a second file under a name, which serves where PostgreSQL would use a schema (Section 8.1).

title: Appendix G — Embedded Databases: SQLite and DuckDB
text:
G.4 DuckDB
DuckDB is an embedded database built for analysis. Like SQLite, it runs inside the program that opens it and keeps a database in one file, and it is open source, under the MIT license. Where SQLite is designed for a program’s many small reads and writes, DuckDB is designed for queries that scan, group, and summarize many rows. Its shell, duckdb, is a single program, installed on macOS with brew install duckdb and downloaded from duckdb.org for Windows and Linux; DataGrip and DBeaver open a DuckDB file as a data source of type DuckDB.
The difference in design lies in how the rows are stored. PostgreSQL and SQLite are row stores: each row’s values are kept together, so finding, inserting, or changing one row touches one place. DuckDB is a column store: each column’s values are kept together, so a query that averages 3 columns of a 20-column table reads only those 3, and a column of like values compresses well. Thus, a row store suits a system that records transactions one at a time, and a column store suits a study that summarizes what was recorded.

G.4.1 The stock tables in DuckDB
The companion script duckdb-stock.sql builds the tables of Section G.3 with the book’s own DDL, VARCHAR columns and all, with one change: DuckDB has no identity columns, so each key draws its values from a sequence, a named counter that nextval advances. (PostgreSQL has sequences too; an identity column is built on one.) Run in a terminal with duckdb -echo stock.duckdb < duckdb-stock.sql, it creates the tables, loads them, and queries them:
.mode column
CREATE SEQUENCE warehouse_seq;
CREATE TABLE warehouse (
    warehouse_pk INTEGER
        DEFAULT nextval('warehouse_seq') PRIMARY KEY,
    warehouse_code VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    city VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL,
    state CHAR(2) NOT NULL
);
CREATE SEQUENCE stock_level_seq;
CREATE TABLE stock_level (
    stock_level_pk INTEGER
        DEFAULT nextval('stock_level_seq') PRIMARY KEY,
    warehouse_fk INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES warehouse,
    product_number VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL,
    quantity_on_hand INTEGER NOT NULL
        CHECK (quantity_on_hand >= 0),
    UNIQUE (warehouse_fk, product_number)
);
INSERT INTO warehouse (warehouse_code, city, state)
VALUES ('W-FAY', 'Fayetteville', 'AR'), ('W-TUL', 'Tulsa', 'OK');
INSERT INTO stock_level
    (warehouse_fk, product_number, quantity_on_hand)
VALUES (1, 'HT-100', 120), (1, 'GC-300', 18), (2, 'HT-100', 60);
SELECT w.warehouse_code, s.product_number, s.quantity_on_hand
FROM stock_level AS s
JOIN warehouse AS w ON w.warehouse_pk = s.warehouse_fk
ORDER BY w.warehouse_code, s.product_number;
warehouse_code  product_number  quantity_on_hand
--------------  --------------  ----------------
W-FAY           GC-300          18
W-FAY           HT-100          120
W-TUL           HT-100          60
The result is the one SQLite and PostgreSQL gave. DuckDB’s SQL is close to PostgreSQL’s, and its types are enforced. One exception is worth knowing: a length in a type, as in VARCHAR(10) or CHAR(2), is accepted and ignored, so a longer value is stored without complaint. A length rule that matters belongs in a CHECK constraint.
The rest of the script repeats SQLite’s two wrong inserts and then changes a warehouse twice:
INSERT INTO stock_level
    (warehouse_fk, product_number, quantity_on_hand)
VALUES (2, 'GC-300', 'forty');
Conversion Error: Could not convert string 'forty' to INT32

LINE 3: VALUES (2, 'GC-300', 'forty');
                             ^
INSERT INTO stock_level
    (warehouse_fk, product_number, quantity_on_hand)
VALUES (9, 'HT-200', 5);
Constraint Error: Violates foreign key constraint because key "warehouse_pk: 9" does not exist in the referenced table
UPDATE warehouse SET city = 'Springdale'
WHERE warehouse_code = 'W-FAY';
UPDATE warehouse SET warehouse_code = 'W-SPR'
WHERE warehouse_code = 'W-FAY';
Constraint Error: Violates foreign key constraint because key "warehouse_fk: 1" is still referenced by a foreign key in a different table. If this is an unexpected constraint violation, please refer to our foreign key limitations in the documentation
SELECT * FROM warehouse;
warehouse_pk  warehouse_code  city        state
------------  --------------  ----------  -----
1             W-FAY           Springdale  AR
2             W-TUL           Tulsa       OK
DuckDB refused both inserts that SQLite accepted: the text in an INTEGER column, and the stock level of a warehouse that does not exist. It accepted the change of the warehouse’s city. But it refused the change of its code, although no stock level refers to the code; the stock levels refer to warehouse_pk, which the update leaves alone. PostgreSQL would accept the update. DuckDB carries out an update of a column in a key or a UNIQUE constraint as a delete of the old row and an insert of the new one, and its foreign key sees the delete of a warehouse that stock levels still refer to. Its foreign keys have two more limits: no ON DELETE CASCADE, and one transaction cannot delete the rows that refer to a row and then the row itself. The last query shows that the refused update changed nothing.
Thus, DuckDB’s constraints suit data that is loaded and then analyzed, not data that is edited row by row. A study’s results are loaded once and queried many times, which is the work DuckDB is built for. A system of record, such as HG Industries’ orders, belongs on a server, or in SQLite when it belongs to one program.


G.4.2 Analysis straight from files
DuckDB can query a file directly: a CSV file’s name, in quotes, may stand where a table’s name would, and DuckDB reads the column names from the header and infers each column’s type from the values. The companion file code/data/frame-line-replications.csv holds three responses of every replication of the frame line’s two scenarios, long, as within_rep_view holds them (Section 12.4.2): 2 scenarios × 30 replications × 3 responses, 180 rows. The companion script duckdb-results.sql, run from the code folder with duckdb -echo < sql/embedded/duckdb-results.sql, first asks what DuckDB made of the file:
.mode column
SELECT column_name, column_type
FROM (DESCRIBE
      SELECT * FROM 'data/frame-line-replications.csv');
column_name  column_type
-----------  -----------
exp_name     VARCHAR
rep_id       BIGINT
stat_name    VARCHAR
rep_value    DOUBLE
DESCRIBE reports each column of a query’s result with its type. DuckDB read rep_id as an integer (BIGINT) and rep_value as a DOUBLE, with no CREATE TABLE and no load step. The script then summarizes the replications by scenario and response:
SELECT exp_name, stat_name, COUNT(*) AS reps,
       ROUND(AVG(rep_value), 3) AS average,
       ROUND(STDDEV_SAMP(rep_value), 3) AS std_dev
FROM 'data/frame-line-replications.csv'
GROUP BY exp_name, stat_name
ORDER BY stat_name, exp_name;
exp_name      stat_name      reps  average  std_dev
------------  -------------  ----  -------  -------
ThreeWelders  LotsCompleted  30    89.567   8.123
TwoWelders    LotsCompleted  30    89.6     8.101
ThreeWelders  TimeInShop     30    33.537   7.282
TwoWelders    TimeInShop     30    33.654   7.258
ThreeWelders  WorkInProcess  30    5.2      1.75
TwoWelders    WorkInProcess  30    5.217    1.748
Each group has 30 rows, one per replication, which accounts for all 180 rows of the file. As a check, the averages and standard deviations agree to three decimals with the across-replication statistics that the KSL computed and stored in across_rep_view (Section 12.2). The two scenarios’ averages differ by a small fraction of a standard deviation, which is why Example 12.1 compares them replication by replication.
The last statement turns the long rows of TwoWelders’ first three replications wide:
PIVOT (
    SELECT rep_id, stat_name,
           ROUND(rep_value, 3) AS rep_value
    FROM 'data/frame-line-replications.csv'
    WHERE exp_name = 'TwoWelders' AND rep_id <= 3
)
ON stat_name
USING MAX(rep_value)
ORDER BY rep_id;
rep_id  LotsCompleted  TimeInShop  WorkInProcess
------  -------------  ----------  -------------
1       85.0           28.126      3.908
2       85.0           28.981      4.094
3       86.0           36.98       5.904
PIVOT names the column whose values become columns (ON stat_name) and the aggregate that fills each cell (USING MAX(rep_value)), and the remaining column, rep_id, gives the rows. The result is Table 12.15, which Section 12.4.2 built by hand and then with one FILTER per response. Notice that PIVOT found the three columns in the data; the FILTER query listed them by hand. PIVOT is DuckDB’s own statement: neither PostgreSQL nor the SQL standard has it. DuckDB’s UNPIVOT goes the other way, and its COPY statement writes a result to a CSV file, or to a Parquet file (a column-store file format that many analysis tools read), for the next tool in a study.

title: Appendix G — Embedded Databases: SQLite and DuckDB
section: G.5 Embedded databases from Kotlin and the KSL
text:
G.5 Embedded databases from Kotlin and the KSL
A program opens an embedded database through JDBC, as it opens PostgreSQL (Section 10.1), with a URL that names a file instead of a server: jdbc:sqlite:stock.db or jdbc:duckdb:stock.duckdb. The driver is the engine, so the program needs only the driver’s library. The companion project’s build includes SQLite’s through the KSL.
The KSL wraps SQLite in classes of its ksl.utilities.io.dbutil package that Section 10.4 introduced: SQLiteDb creates or opens a database in a directory, and the function Database.createSimpleDb creates one with tables defined by DbTableData data classes, the quick tables of Section 12.4. The KSL also supports Apache Derby, an embedded database written in Java, through DerbyDb; its developers retired Derby in October 2025, so use it only to open a database that already uses it. A KSLDatabase created with only a name, KSLDatabase("study.db"), is an embedded SQLite database that holds the KSL’s simulation output. The KSL’s SQLite connections turn on foreign key enforcement, so the problem of the previous section does not arise in them.
The companion program SolverRunsSQLite.kt writes the solver runs of Section 12.4 to a SQLite file and summarizes them. It creates the database and its table from the data class SolverRun:

val dir = Files.createDirectories(Path.of("build", "embedded"))
val db = Database.createSimpleDb(
    tableDefinitions = setOf(SolverRun()),
    dbName = "solver-runs.db",
    dbDirectory = dir
)

It then inserts four runs, as objects of the data class:

val runs = listOf(
    SolverRun(1, "Rosenbrock", "SA-slow", 1, 10.05, 900, 0.005),
    SolverRun(2, "Rosenbrock", "SA-slow", 2, 10.30, 1000, 0.030),
    SolverRun(3, "Rosenbrock", "RS", 1, 10.20, 1000, 0.020),
    SolverRun(4, "Rosenbrock", "RS", 2, 10.90, 1000, 0.090)
)
val inserted = db.insertAllDbDataIntoTable(runs, "solver_run")
println("Inserted $inserted rows into solver_run")

and summarizes them by solver with a grouping query:

val sql = """
    SELECT solverLabel, COUNT(*) AS runs,
           ROUND(AVG(gap), 3) AS average_gap
    FROM solver_run
    GROUP BY solverLabel
    ORDER BY solverLabel
    """.trimIndent()
db.fetchCachedRowSet(sql)?.let { rs ->
    while (rs.next()) {
        println("%-8s %d  %.3f".format(rs.getString(1), rs.getInt(2), rs.getDouble(3)))
    }
}

It prints:

Inserted 4 rows into solver_run
RS       2  0.055
SA-slow  2  0.017

The table is the one whose CREATE TABLE statement Section 12.4 printed, with its DOUBLE columns; SQLite accepts that type, where PostgreSQL refused it. The file build/embedded/solver-runs.db can be opened in DataGrip or with sqlite3 and queried like any other database, and it can be copied, with the study it belongs to, to anyone.
The KSL does not include DuckDB. A program that writes to DuckDB adds its driver, org.duckdb:duckdb_jdbc, to the build; the driver carries DuckDB’s engine compiled for each operating system, and is some 85 MB. A study more often needs DuckDB only for analysis, and then needs no program of its own: every KSL database can write its views as CSV files, one per view, with the function exportAllViewsAsCSV, and DuckDB queries those files as Section G.4 queried frame-line-replications.csv.

title: Appendix G — Embedded Databases: SQLite and DuckDB
text:
G.7 Exercises

Exercise G.1 For each situation, say whether an embedded database or a database server suits it, and why.

A simulation study run by one engineer, whose results are archived with the final report.
HG Industries’ order entry, used by six people in two warehouses.
A tablet application that inspectors carry onto the plant floor, which records measurements while out of network range and sends them later.
A benchmark of optimization solvers run by three students on their own laptops, whose results must be combined for one analysis.



Exercise G.2 Using the SQLite scripts of Section G.3:

Rewrite the stock_level table of sqlite-stock-create.sql as a strict table, and say which of the inserts of sqlite-stock-affinity.sql it would refuse.
The CHECK (quantity_on_hand >= 0) of the original table accepted the text forty. Write a check that refuses any value that is not an integer, for a table that is not strict, using SQLite’s typeof function.



Exercise G.3 A colleague’s SQLite file of stock levels was written for months by a program that never turned on foreign keys.

Write a query that finds every stock level whose warehouse does not exist.
Why does turning the setting on now not find or remove those rows?
What should every program that writes the file do from now on?



Exercise G.4 The same CREATE TABLE warehouse (...) statement is run in PostgreSQL, SQLite, and DuckDB.

Under what name does each database store the table?
A query copied from a database that folds unquoted names to upper case, as the SQL standard specifies, names the table "WAREHOUSE", in double quotes. Does it work in PostgreSQL? In SQLite and DuckDB? Explain.



Exercise G.5 The script duckdb-stock.sql of Section G.4 changed warehouse W-FAY’s city, and DuckDB refused to change its code.

Which column do the stock levels refer to, and did the refused update change it?
Why did DuckDB refuse the update, when PostgreSQL would accept it?
A colleague proposes keeping HG Industries’ order entry in a DuckDB file, since DuckDB’s SQL is so close to PostgreSQL’s. Name two operations of order entry that the limits of Section G.4 would make fail or need a workaround, and recommend where the orders should be kept instead.



Exercise G.6 Using DuckDB and the file code/data/frame-line-replications.csv of Section G.4, run from the code folder:

Write a query that returns, for each scenario, the replication with the longest time in shop: the scenario, the replication, and the time in shop rounded to three decimals. Explain what you notice about the two rows.
Repeat the Little’s law check of Table 12.17 for the first five replications of TwoWelders, building the wide table with PIVOT instead of FILTER. Does your result match Table 12.17?



Exercise G.7 Run SolverRunsSQLite.kt of Section G.5, and open the file it writes in DataGrip, DBeaver, or sqlite3.

Write a query that returns, for each solver, the run with the smallest gap: the solver, the replication, and the gap.
Add a fifth run of your own with a gap of NULL. What does the program’s summary query now report for its solver, and why?

title: Appendix H — NoSQL and Other Data Stores
text:
H.1 Why NoSQL databases exist
This book teaches the relational model because it holds most of the data an industrial engineer works with: orders, parts, routings, inspections, and the results of studies. It is not the only way to store data, however, and you will meet others, in a plant’s historian, in a supplier’s web service, or in a product team’s application. This appendix describes the databases grouped under the name NoSQL, the trade-offs they make against the relational model, and how PostgreSQL itself stores and queries JSON documents, so that you can try the ideas on the server you already have.
Recall from Section 2.7 that two questions separate one way of organizing data from another: where the description of the data lives, and how one record is connected to another. Those two questions run through the whole appendix.
A relational database was designed to run on one server and to keep one copy of each fact, checked against the rules in its catalog on every change. That design suits most business and plant data, and it still does. In the 2000s, however, companies running large web services met three needs it served poorly. Their data no longer fit on one machine, so it had to be spread over many machines and copied for safety. The structure of their records changed every few weeks, as the applications that wrote them changed. And much of their data arrived already shaped as documents, from browsers, phones, and other services.
The databases built for those needs came to be called NoSQL, usually read “not only SQL” (Sadalage and Fowler 2012). The name describes a family, not a rule: several NoSQL databases now accept a query language that looks much like SQL, and relational databases, PostgreSQL among them, have taken on features of NoSQL ones. What the family shares is a different answer to the two questions of Section 2.7. A NoSQL database usually keeps the description of its data in the records or in the programs, not in a catalog, and it connects records by nesting one inside another, or not at all, more often than by keys.
crumbs: H  NoSQL and Other Data Stores

title: Appendix H — NoSQL and Other Data Stores
text:
H.2 The four families
NoSQL databases fall into four families, distinguished by what they store and how a program finds it. Table H.1 summarizes them, with a use for each in a company like HG Industries.



Table H.1: The Four Families of NoSQL Databases












Family
Stores
A program finds a record by
Examples
A use at HG Industries




Key-value
A value of any form under a key
Its key, and nothing else
Redis, Amazon DynamoDB
The current state of each machine, for a dashboard


Document
JSON documents, grouped in collections
Its key, or the values of its fields
MongoDB, Couchbase
Test records whose fields differ from product to product


Wide-column
Rows of many columns, grouped and spread over machines by a key
Its key, often a range of keys
Apache Cassandra, Apache HBase
Sensor readings, by machine and time


Graph
Nodes and the relationships between them
Following relationships from a node
Neo4j
The network of suppliers behind each product






A key-value store is the simplest: it stores a value under a key and returns the value when given the key. The value may be a number, a string, or a document, and the store does not look inside it. That simplicity makes it very fast, which is why it often sits in front of another database, holding the answers to frequent questions. For example, a dashboard on the plant floor that shows each machine’s current state reads one value per machine number, many times a second.
A document database stores each record as a JSON document, as Listing 2.5 showed, and groups documents of one kind into a collection, its counterpart of a table. Unlike a key-value store, it looks inside the documents: a query can ask for every order whose lines include a GC-300. Documents in one collection need not have the same fields. Thus, a document database suits records whose structure varies, such as test records in which a hand truck’s inspection measures different characteristics than a garden cart’s.
A wide-column store holds rows that may have very many columns, grouped by a key that decides which machine stores them. It is built for writing enormous numbers of rows quickly and reading them back by key and range. Sensor readings fit that pattern: each reading is written once, never changed, and read back by machine and time.
A graph database stores nodes, such as suppliers, parts, and products, and the relationships between them as data in their own right. Its queries follow relationships: which products depend, through any number of tiers, on one supplier’s plant. A relational database answers the same question with a recursive query (Section 4.6); a graph database makes following a path its basic operation, which pays off when the paths are long and the questions are about the paths themselves.

H.2.1 Time-series databases and plant historians
The non-relational data you are most likely to meet in a plant is neither of these four. A time-series database records the value of a measurement at each moment: a spindle’s speed, an oven’s temperature, a line’s count of finished units. In manufacturing, the usual one is a plant historian, such as the AVEVA PI System, which collects thousands of such measurements, called tags, from the plant’s controllers, many times a second, and keeps years of them. Other time-series databases include InfluxDB and TimescaleDB, the latter an extension of PostgreSQL.
A historian answers questions about one tag over a span of time well, such as the average oven temperature during each shift. It does not hold orders, parts, or work orders, so the questions an industrial engineer asks usually combine the two: the temperatures during the runs of one lot that failed inspection. The usual design summarizes the readings (an average, a minimum, and a maximum for each tag over each hour or each run) and loads the summaries into a relational database, where they join the rest of the plant’s data. That is the extract, transform, and load of Section 11.3, and the summaries are often the input data of the simulation models of Section 12.1.

title: Appendix H — NoSQL and Other Data Stores
text:
H.3 The trade-offs
Each family gives up something the relational model provides in return for something it does not. This section names the four trade-offs that matter most when you choose.

H.3.1 Schema on write and schema on read
A relational database applies its schema when data is written. Every row is checked against the catalog of Section 2.5 before it is stored, and a row that does not fit is refused. This is called schema on write. A document database usually applies no schema when data is written: it stores whatever document it is given, and the program that reads a document decides what its fields mean. This is called schema on read.
Schema on read lets the structure change without redesigning the database, and it lets one collection hold records of different shapes. Its cost is that every program that reads the data must cope with every shape that has ever been written, including the mistakes. Section H.4 shows a document with a misspelled field being accepted, and a query answering wrongly as a result. Many document databases now let a designer declare rules that documents must obey, which moves them part of the way back to schema on write.


H.3.2 Nesting is denormalization
A document that nests an order’s lines and copies its customer’s and products’ facts is a table that has not been normalized. Recall from Section 7.2 that such a table suffers anomalies, and the order document of Listing 2.5 suffers them all: a product’s description is stored in every order that includes it, a product that has never been ordered has nowhere to be recorded, and removing a customer’s only order removes the only record of the customer.
A designer of documents therefore decides, for each connection, whether to nest or to refer. The class model of Chapter 5 gives a good rule. Nest a composition, whose parts belong to one whole and are created and removed with it (Section 6.3.6): an order’s lines belong in the order’s document. Refer, by key, to anything shared: a customer and a product are shared by many orders, so each belongs in a document of its own, and the order holds its customer number and each line’s product number. A document database that follows this rule copies only what never changes after it is written, such as the price on an order line.


H.3.3 Consistency across copies
A NoSQL database spread over many machines keeps several copies of each record, so that losing a machine loses nothing. Keeping every copy identical at every moment would mean that each change waits for every machine, and that a change is refused whenever the machines cannot reach one another. Many NoSQL databases choose instead to accept a change at one copy and pass it to the others shortly afterward. This is called eventual consistency: for a short time, a read from another copy may return the value from before the change.
Compare the transactions of Section 9.2, in which a change is complete and visible to all, or not made at all. For a dashboard, a value a second old does no harm; for the quantity on hand of a part that two planners are allocating, it does. Most NoSQL databases let a program ask for stronger consistency on the operations that need it, at the cost of speed.


H.3.4 Questions nobody planned for
A relational database answers any question its data can answer: a new question is a new query, joining whatever tables it needs. NoSQL databases are designed the other way round, around the questions known in advance. A key-value store finds a record only by its key, a wide-column store by its key and range, and a document database most easily by the fields of one collection; combining collections is often left to the program. Thus, the designer of a NoSQL database starts from the questions and shapes the records to answer them, while the designer of a relational database starts from the business, as Chapter 5 does, and lets the questions come later. For the data of an industrial engineer, whose next question is rarely the last one, that difference usually decides the matter.

title: Appendix H — NoSQL and Other Data Stores
text:
H.4 Documents in PostgreSQL
PostgreSQL stores JSON documents in a column of type JSONB, a binary form of JSON that it can search and index, and it provides operators to reach inside them. This lets one database hold tables and documents side by side. The type and its operators are PostgreSQL’s own; the SQL standard defines functions for JSON since 2016, and PostgreSQL implements some of them, but other systems store and query JSON differently.
Let’s store the twelve orders of stage D5 as documents. The table has a key, the order number, and one column for the document; the database checks the key and that the document is well-formed JSON, and nothing more.

CREATE TABLE distribution.order_document (
    order_number VARCHAR(10) PRIMARY KEY,
    document     JSONB NOT NULL
);

The next statement builds a document for each order from the relational tables, in the form of Listing 2.5. The function jsonb_build_object builds a document from pairs of a field name and a value, and jsonb_agg gathers the documents of an order’s lines into a list.

INSERT INTO distribution.order_document
SELECT o.order_number,
       jsonb_build_object(
         'order_number', o.order_number,
         'order_date', o.order_date,
         'customer', jsonb_build_object(
             'customer_number', c.customer_number,
             'name', c.name,
             'city', c.city,
             'state', c.state),
         'lines', (
             SELECT jsonb_agg(jsonb_build_object(
                        'line_number', l.line_number,
                        'product_number', p.product_number,
                        'description', p.description,
                        'quantity', l.quantity,
                        'unit_price', l.unit_price)
                      ORDER BY l.line_number)
             FROM distribution.order_line AS l
             JOIN distribution.product AS p
               ON p.product_pk = l.product_fk
             WHERE l.customer_order_fk
                   = o.customer_order_pk))
FROM distribution.customer_order AS o
JOIN distribution.customer AS c
  ON c.customer_pk = o.customer_fk;

Two operators reach inside a document. The operator -> returns the value of a field as JSON, so that another operator can be applied to it, and ->> returns it as text. The following query lists the orders placed in January, with each one’s customer and its number of lines.



Table H.2: January’s Orders, Read from Their Documents


SELECT order_number,
       document -> 'customer' ->> 'name' AS customer,
       jsonb_array_length(document -> 'lines') AS lines
FROM distribution.order_document
WHERE document ->> 'order_date' < '2026-02-01'
ORDER BY order_number;

Notice that the condition compares the order date as text, since ->> returns text; it works here only because dates written in the form 2026-01-05 sort as text in the same order as dates. The customer’s name comes from the copy in each document, without a join. PostgreSQL stores a JSONB document’s fields in an order of its own, which does no harm: a query finds a field by its name, as it finds a column.
The operator @> asks whether a document contains another. The following query finds the orders whose lines include a GC-300, by asking whether the document contains a list of lines with one line for that product.

SELECT order_number,

Example H.1 (Units ordered, from the documents) The system. The twelve order documents of stage D5, loaded into order_document as above.
The request. The production planner asks how many units of each product have been ordered, and the order documents are all the program has.
The units are inside each document’s list of lines, so the query must first turn each list into rows, one per line. The function jsonb_array_elements does that; written in the FROM clause after the table, it produces the lines of each document, which the query names line.



Table H.4: Units Ordered by Product, from the Order Documents


SELECT line ->> 'product_number' AS product,
       SUM((line ->> 'quantity')::INTEGER) AS units
FROM distribution.order_document,
     jsonb_array_elements(document -> 'lines') AS line
GROUP BY line ->> 'product_number'
ORDER BY product;

Notice the cast. A quantity read with ->> is text, so the query must say that it is a whole number before it can be added. The catalog cannot say so, because the catalog knows only that document is a JSONB column. This is schema on read: the query supplies the type that a relational table would have declared once.
The check. The same totals come from the relational tables, grouped as in Section 4.2:



Table H.5: Units Ordered by Product, from the Relational Tables


SELECT p.product_number AS product,
       SUM(l.quantity) AS units
FROM distribution.order_line AS l

  ON p.product_pk = l.product_fk

Table H.4 and Table H.5 agree, product by product, as they must: the documents were built from the tables.
Interpretation. Customers have ordered 130 two-wheel hand trucks, 30 convertible hand trucks, and 55 steel garden carts, the demand the frame line must meet.
Where it breaks. Nothing checks the fields of a document when it is written. Suppose that a program records order SO-5013, for five GC-300 carts, and misspells quantity:

INSERT INTO distribution.order_document
VALUES ('SO-5013', '{"order_number": "SO-5013",
  "order_date": "2026-03-12",
  "customer": {"customer_number": "C-1009"},
  "lines": [{"line_number": 1,
             "product_number": "GC-300",
             "qty": 5, "unit_price": 119.00}]}');

The database accepts the document, since it is well-formed JSON. The same query, run after it, counts the new line and adds nothing for it:



Table H.6: Units Ordered by Product, After the Misspelled Document


SELECT line ->> 'product_number' AS product,
       SUM((line ->> 'quantity')::INTEGER) AS units,
       COUNT(*) AS lines
FROM distribution.order_document,
     jsonb_array_elements(document -> 'lines') AS line
GROUP BY line ->> 'product_number'

Table H.6 shows nine lines for the GC-300 and still 55 units. The line’s quantity is missing, so ->> returns NULL, and SUM ignores a NULL (Section 4.2). The five carts are silently lost. A relational table would have refused the row, since quantity is declared NOT NULL in order_line (Chapter 8). The document also names customer C-1009, who does not exist, and nothing checks it; a foreign key would have refused that too.

The second weakness of documents is the copying of Section 7.2. Suppose that HG Industries renames the GC-300 “Steel utility cart”, and changes the product table:

UPDATE distribution.product
SET description = 'Steel utility cart'
WHERE product_number = 'GC-300';

The following query sets the description in product beside the copies in the documents. The keywords CROSS JOIN before the function produce each document’s lines, as the comma did above, so that a JOIN to product can follow.



Table H.7: The GC-300’s Description in the Table and in the Documents


SELECT p.description AS in_product,
       line ->> 'description' AS in_documents,
       COUNT(*) AS lines
FROM distribution.order_document AS d
CROSS JOIN jsonb_array_elements(d.document -> 'lines')
     AS line
JOIN distribution.product AS p
  ON p.product_number = line ->> 'product_number'
WHERE p.product_number = 'GC-300'
GROUP BY p.description, line ->> 'description';

Table H.7 shows the product renamed and all eight copies still carrying the old name. Each copy must be found and changed by a program, and the database cannot tell the program where they are. Thus, a document should copy only what must not change once it is written. A line’s unit price is such a fact: it records the price the customer was charged, which a later change of list price must not alter. A product’s description is not.
PostgreSQL’s documents are most useful beside tables, not instead of them. A table of test results, for example, can keep the columns every test has (the lot, the date, the inspector, the result) as ordinary columns with keys and constraints, and hold the measurements that differ from product to product in one JSONB column. The rules that matter are kept by the database, and the part of the record that varies is free to vary.

title: Appendix H — NoSQL and Other Data Stores
text:
H.5 Choosing
Most of the data an industrial engineer designs a database for is shared by many people, obeys rules that matter, and will be asked questions no one has thought of yet. That is the data the relational model was made for, and it should be your starting point. The other kinds earn their place for particular data.

Records that are written and read whole, and vary in structure, such as test records, equipment configurations, or the replies of a supplier’s web service: a JSONB column in PostgreSQL, beside the columns that do not vary, or a document database if the volume calls for one.
Measurements at a high rate, such as sensor readings and machine states: a historian or another time-series database, with summaries loaded into a relational database for analysis.
A value read by key many times a second, such as a dashboard’s current state: a key-value store in front of the database that holds the facts.
Networks whose questions are about paths, such as a multi-tier supply network: a graph database, or a recursive query (Section 4.6) while the network is small.

A system that uses several kinds of database, each for the data it suits, is said to practice polyglot persistence (Sadalage and Fowler 2012). A plant’s information systems usually do: a historian on the floor, a relational database for orders and production, and a warehouse for analysis (Chapter 11). The skills of this book carry over to all of them, because each still has to answer the two questions of Section 2.7, and a designer who can answer them for a relational database can see how another database answers them.

title: Appendix H — NoSQL and Other Data Stores
text:
H.6 Exercises

Exercise H.1 For each kind of data, name the family of Table H.1, or a time-series database, that suits it best, or say that a relational database does, and give the reason in one sentence.

The torque reading of every fastening on the HT-100 assembly line, about twenty a minute, kept for two years.
HG Industries’ customers, orders, and order lines.
The suppliers of each purchased part, the suppliers of those suppliers, and so on, where the question asked most is which products depend on one supplier’s plant.
The last known position of each of forty forklifts, shown on a map of the warehouse and refreshed every second.
A record of each customer complaint, whose fields differ by product and by the kind of complaint.



Exercise H.2 A document database holds HG Industries’ orders, one document per order in the form of Listing 2.5. For each of the following, say whether it should be nested in the order’s document, or kept in a document of its own and referred to by key. Justify each answer with the rule of Section H.3, and name the association or composition of the distribution class model behind it.

The order’s lines.
The customer’s name and city.
The unit price on each line.
The product’s description.
The shipments that ship the order.



Exercise H.3 Load stage D5, and run sql/documents/order-documents.sql from the companion code, which leaves the order_document table holding the twelve orders of stage D5 as documents.

Using the documents alone, list each customer’s number and name with the total value of its orders (the sum of quantity times unit price over its lines), largest first.
Write the same query against the relational tables of stage D5, and confirm that the two agree.
Which part of the query in (a) supplies what the catalog would have supplied for the query in (b)?



Exercise H.4 The misspelled document of Example H.1 was accepted without complaint.

List every way in which that document breaks a rule that the relational tables of stage D5 would have enforced.
A developer argues that the program writing the documents should simply be tested more carefully. Give one reason a database’s own rules protect data better than a careful program does. (Recall Section 1.3.)
Describe a query that would find every order line, across all documents, that has no quantity field. You need not write it.



Exercise H.5 A historian records the spindle speed of each of the seven machines in the production.machine table of stage P3 once a second, every hour of the year (365 days).

How many readings does it hold after one year?
The industrial engineers want, for each machine and each hour, the average, minimum, and maximum speed, to join with the work orders run in that hour. How many rows does a relational table of those summaries hold after one year?
Write the relational schema of the summary table in the notation of Section 2.4, with a foreign key to a table of machines.
Name one question about the spindles that the summary table cannot answer and the historian can.
